Live-In Worker Attestations
Daily service documentation
Claim batches, second-person review, remittances and denial follow-up
Monthly reconciliations
Overpayment records and quarterly review results

policies.title: Annual Audit, Fiscal Sustainability Report and DSP Wage Pass-Through
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Executive Director, Finance/Billing staff, payroll staff and the outside CPA
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] stays financially sound and accountable for the public funds it receives. This covers the annual financial statement audit, the Fiscal Sustainability Report to the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD), and passing the DDD-required wage increase through to Direct Support Professionals (DSPs) and DSP Supervisors.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps its financial records so they can be audited and examined by an independent CPA. If the agency claims $350,000 or more in combined Community Care Program (CCP) and Supports Program reimbursement, it obtains an annual financial statement audit performed under generally accepted auditing standards (GAAS). The agency files the Fiscal Sustainability Report with DDD within 120 days after the end of the State fiscal year (about October 30). When DDD raises rates for agency-provided services, the agency passes the required base-wage increase to DSPs and DSP Supervisors. The January 1, 2026 rate change requires about $0.46 per hour, effective 1/1/2026, paid no later than 3/1/2026 and including retroactive pay. The increase is paid as a base-wage increase. It is never paid as a bonus and never used for operating expenses. No employee is paid below the New Jersey minimum wage, which is $15.92 per hour for most employers from 1/1/2026. The licensing application under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(c) requires an independent CPA examination for the two most recent fiscal years, and the agency keeps those materials current and available. This policy is reviewed at least annually as part of the procedure manual.

definitions.definition: The DDD Community Care Program and Supports Program, under which Individual Supports are authorized and paid fee-for-service.
Generally accepted auditing standards, the standard the annual financial statement audit must follow.
The annual report DDD requires from providers, due 120 days after the State fiscal year ends (about October 30).
The portion of a DDD rate increase (about $0.46/hr for the 1/1/2026 change) that the agency must pay as a base-wage increase to DSPs and DSP Supervisors.
The CPA's written communication of internal control findings and recommendations that accompanies the audit or examination.

procedures: By July 31 each year, the Finance Manager totals the CCP and Supports Program reimbursement claimed in the State fiscal year just ended and reports it in writing to the Executive Director. The Finance Manager also compares year-to-date claims to the $350,000 threshold each quarter.

If reimbursement is at or above $350,000, or is projected to reach it, the Executive Director tells the governing body and engages an independent CPA firm before the fiscal year ends. The engagement letter states that the audit will follow GAAS.

The Finance Manager keeps books and records that can be audited. This includes general ledger, bank reconciliations, payroll registers, DDD fee-for-service remittances and claims, and records showing individuals' personal funds are held separately from agency funds (see IR-05).
The Finance Manager gives the CPA all requested records by the dates in the engagement letter. The Executive Director signs the management representation letter only after reviewing it.

The governing body (or its audit committee) reviews the completed audit and the Management Letter. Within 30 days, the Executive Director gives the governing body a written response to each finding, with an owner and a due date for each corrective action.

The Executive Director submits the audit to DDD in the manner and by the date stated in DDD's current instructions. The Finance Manager records the submission date and confirmation in the compliance calendar.

Each year, the Finance Manager opens the Fiscal Sustainability Report template by August 31 and completes a draft by September 30. The governing body reviews the draft before submission. The Executive Director submits the report so that it reaches DDD no later than 120 days after the State fiscal year ends (about October 30), and the Finance Manager files proof of submission.

The Executive Director keeps in the administrative file a current set of the materials required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(c): the CPA independent examination for the two most recent fiscal years, with Management Letters. These are available on request from the Office of Licensing or DDD.

When DDD announces a rate increase with a wage pass-through requirement, the Executive Director assigns the Finance Manager and Payroll Specialist within 5 business days to identify the affected services, the DSP and DSP Supervisor positions, and the required effective date.

For the 1/1/2026 rate change, the Payroll Specialist increases the base hourly wage of every DSP and DSP Supervisor by about $0.46 per hour (or the exact amount in DDD's current guidance), effective 1/1/2026. The Finance Manager confirms the change is paid no later than 3/1/2026 and includes retroactive pay back to 1/1/2026 for all eligible hours worked.

The Payroll Specialist enters the increase as a change to the base rate on the payroll system. It is not a bonus, a one-time payment or a stipend, and it is not counted toward any pay already due. The Finance Manager ensures the increase is not used to cover operating expenses.
The Payroll Specialist gives each affected employee a written notice stating the old rate, the new rate, the effective date and the retroactive amount. Copies go in the personnel record (STF-06).

Before each new hire is offered a rate, the Executive Director confirms the offer is not below the base rate that includes the pass-through and not below the New Jersey minimum wage. The Finance Manager confirms the current minimum wage each January against the NJ Department of Labor and Workforce Development announcement. Questions about how the pass-through applies to a newly licensed agency go to DDD (800-832-9173) before the first payroll.

The Finance Manager prepares a pass-through worksheet that shows the rate change, the affected staff, hours, the amount passed through, and payroll register references. The Executive Director reviews and signs it within 30 days after the retroactive pay is made.

If an error is found, such as an employee not paid the increase, the Payroll Specialist corrects it in the next payroll cycle, pays any retroactive amount owed, and the Executive Director notifies DDD if the error affected a required deadline.
The Executive Director reviews this policy each year with the procedure manual (GOV-04) and updates it after each DDD notice that changes audit, reporting or wage pass-through requirements.

responsibilities.duty: Engage or approve engagement of the CPA, review the audit, Management Letter and Fiscal Sustainability Report, and oversee corrective action.
Ensure audit and report deadlines are met, sign required representations, keep the CPA examination materials current, and certify the wage pass-through.
Track the $350,000 threshold, maintain auditable books, prepare the Fiscal Sustainability Report and the pass-through worksheet.
Change base wage rates, pay retroactive amounts, issue employee notices, and keep payroll records.
Perform the audit under GAAS and issue the audit report and Management Letter.

documentation: Annual reimbursement summary (CCP and Supports Program) and threshold check
CPA engagement letter, audit report, Management Letter and governing body response
Proof of audit submission to DDD
Fiscal Sustainability Report, governing body review record and proof of submission
CPA independent examination materials for the two most recent fiscal years
Wage pass-through worksheet, payroll registers before and after the change, retroactive pay records and employee notices
Compliance calendar showing due dates and completion dates

policies.title: Inspections, Plans of Correction and Enforcement Readiness
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Executive Director, Program Directors, house managers and all staff on duty at any residence
policies.purpose: To keep every [AGENCY NAME] residence ready for announced and unannounced inspection at all times, to make sure citations are answered on time with a written plan of correction, and to protect the agency's license.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with inspections by the NJ DHS Office of Licensing and DDD. Under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(k), DHS may inspect without limitation or notice, and under 1.4(l) an annual on-site inspection is required. Unannounced inspections increase beginning in 2026. The agency does not operate a residence without Office of Licensing authorization (1.4(j)). Inspectors review staff files, schedules, credentials, background checks, physical plant and insurance documents, so the agency keeps these current and available at all times. Partial compliance can result in a provisional license, and two consecutive provisional licenses may result in non-renewal. The agency therefore answers every citation with a written plan of correction by the deadline in the notice. P.L.2025, c.280 expands DHS enforcement authority over developmental disability providers, and the agency has legal counsel review its penalty provisions and updates this policy accordingly. Housing for new sites is cleared with DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development before acquisition.

definitions.definition: A visit by the Office of Licensing or DHS without advance notice, which the agency may not limit or refuse.
A written finding of noncompliance issued after an inspection.
The agency's written response to each citation stating the corrective action, the responsible person and the completion date.
A license issued when compliance is only partial. Two consecutive provisional licenses may result in non-renewal.

procedures: The Executive Director appoints a Compliance Lead ([COMPLIANCE LEAD NAME]) and a backup. They keep the Inspection Readiness Binder (paper or secure electronic) current at the administrative office, and a site copy of items required at each residence is kept on site.

The Readiness Binder includes: staff files; current staff schedules and time records; credential and training verification; criminal history, Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry check records; the procedure manual; the license; insurance documents; the physical plant file (fire drill logs, inspection reports, repair records); and individual files kept at the residence.

The Compliance Lead performs a self-audit of each residence every quarter, using a checklist built from N.J.A.C. 10:44A, and gives the results to the Executive Director within 7 days. Gaps are given an owner and a due date within 30 days.

Each month the Compliance Lead checks expiration dates for licenses, insurance, staff credentials, CPR/first aid, TB screening, training and background check renewals, and sends a list of upcoming expirations to the Executive Director.

Every staff member on duty is told that inspectors may arrive at any time. The person in charge (STF-01) greets the inspector, asks for identification, and lets the inspector in without delay. Staff do not refuse, limit or postpone an inspection.
The person in charge immediately calls the Program Director and Executive Director. Someone from management goes to the site as soon as possible, but the inspection is not delayed while waiting.

Staff escort the inspector, answer questions truthfully and provide requested records. Individuals may speak with the inspector privately if they choose. Staff do not coach, discourage or retaliate against any individual for speaking with inspectors (see IR-01).

The Compliance Lead or manager keeps a log of documents given to the inspector and makes copies of anything the inspector takes. At the exit conference the Executive Director or designee takes notes and asks for clarification of any findings.

If a deficiency can be fixed immediately (for example a missing drill entry or a burned-out smoke detector battery), staff fix it right away and document the date, time and who did it. Falsifying or back-dating records is never permitted.
When a written citation is received, the Executive Director logs the date of receipt and the response deadline stated in the notice within 1 business day, and assigns each citation to an owner.

The Compliance Lead drafts the written plan of correction for each citation. Each entry states the cause, the specific corrective action, how similar problems will be prevented for other individuals and residences, the person responsible and the completion date. The Executive Director signs it.

The Executive Director submits the plan of correction to the Office of Licensing by the deadline in the notice. If more time is needed, the Executive Director asks the Office of Licensing in writing before the deadline. The submission and any response are filed in the Readiness Binder.

The Compliance Lead checks completion of each corrective action by the due date and keeps evidence (photos, revised schedules, training sign-in sheets, repair invoices). The results are reported to the governing body and used in quality improvement (GOV-05).

If the agency receives a provisional license, the Executive Director notifies the governing body within 2 business days, develops a written plan to reach full compliance before the next inspection, and reviews progress with the governing body every month. The agency recognizes that two consecutive provisional licenses may result in non-renewal.

The Executive Director arranges for legal counsel to review P.L.2025, c.280, including its penalty provisions, and reports the review to the governing body. Counsel's advice is used to update this policy, the monitoring checklist and staff training.

Before acquiring or leasing any new site, the Executive Director obtains clearance from DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development and confirms Office of Licensing authorization before any individual moves in (see ENV-01).
The Executive Director reviews this policy yearly and after each inspection, and updates it when licensing or enforcement requirements change.

responsibilities.duty: Review inspection results, provisional license status and enforcement developments, and hold management accountable for correction.
Ensure inspection readiness, sign and submit plans of correction on time, and engage legal counsel on enforcement authority.
Maintain the Readiness Binder, perform quarterly self-audits, track expirations, draft and monitor plans of correction.
Admit inspectors without delay, escort them, provide records and notify management.
Cooperate truthfully with inspectors, never limit access, and never alter records.

documentation: Inspection Readiness Binder contents and expiration tracking list
Quarterly self-audit checklists and corrective action tracking
Inspection log: date, inspector, documents copied, exit conference notes
Citations received, date received and response deadline
Plans of correction, submissions, extension requests and evidence of completion
Provisional license compliance plan and governing body minutes
Legal counsel review of P.L.2025, c.280 and resulting policy updates

policies.title: Individual Rights and HCBS Settings Requirements
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors, individuals receiving services, guardians and families
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals living in [AGENCY NAME] residences enjoy the same rights as other citizens, are taught and supported to exercise those rights, and live in settings that meet New Jersey's Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) settings requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes that people with disabilities have the same rights as other citizens, and exercising a right is never a cause for retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a)). The agency complies with the Developmentally Disabled Rights Act, N.J.S.A. 30:6D-1 et seq. (3.1(b)). All staff are familiar with and observe the rights listed in the Division's rights document, and the agency gives that document to each individual at admission and obtains a signed acknowledgment (3.1(c)). The agency trains and supports individuals to understand their options, make choices and exercise their rights, and rights are not limited because an individual has a guardian or family (3.1(d)). DDD services are authorized under the NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration (Section 1115), and New Jersey's HCBS settings transition plan applies to homes licensed under N.J.A.C. 10:44A. The agency therefore operates each residence consistently with 42 CFR 441.301(c): the setting is integrated in the community, individuals choose their setting and services, and individuals have privacy, dignity and respect and freedom from coercion and restraint. Individuals also control their own schedules and activities, have access to food at any time, have visitors of their choosing at any time, and have a lease or residency agreement and a lockable bedroom door where applicable, with choice of roommates and freedom to furnish and decorate their own space.

definitions.definition: N.J.S.A. 30:6D-1 et seq., the State law that sets out the rights of people with developmental disabilities.
The document of rights issued by DDD that the agency must give to each individual and obtain signed acknowledgment of.
The federal standards at 42 CFR 441.301(c) for settings where Medicaid home and community-based services are delivered, as applied in New Jersey's HCBS Statewide Transition Plan.
Any adverse action, threat, loss of privilege or change in treatment taken because an individual exercised a right or made a complaint.

procedures: Before or at admission, the Program Director gives each individual, and the guardian or family member if there is one, the Division's rights document in the individual's preferred language and format (see IR-09). The Program Director goes through it in plain language and with the communication supports the individual uses.

The individual (and the guardian, where applicable) signs an acknowledgment of receipt of the rights document. If the individual cannot or will not sign, the Program Director records how the rights were explained and who witnessed it. The acknowledgment is filed in the individual's record (REC-01).

During new employee orientation, before working alone with individuals, each staff member receives the Division's rights document and this policy, and signs that they have read it and been trained (STF-03). The Program Director repeats rights training for all staff at least annually.

Each individual's person-centered plan (PCS-02) includes goals and supports for learning about rights, choice-making and self-advocacy. The Program Director reviews progress at each plan review, and staff provide the training and support during daily routines and in house meetings.

Staff offer real choices every day, including what to eat, when to wake and sleep, what to wear, how to spend free time and who to spend it with. Choices and the support given to make them are recorded in daily documentation (PCS-03).

A guardian's or family member's involvement does not remove an individual's rights. Staff continue to ask the individual for preferences, support supported decision-making (IR-08), and record any limits that have been legally imposed.

The Program Director ensures each residence meets the HCBS settings conditions: the individual has a written residency agreement or lease, private bedroom or choice of roommate where applicable, privacy in bedroom and bathroom, a key or lock where assessed, access to food at all times, freedom to have visitors at any time, and the ability to come and go in the community.
Staff never deny a right as punishment or for staff convenience. Any limit on a right is treated as a rights restriction and handled only under IR-02.

No staff member may threaten, penalize, discipline, treat differently or otherwise retaliate against any individual who exercises a right, files a grievance or speaks with an inspector, advocate or family member. Suspected retaliation is reported to the Program Director immediately and handled under BEH-03.

The Program Director holds a house meeting at least monthly, in an accessible format, to hear individuals' ideas and concerns about rights, house practices and community activities. Minutes and follow-up actions are recorded.

Individuals are told how to make a complaint (IR-03) and how to reach outside help, including the Office of Licensing and DDD (800-832-9173). Contact information is posted where individuals can see it, in accessible formats.

Each quarter the Compliance Lead completes an HCBS settings review at each residence, using a checklist that covers each condition in Procedure 7 and in 42 CFR 441.301(c). Findings go to the Executive Director, and the data are used in quality improvement (GOV-05).

The Executive Director monitors DDD notices and updates to the HCBS Statewide Transition Plan and the Section 1115 demonstration, and revises this policy and staff training within 60 days of any change.
The Executive Director reviews this policy yearly with the procedure manual (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure the agency complies with the Developmentally Disabled Rights Act and HCBS settings requirements, and monitor DDD updates.
Distribute rights information, obtain acknowledgments, train staff, supervise choice-making and hold house meetings.
Observe individuals' rights, offer choices daily, support self-advocacy and report rights concerns.
Perform quarterly HCBS settings reviews and report findings.
Receive rights information, ask questions, and raise concerns without fear of retribution.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of receipt of the Division's rights document, filed in the individual record
Staff rights training sign-in sheets and signed acknowledgments
Person-centered plan goals and progress notes on rights and self-advocacy
Daily choice documentation
House meeting minutes
Quarterly HCBS settings review checklists and corrective actions
Residency agreements or leases

policies.title: Rights Restrictions, House Rules, Human Rights Committee and Due Process
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Human Rights Committee, individuals receiving services, guardians and the person-centered planning team
policies.purpose: To make sure that no individual's rights are limited without a documented reason, review, consent and a way to challenge the limit, and that house rules are fair, necessary and developed with the people who live in the home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses a Human Rights Committee (HRC) under N.J.A.C. 10:41A, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(e). House rules are developed with the involvement of the individuals they affect, are necessary to promote order, and do not infringe on the rights of others (3.1(e)). Any individual-specific restriction or modification of a right must meet 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F). It must be based on a documented assessed need, a less-intrusive alternative must have been tried first, the individual (or guardian) must give informed consent, it must be reviewed periodically, and the plan must include a sunset date. Individuals and guardians are told how to appeal or file a grievance (see IR-03). Rights are not limited for staff convenience, as punishment, or because the individual has a guardian or family. Restraint and seclusion are governed by BEH-02 and are not authorized by this policy.

definitions.definition: The committee established under N.J.A.C. 10:41A that reviews proposed restrictions on rights and restrictive practices for the agency.
Any individual-specific limit on a right, freedom or HCBS setting condition, such as access to food, visitors, money, personal items, privacy or movement.
A rule that applies to everyone living in a residence, developed to promote order and not to limit any individual's rights.
The date on which a restriction automatically ends unless it is formally reviewed and renewed.

procedures: The Executive Director appoints the Human Rights Committee in line with N.J.A.C. 10:41A, including members who are not agency employees where required. The HRC meets at least [HRC MEETING FREQUENCY] and as needed for urgent referrals, and keeps minutes.

Staff do not impose any individual restriction on their own. If staff believe a restriction may be necessary, they notify the Program Director and the person-centered planning team (PCS-02) within 1 business day, and no restriction begins until Procedures 3 to 7 are complete, except under BEH-02 in an emergency.

The planning team documents the specific assessed need, including the health or safety risk that the restriction would address, the evidence for it (incident data, assessments), and how it was determined.
The team documents the positive supports and less-intrusive alternatives already tried, and why each was not enough. If none have been tried, they must be tried first, with data collected.

The team writes the proposed restriction in the individual's plan: exactly what is limited, when, where and by whom, and how it is proportionate to the need. It also records how data will be collected, the criteria for ending it, and a sunset date no later than [PERIOD, e.g., 90 days] from the start.

The Program Director explains the proposed restriction to the individual in plain language and in the individual's communication method. The individual and the guardian, if any, are asked for informed consent (see IR-08). The consent or refusal is documented and signed. A restriction does not start without informed consent.

The Program Director submits the proposal and supporting documentation to the HRC. The HRC reviews it and records its recommendation (approve, modify or reject) and the reasons. The individual and guardian may attend or send a representative or advocate.
If the HRC approves, the restriction is added to the plan and staff are trained on exactly how to implement it. Staff record its use and the data collected in daily documentation (PCS-03).

The Program Director reviews the data for each restriction at least monthly and the team reviews it at the sunset date. If the need is gone, the restriction ends. If it is to continue, the team repeats Procedures 3 to 7 and the HRC reviews it again.

For house rules, the Program Director holds a house meeting with the people who live in the residence before a rule is made or changed. The rule is written in plain language, explains why it is necessary to promote order, and is posted. A house rule may not limit visitors, food access, privacy, movement or other HCBS setting rights.
The Program Director reviews each house rule with the HRC at least annually. Any rule found to infringe on an individual's rights is withdrawn or revised within 7 days.

At the time a restriction is proposed and approved, the individual and guardian are told in writing how to appeal or file a grievance (IR-03), including the right to ask for review by the Executive Director, and how to contact the Office of Licensing and DDD (800-832-9173). Staff offer help in making the appeal.
No one may be treated differently or punished for objecting to a restriction, filing a grievance or appealing (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a)).

The Compliance Lead audits all active restrictions and house rules each quarter against this policy and reports to the Executive Director and HRC. Any restriction lacking documentation is ended or corrected immediately.
The Executive Director reviews this policy yearly with the HRC and the procedure manual (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Review proposed restrictions and restrictive practices, record recommendations, and review house rules.
Appoint the HRC, hear appeals and ensure no unauthorized restrictions exist.
Coordinate assessment, consent, HRC submission, staff training and monthly data review.
Document assessed need, less-intrusive alternatives, sunset date and periodic review in the plan.
Implement only approved restrictions exactly as written, record data, and report concerns.
Participate in decisions, give or refuse consent, and use the appeal and grievance process.

documentation: HRC membership list, meeting minutes and recommendations
Written assessment of need and record of less-intrusive alternatives tried
Plan language for each restriction, with sunset date
Signed informed consent or documented refusal
Monthly data review and sunset review records
House meeting minutes and posted house rules
Written notice of appeal and grievance rights
Quarterly audit of restrictions and house rules

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All staff, individuals receiving services, guardians, families and advocates
policies.purpose: To give individuals, guardians and families a clear and safe way to raise a complaint or grievance and have it heard, resolved and tracked, with at least two levels of review.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)13 — a procedure for resolving complaints and grievances of individuals that has a minimum of two levels at which the grievance shall be heard, the last of which involves the licensee or the executive director. At [AGENCY NAME], Level 1 is review by the Program Director, and Level 2 is review by the Executive Director [or licensee]. Individuals may file a grievance without retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a)). The written procedure is given to individuals, guardians and families at admission. Every grievance and its outcome is logged, and the data are reviewed in quality improvement (GOV-05). Allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation, and reportable unusual incidents, are not handled as grievances. They are reported at once under BEH-03 and BEH-04, even if the person also files a grievance.

definitions.definition: An expression of dissatisfaction that may be resolved informally on the spot.
A formal complaint, oral or written, that is logged and handled through the levels of review in this policy.
Review by the Program Director.
Final agency review by the Executive Director [or licensee], who was not involved in the Level 1 decision.
Any adverse action or change in treatment taken because a person filed a complaint or grievance.

procedures: At admission, the Program Director gives each individual, guardian and family member the written grievance procedure in plain language and the individual's preferred format (IR-09). The Program Director goes through it with them and records the date in the individual's record. The procedure is also posted in an accessible place in each residence.

The procedure tells individuals they may complain orally or in writing, to any staff member, in any communication method; that staff will help write it down; that they may bring a guardian, family member, friend or advocate; and that no one will retaliate.

Any staff member who receives a complaint or grievance writes it down the same day on the Grievance Form (or helps the individual do so), records the date, the person's words as closely as possible and what outcome the person wants, and gives it to the Program Director within 1 business day.

If a complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, or involves an incident that must be reported, staff immediately follow BEH-03 and BEH-04 and notify the Executive Director. The grievance process does not delay or replace the required report or investigation.

The Program Director enters the grievance in the Grievance Log with a number, date received, name, nature of complaint and the date Level 1 is due, and gives the individual a written or accessible acknowledgment within 2 business days.

Level 1: The Program Director meets with the individual (and any support person the individual chooses), reviews the facts, and tries to resolve it. The Program Director gives a written or accessible response with the decision and the reasons within 5 business days of receipt, and records it in the log.

If the individual is satisfied, the Program Director documents the resolution and closes the grievance. If not satisfied, or if the Program Director is the subject of the complaint, the individual may go directly to Level 2. Staff tell the individual how and help with this.

Level 2: The Program Director sends the file to the Executive Director [or licensee] within 1 business day of the request. The Executive Director reviews the file, meets with the individual and any support person and anyone involved, and issues a written or accessible final agency decision within 10 business days of the request.

The decision states what was found, what action will be taken, by whom and by when, and tells the individual how to contact outside help: the Office of Licensing and DDD (800-832-9173). The Executive Director signs it and gives a copy to the individual and guardian.
The Program Director follows up within 10 business days to confirm any promised corrective action was taken, and documents it in the log.
If the grievance is about a rights restriction, staff also notify the Human Rights Committee chair so the HRC may review it (IR-02).

Staff may not discourage a grievance, delay forwarding it, or treat an individual differently because of it. Suspected retaliation is reported to the Executive Director immediately and investigated (BEH-05).
Grievance information stays confidential and is shared only with people who need it to resolve it (IR-04).

The Compliance Lead summarizes the Grievance Log quarterly (number, topics, time to resolution, outcomes, repeat issues) and presents it to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-05) for trend review.
The Executive Director reviews this policy yearly with the procedure manual (GOV-04) and revises it if the review shows barriers to filing or resolution.

responsibilities.duty: Conduct Level 2 review, issue final decisions, and prevent retaliation.
Conduct Level 1 review, maintain the Grievance Log, give the procedure at admission and follow up on corrective action.
Accept and record any complaint, help the individual, forward it within 1 business day, and never retaliate.
Summarize grievance data quarterly for quality improvement.
May raise concerns at any time and appeal to Level 2 and to outside agencies.

documentation: Written grievance procedure and record of its delivery at admission
Grievance Forms and acknowledgments
Grievance Log with dates, levels, outcomes and follow-up
Written Level 1 and Level 2 decisions
Quarterly grievance trend summary and QI committee minutes

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors, board members, students and visitors who may see or hear information about individuals
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of individuals receiving services and the confidentiality of their records, and to make clear when and how information may be shared.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)16 — a statement regarding maintaining confidentiality of individuals receiving services and records, as required at N.J.A.C. 10:41-2. [AGENCY NAME] keeps the identity, health, behavioral, financial and service information of every individual confidential. The agency follows N.J.A.C. 10:41-2 and, as a provider that bills Medicaid, the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR 160 and 164). An individual file is kept for each person (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(a)), and files for group home and supervised apartment residents are kept at the residence (2.9(b)). Information is released only with the consent of the individual or the person legally authorized to consent, or as the law requires, and each disclosure is logged. Staff use and share only the minimum information needed to do their jobs. This policy covers paper and electronic records, photographs and recordings, and any video or audio monitoring (see IR-11). Breaching confidentiality is grounds for discipline up to termination.

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies or relates to an individual, including name, photo, diagnosis, medications, behavior, finances, service plans, incidents and the fact that the person receives services.
Individually identifiable health information, in any form, protected by 45 CFR 160 and 164.
Using or sharing only the amount of information needed for a given purpose.
A record of each release of information outside the agency, showing who, what, when, why and under what authority.
The person designated by the agency to oversee HIPAA compliance and handle privacy complaints.

procedures: The Executive Director designates a Privacy Officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) in writing, and gives the person's name to individuals, guardians and staff.
At admission, the Program Director gives the individual and guardian the agency's Notice of Privacy Practices and explains it. The signed acknowledgment is placed in the record (REC-01).

Before working with individuals, each employee, volunteer, student and contractor signs a confidentiality agreement and is trained on this policy, N.J.A.C. 10:41-2 and HIPAA during orientation (STF-03). The Program Director repeats the training at least annually.

Each individual's file is kept at the residence in a locked cabinet (or access-controlled electronic system with equal protection) in the office or other secure area, not in common areas. Only staff with a job-related need may access it (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)).

Staff do not discuss individuals in public places, with people not involved in the individual's care, or where other individuals or visitors can overhear. Shift reports and phone calls about individuals are held in private areas.

Staff do not post, text, email or share information, photos or videos of individuals on personal devices or social media. Photos or recordings for agency purposes are taken only on agency equipment with written consent of the individual or guardian.

Before releasing information to anyone outside the agency, the Program Director confirms the person's identity and checks for a signed authorization from the individual or the person legally authorized to consent, or a legal basis such as a court order, required reporting, or oversight by the Office of Licensing or DDD. The agency discloses only the minimum necessary.

The Program Director records every release in the Disclosure Log: date, recipient, information released, purpose, authority and staff member. Authorization forms are filed in the record and expire as stated in them.

Families and guardians receive information about individuals as allowed by the individual's consent or the guardian's legal authority. Staff ask the individual about sharing and respect the answer where the law permits.

Electronic information is protected by unique user logins, passwords, automatic log-off and encryption of laptops, phones and portable drives that hold PHI. Staff do not share passwords. Access is removed on the day a staff member leaves.
Paper records with PHI are shredded when no longer required to be kept (see REC-01 for retention). Faxes and emails with PHI use secure methods, and the sender checks the recipient before sending.

Staff report any suspected breach (lost record, misdirected email, unauthorized access or disclosure) to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits harm, notifies individuals and agencies as required by HIPAA and other law, and documents the outcome.

Individuals and guardians may ask to see their record, ask for corrections, ask for an accounting of disclosures, and file a privacy complaint without retribution. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within 30 days. Complaints are also handled through IR-03.
If video or audio monitoring is used, it follows IR-11, and recordings are protected and used only as that policy allows.
The Privacy Officer reviews access and disclosure logs at least quarterly, reports results to the Executive Director, and the data feed quality improvement (GOV-05).
The Executive Director reviews this policy yearly with the procedure manual (GOV-04), including any change in N.J.A.C. 10:41-2, HIPAA or DDD requirements.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure the agency complies with confidentiality and HIPAA requirements and designate the Privacy Officer.
Oversee the Notice of Privacy Practices, investigate breaches, respond to privacy requests and complaints, and review logs.
Keep records secure at the residence, approve releases of information, maintain the Disclosure Log and train staff.
Keep information confidential, use only what is needed, and report breaches immediately.
Give or refuse consent for release of information and may ask to review their records.

Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments
Signed staff, volunteer and contractor confidentiality agreements and training records
Authorizations for release of information
Disclosure Log
Breach reports, investigation notes and notifications
Record access, correction and privacy complaint requests and responses
Quarterly access/disclosure log review

policies.title: Personal Funds Management
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers who handle, record, review or have access to the personal funds of individuals served by [AGENCY NAME]; the Program Director; fiscal staff; and all residences and supervised apartments.
policies.purpose: To make sure the money that belongs to individuals is handled honestly, kept separate from agency money, fully recorded, open to the individual and guardian, and managed so that the individual's public benefits are not put at risk.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)10 — a procedure to ensure sound fiscal management of individuals' personal funds. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written record of every financial arrangement and transaction involving funds entrusted to it, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10. Each individual and guardian may see the record on request and receive copies on request. Funds belonging to individuals are never mixed with agency funds, and they are reconciled monthly. Individuals manage their own money to the greatest extent they are able and choose, with only the support they ask for or need. Funds are managed so that entitlement to benefits such as Supplemental Security Income (federal benefit rate $994 per month in 2026) is not jeopardized. At each annual policy review [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms the current text and subsection of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10 and updates this policy if it has changed. No employee may borrow from, lend to, accept gifts from, or use the money of an individual. Any loss or suspected misuse of an individual's funds is treated as possible exploitation and reported under BEH-03 and BEH-04.

definitions.definition: Any money of an individual that [AGENCY NAME] holds, deposits, safeguards, or helps spend, including benefit payments, wages, gifts, allowances and petty cash.
The written running record for each individual showing every deposit, withdrawal, purchase and balance, with date, amount, purpose, receipt and signatures.
A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to receive and manage an individual's benefits for that individual's use and benefit.
Placing an individual's money in the same account or cash container as agency money or another person's money, or in any employee's personal account.
An individual's eligibility for income-based or resource-limited public benefits, such as SSI and Medicaid, which can be lost if income or resources are mishandled or unreported.

procedures: At admission, and at each annual IHP meeting, the planning team asks each individual and guardian how they want to manage money, who will help if help is wanted, and which expenses are approved. The decision is written in the IHP and the personal funds record. The least restrictive arrangement that meets the person's wishes and safety needs is used.

The Program Director or designee records every source of income (for example SSI, SSDI, earnings, family gifts) and the representative payee, if any, in the individual's financial record within seven days of admission. The individual or guardian signs a written authorization before [AGENCY NAME] holds or spends any funds.

Where [AGENCY NAME] holds funds for an individual, fiscal staff open a separate account in the individual's name, or a properly titled account that identifies the individual's balance separately. The account is never combined with agency operating funds and never held in an employee's personal account.

Cash kept at the residence is held in a locked container in a secure location. Only staff designated in writing by the Program Director have access. Each individual's cash is kept in a separate envelope or compartment.

Staff record every deposit and withdrawal in the individual's personal funds ledger at the time it occurs. Each entry shows date, amount, purpose, running balance, staff signature, and the individual's signature when able. Receipts are attached for every purchase.
Two staff members count petty cash and compare it to the ledger at each shift change and sign the count log. Any difference is reported to the Program Director the same day.
Funds received for an individual are deposited within two business days, and the receipt is filed in the financial record.

Individuals decide how to spend their own money. Staff may advise but may not refuse a purchase unless the individual's IHP or a documented rights restriction approved under IR-02 says otherwise. Staff may not buy items for themselves with an individual's money, charge for time or transport out of an individual's funds, or borrow or lend money.

Purchases that are large or unusual (above [DOLLAR AMOUNT]) are discussed with the individual and guardian in advance and are consistent with expenses approved in the IHP, except for emergencies, which are documented afterward.

Before any deposit, gift, purchase or savings arrangement, the Program Director considers its effect on benefit eligibility. Where it may affect eligibility, the Program Director consults the individual's DDD support coordinator or a benefits counselor before proceeding. Balances are reviewed quarterly, and the team is alerted when a balance approaches a resource limit.

[AGENCY NAME] reports changes in income, living arrangement or resources to the Social Security Administration or other benefit agency within the required time when [AGENCY NAME] is the representative payee or has been asked to do so by the individual or guardian.

Fiscal staff reconcile each individual's ledger to the account or cash on hand by the 10th day of each month and sign and date the reconciliation. The Program Director reviews and signs it by the 15th. Discrepancies are investigated immediately and reported to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

Any unexplained shortage, missing receipt pattern, or suspected misuse is reported the same day to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and handled as possible exploitation under BEH-03, BEH-04 and BEH-05. The individual and guardian are told, and funds are restored while the matter is investigated.

Each individual and guardian may see the financial record on request and receive copies. Fiscal staff or the Program Director provide access within two business days, in a form the person can understand, and explain entries if asked. A statement is offered to each individual and guardian at least quarterly.

Any limit on an individual's access to their own money is treated as a rights restriction and goes through IR-02, including documented reason, team and guardian agreement, Human Rights Committee review and periodic review.

At discharge, transfer or death, fiscal staff complete a final accounting within [30] days, return the balance and records to the individual, guardian or legal representative (or the estate on death), and obtain a signed receipt, consistent with PCS-05 and HW-05.

Before handling funds, each employee is trained on this policy and signs an acknowledgment, as part of STF-03. Fiscal procedures are included in the annual audit and quality review under GOV-05 and GOV-07.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy, ensures separate accounts and monthly reconciliation occur, receives reports of discrepancies, and confirms the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10 at each annual review.
Designates staff with fund access, reviews and signs monthly reconciliations by the 15th, consults on benefit impact, and ensures access to records is given on request.
Maintain separate accounts, deposit funds within two business days, prepare monthly reconciliations, and produce statements and copies.

responsibilities.role: Direct support professionals and residence supervisors
responsibilities.duty: Record every transaction at the time it occurs, keep receipts, count petty cash at shift change, never borrow or lend, and report shortages immediately.
Direct how funds are spent within the IHP, review records and statements, and sign authorizations.

Personal funds ledger for each individual with receipts
Petty cash count logs signed each shift change
Monthly reconciliation signed by fiscal staff and the Program Director
Benefit and income record, and notes of consultations on benefit impact
Quarterly statements and record of requests for access and copies
Final accounting and signed receipt at discharge or death
Incident and investigation reports for any shortage or suspected misuse
Employee training acknowledgments

policies.title: Safekeeping of Valuable Personal Possessions and Property
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals served in community residences and supervised apartments.
policies.purpose: To protect the valuable belongings of each individual, keep them under the individual's own control, and make sure their handling is recorded from admission through discharge or death.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)11 — a procedure for the safekeeping of valuable personal possessions. Personal belongings belong to the individual. Individuals control, use and may secure their own possessions, and [AGENCY NAME] holds an item only when the individual or guardian asks or agrees. [AGENCY NAME] inventories valuables at admission, updates the inventory whenever items are added, removed or replaced, and has the individual or guardian sign it. Handling of belongings at discharge and at death is documented. Cash and bank accounts are handled under IR-05, which follows N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10. No employee may borrow, use, keep or accept any belonging of an individual.

definitions.definition: An item of monetary or personal importance to the individual, such as jewelry, electronics, phones, cameras, musical instruments, important papers, keepsakes, religious items, collectibles, mobility or communication devices, or any item the individual identifies as valuable.
A dated written list of the individual's valuables, with description, identifying marks or serial numbers, condition, and location, signed by the individual or guardian and a staff member.
Holding an item in a secure place at the individual's or guardian's request, with a written receipt, while the item remains the individual's property.

procedures: At admission, and within 24 hours of arrival, a staff member and the individual (with the guardian or advocate if the individual wishes) walk through the belongings and list valuables on the personal property inventory, with description, serial number where there is one, condition and location. Photographs are taken only with the individual's or guardian's consent.
The individual or guardian and the staff member sign and date the inventory. The individual or guardian receives a copy and the original is filed in the individual's record.

The individual is told, in plain language and in the way they communicate best, that they may keep their belongings in their own room, use a lockable drawer, closet or box (the key remains with the individual), or ask staff to hold an item in the agency's secure storage.
Each bedroom has a lockable storage option available to the individual at no charge unless the individual declines it. A limit on this is a rights restriction handled under IR-02.

When an individual asks staff to hold an item, staff write a dated receipt describing the item. The individual signs it, the item is stored in a locked location with limited access, and the individual may retrieve the item at any time without delay or explanation.
Staff update the inventory within seven days whenever an individual acquires, gives away, sells, loses or replaces a valuable item. The individual or guardian signs the update.
The residence supervisor reviews each inventory with the individual at least quarterly and the full inventory is reviewed at each annual IHP meeting.

Staff do not search, remove, withhold or restrict an individual's belongings except under a documented rights restriction approved under IR-02, or in an immediate health or safety emergency, which is documented and reported to the Program Director the same day.
Staff may not borrow, use, buy, sell, accept as gifts or keep for themselves any belonging of an individual. Violations are reported under BEH-03 and handled under STF-07.

If an item is reported lost, damaged or missing, the staff member who learns of it notifies the residence supervisor immediately and the Program Director within 24 hours. A written report is made and a documented search is completed.

Where the cause appears to be theft or misuse, the matter is reported under BEH-03 and BEH-04 and investigated under BEH-05. The individual and guardian are informed promptly. [AGENCY NAME] repairs or replaces items lost or damaged through staff error or neglect, or compensates the individual, as approved by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
Valuable papers (for example identification, benefit letters, guardianship documents) are kept by the individual or, if requested, in locked storage, and are listed on the inventory.

At discharge or transfer, the staff member and the individual or guardian check all belongings against the current inventory, release them, and both sign a receipt before the individual leaves. Items stored by staff are returned at that time.

After the death of an individual, the Program Director secures the room and belongings, makes a joint inventory with a second staff member, notifies the guardian or legal representative, and releases items only to the guardian, next of kin or estate representative against a signed receipt, consistent with HW-05.

Employees are trained on this policy at orientation (STF-03). The Program Director spot-checks inventories during quarterly record reviews, and findings are reported to the quality improvement process (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures inventories are done and updated, reviews loss reports, arranges replacement or compensation approved by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], and checks inventories during quarterly reviews.
Completes the admission inventory, updates changes within seven days, reviews quarterly with the individual, and manages safekeeping receipts and secure storage.
Respect the individual's control of belongings, report lost or damaged items immediately, and never borrow or keep an individual's property.
Decide what belongings to keep, secure or store, sign inventories, and review them.
Approves compensation for losses caused by the agency and receives reports of suspected theft.

Safekeeping receipts for items held by staff
Loss, damage or missing item reports and search record

Discharge or transfer receipt signed by the individual or guardian

Quarterly inventory review notes

policies.title: Charges, Fees and Room and Board
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the Program Director, fiscal and admissions staff, and all staff who explain charges to individuals and guardians in all residences and supervised apartments of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals and guardians know in advance every charge or fee they may be responsible for, that charges are fair, written, and consistent with benefit rules, and that nobody is billed for anything not on the schedule.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)12 — a list and schedule of all charges and fees for which an individual shall be held responsible. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a current written list and schedule of every charge and fee an individual may be held responsible for, and may not charge any individual an amount that is not on the schedule. The schedule is given to every individual and guardian at admission and again whenever it changes. Services approved and paid for by the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD) are not charged to the individual. Before any room and board or other charge is set against an individual's income, including Supplemental Security Income (federal benefit rate $994 per month in 2026), [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms in writing with DDD what may be charged, so that benefit eligibility is not jeopardized and the individual keeps adequate personal spending money. Individuals and guardians may see their financial records on request as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10.

definitions.definition: The written list of every charge for which an individual may be responsible, with description, amount, how it is calculated, when it is due and who is told about changes.
The portion of an individual's income, if any, that the individual contributes toward housing and food, set in writing and confirmed with DDD.
Money that belongs to the individual to spend as the individual chooses, which is not subject to any agency charge.
An item or service the individual chooses to buy, such as a personal phone plan, streaming service or social outing, that is charged only with the individual's agreement.

procedures: Before the residence opens, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and fiscal staff draft the schedule, listing each charge: room and board contribution, if any; items and services that are optional and individual-choice; and a statement that DDD-funded services carry no charge to the individual.

Before adopting any room and board or other charge, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms in writing with DDD what may be charged against an individual's income, including SSI, and keeps the written confirmation on file. If DDD has not confirmed, no charge is made.
The governing body approves the schedule, and the approval is recorded in its minutes (GOV-01).

Charges are set so that each individual retains personal spending money and the charge does not jeopardize benefit eligibility. Fiscal staff check each individual's income sources before a charge is applied.

At admission, admissions staff review the schedule with the individual and guardian in plain language and in the individual's preferred form of communication (IR-09), answer questions, and give a copy. The individual or guardian signs an acknowledgment of receipt.
Any charge applied to an individual is written in a signed agreement stating the amount, what it covers, and how and when it is paid. The individual or guardian receives a copy.

No staff member may collect or deduct an amount that is not on the schedule. No fee may be charged as a penalty, for behavior, for damage caused by a symptom of disability, or for the cost of any service paid by DDD.

When the schedule changes, the Program Director gives each individual and guardian written notice of at least 30 days before the change takes effect, unless a law or DDD directive requires a different timing. The new schedule is reviewed with each person and a new acknowledgment is signed.
Optional items are charged only with the individual's prior agreement, recorded in the personal funds ledger under IR-05, with a receipt.
Each charge is recorded in the individual's financial record, and individuals and guardians may see the record and receive copies on request, within two business days.

Fiscal staff reconcile charges against the schedule monthly. Any charge not on the schedule is reversed and refunded within 10 days, and the Program Director reports the error to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

Where an individual or guardian disagrees with a charge, they may use the grievance procedure under IR-03. The charge is reviewed by the Program Director within five business days. No retaliation occurs.
Failure to pay a charge is never a reason to discharge or to reduce services without going through the notice and due process requirements of PCS-05.
At discharge or transfer, fiscal staff prepare a final statement, refund overpayments within [30] days, and document it per IR-05 and PCS-05.
The schedule is reviewed at least annually as part of the policy review under GOV-04, and any change to DDD rules or SSI amounts is checked and reflected.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the schedule of charges and fees and each change.
Obtains DDD written confirmation before any charge is set, keeps it on file, and reviews the schedule annually.
Explains the schedule, gives written notice of changes, resolves disputes and ensures no unscheduled charge is made.
Apply only scheduled charges, record them, reconcile monthly, refund errors and prepare final statements.
Review the schedule with each individual and guardian at admission and obtain signed acknowledgment.

Written DDD confirmation of permissible charges
Signed acknowledgment of receipt of the schedule at admission and at each change
Signed charge agreements
Financial record entries and monthly reconciliations

Grievances about charges and their resolution

policies.title: Informed Consent and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All employees and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] who ask for, explain, record or act on an individual's consent, and all individuals and guardians served.
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual is supported to understand choices and make their own decisions, that consent is obtained from the right person in the right way, and that guardianship does not take away rights that the individual retains.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual to understand options, make choices and exercise rights, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(d). Rights are not limited because an individual has a guardian or family. The terms guardian and fiduciary capacity are used as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. Where an individual has no guardian, the individual gives their own consent. Where a guardian has authority over a decision, the guardian consents, and the individual is still told about the decision and supported to take part and to say what they want. Consent is informed: it is given voluntarily, after the information is explained in a way the person understands, and it can be withdrawn. The Individual Habilitation Plan (IHP) includes a guardianship review under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c). In keeping with 42 CFR 441.301(c), the person-centered service plan reflects the individual's informed choices and is signed by the individual and those responsible for carrying it out. Consent is obtained for medical treatment, medications, behavior support plans, rights restrictions, photo and media release, release of information, and other significant decisions.

definitions.definition: Voluntary agreement to a service, treatment or action given by the individual or guardian after receiving, in an understandable way, the nature, benefits, risks and alternatives, including the option to refuse.
A person appointed by a court with legal authority to make certain decisions for an individual, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. The scope of authority is as stated in the court order.
A position of trust in which a person or organization is responsible for managing another person's money, property or affairs for that person's benefit, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
An individual's agreement or expressed wishes about a decision legally made by a guardian.
Help given to an individual to understand information, weigh choices and communicate a decision, such as plain-language explanation, visuals, extra time or a trusted person present.

procedures: At admission, the Program Director obtains and files copies of any guardianship order, power of attorney, or other legal authority, and records exactly which decisions each person is authorized to make. If there is no guardian, the file states that the individual makes their own decisions.
The Program Director tells every staff member who works with the individual, at orientation and when authority changes, which decisions the individual makes and which require the guardian.

Before asking for consent, the staff member or nurse explains in plain language, in the individual's preferred form of communication (IR-09), what is proposed, why, benefits, risks, alternatives and what happens if the person says no. Visuals, demonstrations, interpreters, assistive communication and a trusted support person are used as needed.
The individual is given enough time to ask questions and decide. Staff do not pressure, hurry or reward agreement, and do not treat a refusal as noncompliance.

For decisions the individual may make, the individual gives consent and signs the form where able. Staff record how the information was explained and how the individual showed agreement. Staff do not seek guardian or family consent for decisions the individual is entitled to make.

For decisions within the guardian's authority, written consent is obtained from the guardian. The individual is told about the decision, the individual's own wishes are asked and documented, and any disagreement is recorded and raised with the planning team.

Written consent is obtained before: nonemergency medical treatment and medications (HW-01, HW-02); a behavior support plan or any rights restriction (BEH-01, IR-02); release of information (IR-04); photos, video or media (IR-04); and handling of funds (IR-05). Consents are filed in the record and renewed at least annually or sooner when the proposal changes.

Consent for emergency care is handled under HW-04. If the guardian cannot be reached, staff call 9-1-1 for any life-threatening emergency without waiting for consent, then notify the guardian as soon as possible.

An individual or guardian may withdraw consent at any time. Staff stop the activity unless doing so would create immediate danger, notify the Program Director, and document it. The planning team reviews what to do next.

At each IHP meeting, the team completes the guardianship review required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c): whether the guardianship is still needed and its scope, whether the individual has gained skills to decide more for themselves, and whether less restrictive alternatives or supports could be used. Findings are recorded in the IHP.

If the team thinks an individual could make more decisions independently, the Program Director gives the individual and guardian information on how to ask the court to change the guardianship and on legal resources, and records that this was done.

Where a guardian is not acting in the individual's interest or is unreachable for decisions, the Program Director notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], who consults DDD and, where appropriate, reports under BEH-03.
Individuals and guardians are never asked to waive rights as a condition of admission or service, and exercising rights is never a cause for retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation (STF-03) and annually, and the Program Director audits a sample of consents at least quarterly through the quality improvement process (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures consent practices follow this policy and consults DDD where a guardian is unreachable or not acting in the individual's interest.
Files legal authority documents, informs staff of decision-making authority, completes the guardianship review with the team, and audits consents.
Obtain and document informed consent for treatments and medications in an accessible manner.
Support individuals to understand and make choices, respect refusals, and report concerns about decision-making.
Make decisions within their authority, ask questions, and may withdraw consent at any time.
