policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All governing body members, employees, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all applicants, individuals, guardians and family members.
policies.purpose: To prevent discrimination in admission, services and employment, to make information about the agency available to everyone who needs it, and to make sure every person can understand and be understood.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any applicant, individual, guardian, family member, employee or applicant for employment because of disability, race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age or any other protected status, as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq.) and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 2000d). The Office of Licensing may not issue a license where there is a final finding of discrimination (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(n)), so [AGENCY NAME] treats any discrimination complaint as a priority. In accordance with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.1(a), the purposes of [AGENCY NAME] and a description of its services are available to individuals, parents, guardians, advocates and the general public. Direct support professionals must be able to communicate with the individuals they support (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5(d)). [AGENCY NAME] provides interpreters, translation, language access and accessible formats at no cost to the person.

definitions.definition: Treating a person less favorably, denying or limiting access to services, housing or employment, or applying rules differently, because of a protected characteristic such as disability, race or national origin.
A change to a rule, practice, service or environment that gives a person with a disability equal access, unless it would impose an undue burden or fundamentally alter the service.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to use services without language help.
Information provided in a way the person can use, such as large print, plain language, Braille, audio, pictures, captioned video, electronic text or sign language.
Tools or methods used to communicate other than speech, such as picture boards, speech-generating devices, gestures or sign.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a Nondiscrimination Coordinator ([NAME/TITLE], [PHONE]) who receives and tracks questions and complaints about discrimination and access, and the name is posted in each residence and on printed materials.

[AGENCY NAME] posts a notice of nondiscrimination and how to complain in each residence in plain language and in the languages commonly used by the individuals served, and gives it to every individual and guardian at admission.

The admissions decision follows the criteria in PCS-01 only. Applicants are not rejected because of race, national origin, language, religion, sex, age, type or severity of disability beyond the program's documented capacity to serve safely, or other protected status. Each non-admission and its reason is documented and reviewed by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

A written description of the agency's purposes and services (the program description under GOV-03) is kept current, offered to every individual, guardian, advocate and visitor on request, available at the residence and on request by mail or electronically, and provided in an accessible format and, where needed, in the person's language (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.1(a)).

At admission, and at each IHP meeting, the team completes a communication profile for each individual: how the person expresses wants, yes and no, distress and pain; preferred language; hearing, vision and literacy needs; and any AAC or assistive technology. The profile is kept at the residence for staff to use.

Before assigning a direct support professional to an individual, the residence supervisor confirms the professional can communicate with that individual (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5(d)), through shared language, sign, AAC or other documented method. Staff receive training on the individual's communication method before working alone.

When an individual, guardian or family member needs language help, [AGENCY NAME] arranges a qualified interpreter or translation at no cost, including for the IHP meeting, medical visits, rights review and grievances. Staff do not ask family members, other individuals or children to interpret except at the person's own request and when documented.

Important documents (rights notice, grievance procedure, schedule of charges, consent forms, IHP) are provided in plain language and in accessible formats and in the person's preferred language. Staff read them aloud or explain them when requested.

Reasonable accommodation requests may be made orally or in writing to any staff member. The Program Director responds within five business days, documents the request, the decision and the reason, and informs the person of their right to complain if denied.
Facilities and programs are reviewed for accessibility under ENV-01. Barriers that limit access to common areas, entrances, bathrooms or activities are corrected or an alternative is provided.

Any person who believes they have been treated in a discriminatory way may complain to any staff member, the Nondiscrimination Coordinator, or the grievance procedure (IR-03). Staff who receive a complaint report it to the Coordinator the same business day. The Coordinator begins review within two business days and informs the person of the outcome in writing within 30 days.

Complaints are also shared with the individual's right to contact outside agencies, including the Office of Licensing, DDD and civil rights agencies. Retaliation against anyone who complains is prohibited and is reported under BEH-03.
Employment decisions follow STF-10 and are made without discrimination. Reasonable accommodations are provided to employees with disabilities and for religious practices where required by law.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies the governing body and DDD or the Office of Licensing as required if a government agency finds discrimination, and no final finding of discrimination may be left unaddressed because it can prevent licensure (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(n)).
Staff training on this policy occurs at orientation (STF-03) and annually. Complaints, accommodation requests and language services are reported quarterly to the quality improvement process (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, reviews quarterly data on complaints and accommodations, and acts on any finding of discrimination.
Ensures resources for interpreters, translations and accessible formats, and reports required findings.
Receives and tracks complaints and accommodation requests, begins reviews within two business days, and reports outcomes.
Maintain communication profiles, assign staff who can communicate with each individual, and arrange accommodations and language help.
Treat everyone without discrimination, use each person's communication method, and report complaints the same business day.

documentation: Notice of nondiscrimination, with date posted and distribution record
Nondiscrimination Coordinator designation
Current program description and records of distribution
Communication profile for each individual
Interpreter and translation requests and records of services provided
Accommodation requests, decisions and reasons
Discrimination complaints, review notes and outcomes
Staff training records
Quarterly reports to the quality improvement process

policies.title: Exchange of Contact Information with Families and Guardians
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the Program Director, residence supervisors, admissions staff and all direct support professionals of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals, families and guardians served.
policies.purpose: To give parents, actively involved family members and guardians a safe and voluntary way to exchange contact information, while respecting the choices of the individual and the guardian and keeping their information private.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)19 — written procedures for the exchange of contact information of parents, family members who are actively involved in ensuring the individual's welfare, or guardians who choose to, as set forth at N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6. It also meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)8 — new employee orientation includes training consistent with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6. Participation is voluntary. Contact information is exchanged only with those who choose to take part, and no one's information is shared without that person's agreement. The individual's own preferences and the individual's guardianship status are honored, consistent with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1, which provides that rights are not limited because an individual has a guardian or family. [AGENCY NAME] records each exchange in the individual's record and does not use the exchange to share clinical or other confidential information about any individual, which remains protected under IR-04.

definitions.definition: A parent, relative or other person who takes part in ensuring the individual's welfare, such as by visiting, communicating regularly, attending planning meetings or advocating for the individual.
A court-appointed person with legal authority to make certain decisions for an individual.

The voluntary sharing, among parents, actively involved family members and guardians who choose to take part, of names, phone numbers, email and mailing addresses so they can communicate with each other.

A written form on which a parent, family member or guardian says whether they choose to share their own contact information and with whom, and which the individual (or guardian) signs to show the individual has been asked.

procedures: At or before admission, admissions staff explain the contact information exchange to the individual and to each guardian, parent or actively involved family member, in plain language and an accessible format. They state clearly that taking part is optional and that declining has no effect on services.

Staff ask the individual about their own wishes. If the individual has a guardian, the guardian's decision governs where the guardian has authority, and the individual's wishes are still recorded and respected whenever possible. Where an individual objects and a guardian does not, the Program Director records the disagreement and refers it to the planning team.

Each person who chooses to take part completes the exchange consent form, listing the contact information they agree to share (for example name, phone, email), whether they share with all participating families and guardians of individuals at [AGENCY NAME] or only certain people, and how long the consent lasts. A person may decline altogether.

The Program Director or designee keeps a contact exchange list limited to the people who have signed an exchange consent form. The list is kept in a locked file or in a password-protected electronic file with restricted access.

Within 14 days of receipt of a signed consent form, the Program Director provides, to each participating parent, family member or guardian, the contact information of the others who have consented to share, in the form each has agreed to. Staff record the date and the information provided.

The exchange list contains only contact information. It does not include any person's diagnosis, address of the individual's room, medical, behavioral, financial or other protected information about any individual, which remains confidential under IR-04.

A person may change or withdraw consent at any time, orally or in writing. Staff stop sharing the person's information within two business days, update the list, and tell the person that information already shared cannot be taken back.

When a new individual is admitted, or an individual leaves, the Program Director updates the list within 14 days and offers new participants the exchange. Individuals who have left have their entries removed unless the person asks to remain on the list.

Each exchange, refusal, change and withdrawal is documented in the individual's record with date, who was involved, and the staff member's signature, and the consent form is filed in the record (REC-01).

Individuals and guardians are told in the admission rights review (IR-01) that they may ask to meet or communicate with other families. [AGENCY NAME] does not control, monitor or restrict communication that families set up with each other after the exchange.

Concerns or complaints about the exchange, including sharing without consent, are handled through the grievance procedure (IR-03). An unauthorized disclosure is reported to the Program Director the same day and handled as a privacy incident under IR-04.

Orientation under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)8: during new employee orientation (STF-03), before working alone, each new employee is trained on N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6 and on this procedure. The training covers that participation is voluntary, how consent is obtained, what may and may not be shared, how to refer family requests to the Program Director, and how to document. The trainer and employee sign the orientation checklist when completed.
Employees are retrained annually as part of the in-service training under STF-04, and a copy of this policy is given to each employee at orientation and whenever it changes.

The Program Director reviews the contact list and consent forms every six months to make sure that all information is current and consents are on file, and reports the results to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy, ensures staff are trained, and receives the six-month review and any report of unauthorized disclosure.
Keeps the consent forms and contact exchange list, provides the information to participants within 14 days, updates the list, and resolves disagreements with the team.
Explain the exchange at admission, state that it is voluntary, and obtain completed consent forms.
Delivers and documents the orientation training on N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6 for every new employee.
Refer family requests to the Program Director, never give out family contact information themselves, and report any improper disclosure the same day.

responsibilities.role: Individuals, parents, family members and guardians
responsibilities.duty: Decide whether to take part, keep their own information current, and tell [AGENCY NAME] if they wish to change or withdraw consent.

documentation: Signed exchange consent forms and any declinations
Contact exchange list with dates updated
Record of each exchange, change and withdrawal in the individual's record
Disagreement notes and planning team referral, if any
Orientation checklist showing training on N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6, signed by trainer and employee
Annual in-service training records
Six-month review reports
Privacy incident reports and grievances related to the exchange

policies.title: Video and Audio Monitoring in Common Areas
policies.applies_to: All residences, supervised apartments and supportive living settings operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all staff, individuals, guardians, visitors and contractors
policies.purpose: To state whether [AGENCY NAME] uses video or audio monitoring in the common areas of its residences and to set firm limits on any future use. These limits protect the privacy, dignity and rights of the people we support. The policy also keeps any recording subject to confidentiality rules.
policies.policy:
This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)21 — a procedure to address the use of video/audio monitoring in the common areas of the residences, if applicable.

Current status: At the time this manual is adopted, [AGENCY NAME] does NOT use video or audio monitoring, recording or live-streaming devices in any common area of any residence. No camera, microphone, baby monitor, smart speaker with recording function or similar device is installed or used to observe individuals.

Monitoring is not adopted unless the conditions below are met. Staff may not install, bring or use any monitoring device on their own initiative.

1. Bedrooms and bathrooms are never monitored by video or audio. This applies to every residence, whether or not monitoring is used elsewhere.
2. Monitoring may be considered only for common areas (for example the living room, kitchen, hallways and entrances) and only to address a documented safety or security need that less intrusive measures have not met.
3. The Human Rights Committee must review and approve the proposal first. The Committee operates under N.J.A.C. 10:41A, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(e).
4. Every individual living in the home, and each guardian, must be told in writing before any device is installed and must have the chance to object. Staff must also be notified in writing. Monitoring is not used over the documented objection of an individual unless the Human Rights Committee, the planning team and the process in IR-02 have addressed the objection.
5. Monitoring may never be used in place of required staffing or supervision, and never as a substitute for positive behavior support or as a form of punishment.
6. Recordings that identify an individual are confidential. They are treated as protected information under HIPAA (45 CFR Part 164) and the confidentiality rules in IR-04.
7. Exercising a right to object to or question monitoring is never a cause for retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a)).

This policy supports the individual's rights under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1, including that house rules and practices must not infringe on the rights of others, and it works with the HCBS settings privacy protections in IR-01.

definitions.definition: A shared space in a residence used by all residents and staff, such as a living room, dining room, kitchen, hallway or entrance. Bedrooms, bathrooms and any space where personal care is given are not common areas for this policy.
Any camera, video doorbell, microphone, audio recorder, baby monitor, smart speaker or similar equipment that can transmit, view or record images or sound of people in the residence.
The committee established under N.J.A.C. 10:41A that reviews practices and restrictions affecting individuals' rights.
Any stored image or sound captured by a monitoring device, including footage retained on a device, server or cloud service.

procedures: Standing rule: The Executive Director/[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms at each annual policy review (GOV-04) whether any monitoring device is in use in any residence, and records the finding on the review sign-off sheet. At adoption the finding is 'none in use'.

Staff must report immediately to the Program Director any device in a residence that could view or record people (for example a device brought in by a staff member, visitor or family member). The Program Director removes or disables it the same day, unless it is the individual's own property, and documents the action in the critical information log (REC-03).

If an individual brings a personal device (for example a smart speaker or tablet), the Program Director meets with the individual, and the guardian if any, to discuss housemates' privacy. Agreement about where the device may be used is documented. This is not agency monitoring, but the individual is not allowed to place devices in bathrooms or in another resident's room.

If the governing body wishes to propose monitoring of a common area, the Executive Director prepares a written proposal. It states the specific need, the incidents or risks involved, less intrusive alternatives already tried, the exact location of each device, whether audio is included, who may view the footage, and the retention period.
The Executive Director seeks advice from legal counsel on applicable recording and consent laws before any device is purchased or installed. The advice is kept in the governance file.

The Executive Director submits the proposal to the Human Rights Committee. No device may be installed until the Committee's written approval is on file. The approval date and any conditions are recorded in the minutes.

Before any installation, the Program Director gives written notice to every individual in the home, each guardian, and all staff assigned to the home. The notice is in plain language and the individual's preferred communication format (IR-09). It describes the device, location, purpose, who can view recordings, how long recordings are kept, and how to object or file a grievance (IR-03).

The Program Director meets with each individual, and with the guardian if applicable, to explain the plan and hear objections. Objections and the individual's wishes are recorded. Unresolved objections go back to the Human Rights Committee and are handled under IR-02 before installation.

Devices must be installed only in approved common-area locations, and the field of view must not include any bedroom or bathroom doorway interior. Signs are posted at the entrance to the home and in each monitored room stating that monitoring is in use.

The Executive Director appoints, in writing, a short list of staff authorized to view recordings (by title). Viewing is limited to the authorized persons and to the purposes in the approved proposal, such as investigating an incident (BEH-05) or a safety review.

Recordings are retained for [30] days and then deleted automatically or manually, unless a recording relates to an unusual incident, an allegation of abuse, neglect or exploitation, an investigation or a legal hold. In those cases the relevant recording is exported, logged and kept until the matter is closed and the Executive Director authorizes deletion.

Every viewing or export of a recording is logged with date, person viewing, reason and incident number. Recordings may not be copied to personal phones or personal accounts, posted or shared outside the agency except to the Office of Licensing, DDD, law enforcement or other authorities as the law requires, or to an individual or guardian requesting access to the individual's own information with Executive Director approval (IR-04).

The Program Director reviews monitoring use quarterly with the Human Rights Committee chair. The review covers complaints, access logs, any misuse and whether the need still exists. If the need no longer exists, the devices are removed and the individuals and guardians are notified in writing.

Any staff member who misuses a device or recording (for example viewing without authorization, copying or sharing) is subject to discipline up to termination under STF-07. If the misuse suggests abuse, exploitation or a rights violation, it is reported under BEH-03 and BEH-04.
Individuals, guardians and staff who object to monitoring or to a recording may use the grievance process in IR-03 without retribution.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether any monitoring is proposed. Obtains legal advice and Human Rights Committee approval first. Confirms status annually and ensures this policy is followed.
Removes unauthorized devices. Gives all notices, meets with individuals and guardians, manages access logs and retention, and conducts quarterly reviews.
Reviews and approves or rejects any proposal. Reviews objections and periodic use reports under N.J.A.C. 10:41A.

responsibilities.role: Direct Support Professionals and other staff
responsibilities.duty: Do not bring or install devices. Report any device found. Protect confidentiality of recordings.
May ask questions, object and file a grievance at any time without retribution.

documentation: Annual policy review sign-off stating monitoring status
Written proposal, legal advice and Human Rights Committee minutes and approval (if monitoring is ever proposed)
Notices to individuals, guardians and staff, with acknowledgments and recorded objections
Recording access and export log
Quarterly monitoring review notes
Critical information log entries for any unauthorized device or misuse (REC-03)

policies.title: Referral, Admission and Transition In
policies.applies_to: All referrals and admissions to [AGENCY NAME] residences, supervised apartments and supportive living; Program Director, Executive Director, nursing staff, DSPs and the planning team
policies.purpose: To make sure each person is admitted by informed choice, is eligible and appropriately matched to the home, and is introduced to the home, their rights and the agency's charges in a planned and respectful way.
policies.policy:
This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)15 — a procedure for admissions that complies with the requirements at N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.

[AGENCY NAME] admits only individuals who:
1. are age 21 or older,
2. are eligible for Medicaid and enrolled in the DDD Community Care Program,
3. have services approved by DDD, and
4. have chosen [AGENCY NAME] as their provider after learning about their options.

The individual's choice of provider and setting is central. Admission is consistent with the HCBS settings requirements applied to N.J.A.C. 10:44A homes through New Jersey's NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration and the Statewide Transition Plan, and with 42 CFR 441.301(c) (person-centered planning and home- and community-based setting characteristics).

Before the agency accepts any individual, the Executive Director confirms that the person's assessed needs, the housemates and the home's supervision and staffing match the program description (GOV-03 and STF-01). The agency does not admit a person whose needs it cannot safely meet and does not exceed the capacity on its license (a community residence of up to 16 individuals; a supervised apartment of up to 4 individuals per apartment).

On or before the day of admission, each individual (and guardian, if any) receives the Division's rights document and the agency's schedule of charges and fees, and the acknowledgments are signed and filed. The agency verifies the admission steps required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4 against the current regulatory text at each annual policy review and whenever the rules change (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: The DDD program under the NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration (Section 1115) that authorizes and funds Individual Supports and related services.
The DDD-funded support coordinator or Support Coordination Agency worker who helps the individual develop and monitor the service plan and select providers.
The planned period before and after the move, including visits, preparation of the home and first-30-day review.
The Division's document listing the rights of individuals with developmental disabilities, which the agency must provide and for which it must obtain acknowledgments.

procedures: The Program Director receives each referral from the individual, family, guardian, support coordinator or DDD. The inquiry is logged with date, source and contact information.

Within [5] business days the Program Director confirms the person's age (21+), Medicaid eligibility, CCP enrollment and DDD service approval (or approval pending) through the support coordinator and the DDD authorization. Anything not confirmed is noted and followed up.

The Program Director requests and reviews current information: the most recent Individual Habilitation Plan or service plan, assessments, medical and psychiatric history, medication list, any behavior support plan, guardianship papers, and prior incident or restriction history. The review is limited to what is needed for placement.

The Program Director and nurse review health, behavioral and support needs. They decide whether the program description, staffing pattern, home accessibility and housemate mix can meet them. The decision and reasons are written and signed by the Executive Director. If the answer is no, the individual and support coordinator are told in writing within [5] business days with the reasons and are offered help to find alternatives.

The individual (and guardian) tour the home, meet housemates and staff, and choose whether to proceed. The Program Director records the individual's own words about their wishes. Several visits, including a meal or overnight stay, are offered when possible.
The Program Director asks existing residents about a new housemate and records their views. Existing residents' rights are weighed in the match.

The Program Director explains the schedule of charges and fees (IR-07), including any room and board and how personal funds are handled (IR-05, IR-06), and gives a written copy. The individual or guardian signs an acknowledgment.

The Program Director provides the rights document, explains it in plain language and the person's preferred communication method (IR-09), and obtains signed acknowledgments. The explanation also covers the grievance process (IR-03), how to report abuse, neglect or exploitation (BEH-03), and the Human Rights Committee.
The Program Director obtains signed consents and releases as needed (IR-04, IR-08), emergency contacts, and copies of guardianship documents, and records the person's Medicaid and insurance details.

The nurse completes a health and medication review and obtains current prescriber orders before the first dose (HW-01). Allergies, choking risks, seizure plans and dietary needs are entered into the record (HW-02, HW-03, ENV-05).

The Program Director prepares the home before arrival: bedroom set up as the person chooses, accessibility checked, evacuation plan updated for the new resident (ENV-02), and staff briefed on the person's preferences, supports and risks.

On the admission date the Program Director or designee welcomes the person, reviews belongings with an inventory the individual signs (IR-06), and confirms the date of admission in the individual's record (REC-01).
The record is opened at the residence with required identifying information and the dates of admission (REC-01), and the critical information log is updated for staff (REC-03).

The planning team confirms the existing IHP is in place and, where it is not, schedules the IHP meeting (PCS-02) so that services begin without delay. Any gap between the plan and what the agency can deliver is raised with the support coordinator.

The Program Director checks in with the individual weekly for the first 30 days and holds a transition review with the individual, guardian and support coordinator at about 30 days. Changes to supports, housemate concerns or a request to move are documented and addressed.
The Executive Director reviews admissions quarterly in the quality improvement process (GOV-05), including declined referrals, early moves out and complaints from new residents.

responsibilities.duty: Approves or declines admission. Ensures the match fits the program description and licensed capacity.
Manages referral, verification, visits, rights and fee acknowledgments, the admission day and the 30-day review.
Completes health and medication review and obtains orders before admission.
Welcome the person, follow the person's preferences and report concerns during the transition.
Choose the provider, take part in visits and planning, and sign acknowledgments.

documentation: Referral log and eligibility confirmations (age, Medicaid, CCP, DDD authorization)
Admission decision, with written reasons
Signed rights document acknowledgment and schedule of charges and fees acknowledgment
Consents and releases, guardianship papers, emergency contacts
Health and medication review, prescriber orders
Belongings inventory
Admission date entry in the record
30-day transition review

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning and the Individual Habilitation Plan
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services; Program Director, qualified staff, DSPs, nurse, planning team members
policies.purpose: To make sure each person's Individual Habilitation Plan (IHP) is developed, implemented, reviewed and evaluated with the person leading, in a way that reflects their preferences, builds on strengths and meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3.

definitions.definition: The written comprehensive plan of goals, objectives, methods and services developed under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3 for each individual.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, the group that develops the service plan, including the individual, guardian, support coordinator and others who provide supports.
A person legally appointed to make decisions for an individual, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. The guardian's scope is verified from the court order.
A step toward a goal that states what the person will do, how often or to what standard, and how progress will be counted.
A plan, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, to teach new skills and reduce challenging behavior; it is part of the IHP when used (BEH-01).

procedures: Within [30] days of admission, or before if an existing plan is in place, the Program Director schedules the IHP meeting with the individual and sends invitations to the guardian, support coordinator, family or friends the individual chooses, the nurse and key DSPs. The Program Director asks the individual where, when and how the meeting should be held.

At least [10] days before the meeting, the Program Director prepares a draft packet: cover page information, current evaluations and assessment summaries, progress on previous goals from monthly summaries, and a one-page profile of the person's preferences. The profile is built with the individual using their own words, photos or other communication supports (IR-09).

The Program Director offers the individual practice, advocacy and training to understand options and choices (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(d)) before the meeting and uses plain language and accessible formats.

The meeting is led by or with the individual. The team reviews progress on prior goals, preferences, capabilities and needs, health and safety, community, work and relationship goals (PCS-04), and any barriers.

The team writes goals the individual wants. For each goal, the team writes measurable, sequential objectives and the method staff will use to teach or support each objective, and names the responsible person for each.
The team lists services with start dates, duration and frequency, consistent with the DDD authorization, and lists the team members and responsible persons.
The team reviews guardianship status and decision-making supports (IR-08) and records any needed changes or referrals.
The team identifies barriers (such as transport, staffing, health, funding or communication) and assigns an action and a date for each.
The team lists any individual expenses that need authorization (for example a major purchase or an agency-managed fund use), and the individual or guardian signs the authorization (IR-05).

The Program Director writes the meeting summary or addendum. Any disagreement by the individual, guardian or a team member is recorded in their words, together with how it will be resolved or appealed. Disagreement does not stop the plan from being finalized.
All attendees sign the attendance sign-off. Anyone who joined by phone is documented and signs within [5] business days.

The completed IHP with all 14 elements is typed and signed within [14] days of the meeting. The Program Director checks the 14-element checklist before filing. A copy goes to the individual, guardian and support coordinator and the plan is explained to them in an understandable way.

The Program Director trains all staff who support the individual on the IHP within [7] days of finalization, including methods, responsible persons and data collection (PCS-03). Staff sign that they have read it.

Monthly, the Program Director or qualified designee writes a progress summary for each objective, based on daily documentation, and files it in the record (PCS-03). Lack of progress prompts a team review and a change of method rather than closing the goal.

The team meets to review and evaluate the IHP at least annually, and sooner when the person asks, when needs change, after hospitalization, after a rights restriction is proposed, or when an objective is mastered or not working. A change that requires a new service authorization is shared with the support coordinator.
The Executive Director samples IHPs in the quality improvement process (GOV-05) for completeness of the 14 elements, individual participation, timeliness and goals tied to preferences.

responsibilities.duty: Leads or takes part in the meeting, chooses attendees, states preferences and goals.
Schedules and facilitates, writes the IHP and monthly summaries, and ensures all 14 elements are present and implemented.
Takes part in planning and decisions within the scope of the guardianship, and signs authorizations where required.
Takes part in the meeting and ensures consistency with DDD service authorization.
Provides health information and plans for health goals.
Implement methods, collect data and give input to the team.
Ensures the process is resourced and audits it.

documentation: Invitations and individual preference profile
Signed IHP with all 14 required elements and checklist
Meeting summary or addendum including any recorded disagreement
Signed attendance sign-off
Authorization for approved individual expenses
Staff read-and-sign sheet for the IHP
Monthly progress summaries in the record
Annual and interim review records

policies.title: Implementation of Supports and Daily Documentation
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the nurse, Program Director and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure supports in the Individual Habilitation Plan are actually delivered, are documented accurately and on time, and match the services billed and the EVV records.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] implements each person's IHP as written. Each objective has a method and a responsible person (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c)). Progress is documented monthly and filed in the individual's record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(b)); the record is kept at the residence (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9).

Daily notes and data sheets must support every service billed. Billing is done only for services that were delivered, documented and authorized (GOV-06). Where Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) applies — New Jersey requires it for DDD Individual Supports, In-Home Respite and Community Based Supports through HHAeXchange under section 12006(a) of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)) — EVV visit records must match the schedule and the daily documentation. Where a worker lives with the person served, a Live-In Worker Attestation may allow EVV exclusion, if DDD approves it.

Every entry is dated and signed with the writer's full name and title (initials alone are not accepted unless tied to a signature log). Entries are factual, written at the time of the event or as soon as possible, and never altered to hide an error. Falsification (as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3) is a serious violation. It is cause for discipline up to termination and may be reported as required.

definitions.definition: A dated and signed entry written each shift describing supports given, the person's activities, mood, health observations, incidents and communications.
A form used to record counts, prompts or results for a specific IHP objective.
An electronic system (HHAeXchange for DDD) that records the date, time, place, worker and service of a visit.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: making a false entry or altering a record or document to misrepresent facts.
A DDD form that allows exclusion from EVV where the worker lives with the person being served.

procedures: The Program Director trains each DSP on the IHP, methods and data collection before the DSP works alone with the person (PCS-02) and at each plan change. The training is documented and signed.

The Program Director posts or provides a weekly schedule that assigns each IHP activity and objective to a named staff member and time, including community activities the individual has chosen (PCS-04).

Each shift, assigned staff provide the supports described in the IHP, using the specified method, and respect the person's choices. When a person declines, staff record the refusal, offer alternatives and report to the Program Director if the pattern continues.
During each shift staff complete data sheets for assigned objectives at the time of the activity.

Before the shift ends, each staff member completes a daily note for each individual with the date, shift hours, supports given, activities, health observations, mood and behavior, visitors, outings, and anything staff communicated. The note is signed with full name and title.

Staff write only facts and direct quotes, avoiding labels and opinions. If an error is made, staff cross out with a single line, write 'error', date and sign. Staff never use correction fluid, deletion or backdating. Electronic entries are corrected by a dated addendum.

Staff record any incident, injury, change in condition or medication issue in the note and report it by the required process (BEH-04, HW-04, HW-01). Critical information is also entered in the critical information log (REC-03).
Each service day, staff who are required to use EVV clock in and out in HHAeXchange at the service location, for the service delivered. Staff do not clock in for another person or clock in remotely.

If a worker forgets to clock or the system fails, the worker notifies the Program Director the same day. The Program Director completes the agency's EVV correction process with a reason code, a note and supporting documentation. Corrections are not made without a documented reason.
If a live-in worker arrangement is proposed, the Executive Director obtains DDD's Live-In Worker Attestation before excluding the worker from EVV and files it.

At the end of each week, the Program Director or designee compares schedules, EVV records and daily notes to identify gaps, missing notes or mismatches. Differences are resolved within [3] business days and documented.
The Program Director reviews daily notes and data sheets weekly, signs the review, and gives staff feedback on missing or unclear entries.

By the [10th] of each month, the Program Director or qualified designee writes the monthly progress summary for each individual. It addresses each objective with data from the prior month, the individual's own comments and recommended changes, and files it in the record (4.3(b)).

Billing staff bill only from authorized services that are supported by a signed daily note and a matching EVV record (where applicable). Any service lacking support is not billed, or is corrected under GOV-06.
Records are kept at the residence in the individual's file (REC-01). Daily notes may be stored in a secure electronic system with access limited to authorized staff (IR-04).

The Executive Director includes documentation timeliness, EVV matching and objective progress in quality improvement reviews (GOV-05). Falsified or missing documentation leads to corrective action and, when appropriate, refund of any related payment.

responsibilities.duty: Provide supports, complete data sheets and daily notes accurately and on time, and use EVV correctly.
Assigns supports, trains staff, reviews documentation weekly, writes monthly summaries and corrects EVV records.
Compare services billed to notes and EVV and withhold unsupported claims.
Ensures resources and audits documentation and EVV performance.

documentation: Staff training on IHP read-and-sign sheets
Weekly schedules
Daily notes and data sheets (dated and signed in full)
EVV visit records and correction logs
Live-In Worker Attestation, if used
Weekly documentation review sign-off
Monthly progress summaries filed in the record

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: All individuals served; Program Director, DSPs, planning team
policies.purpose: To make sure each person lives as a full member of the community: choosing activities, work, relationships, visitors and daily routines, as required of HCBS settings under New Jersey's NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration and Statewide Transition Plan, which applies to N.J.A.C. 10:44A homes.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] supports each individual to take part in community life to the same degree as people who do not receive services. Each person has access to the community, chooses how to spend time, and may seek and keep competitive integrated employment if they wish (42 CFR 441.301(c)).

Employment and integration goals that the person chooses are reflected in the Individual Habilitation Plan, with measurable objectives, methods and responsible persons (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c)), and are reviewed at least annually (PCS-02).

The agency does not restrict visitors, community access, meals, schedules or privacy except through a documented rights restriction under IR-02 that meets the required criteria. House rules may not infringe on individuals' rights (IR-02). Staffing and transportation are arranged to make community participation possible, not to limit it (STF-01, ENV-06).

definitions.definition: Opportunity to live, work, shop, worship, learn, socialize and use public services in the community alongside people without disabilities.
Work in the community, at or above minimum wage, in a setting where the person interacts with people without disabilities.
A limit on a right, imposed only through the due process in IR-02, with documented justification, review and consent.

procedures: At admission and at each IHP meeting, the Program Director asks each person about interests, work history and goals, friends and family, faith, clubs, hobbies and places they want to go. Answers are recorded in the person's words and in the IHP preferences section.

The planning team writes integration and employment goals when the person chooses, with measurable objectives and a responsible person (PCS-02). A person who is not interested in work is not pressured; the question is asked again at each annual review.

If a person wants to work, the Program Director gives information about employment options and supports and refers the person and support coordinator to DDD employment services and other community resources, and records the referral. The agency adjusts schedules and supports to fit work hours.

The Program Director builds a weekly activity plan with each person that includes activities in the community outside the home, based on the person's choices and not on staff convenience or group outings only. Staff record where each person went and who chose it in the daily note (PCS-03).

Transportation is provided or arranged (agency vehicle, public transit, ride share, family or travel training) so that scheduled activities, work and appointments can occur (ENV-06). If a vehicle or staff is not available, the Program Director arranges an alternative or reschedules within [24] hours, and the person is told the reason.

Staff support people to keep and build relationships: helping with phone calls, video calls, letters, social media safety, and visits with friends, family and partners. Visitors are welcome at times chosen by the individual, subject to the person's wishes and to reasonable safety needs of housemates only through IR-02.
The Program Director teaches and supports personal safety, money skills and travel skills as chosen by the person, with objectives in the IHP.

No limitation on access to the community, food, visitors, phone, internet, privacy, or personal schedule is imposed by staff on their own. A staff member who thinks a limit is needed reports it to the Program Director, who follows IR-02 and the Human Rights Committee process.

Each quarter, the Program Director reviews each individual's community activity log with them, checking that activities are chosen, varied and in integrated settings, and updates the plan if the person wants something different.

The Executive Director reviews integration and employment indicators (hours in the community, employed individuals, new relationships, complaints) quarterly in the quality improvement process (GOV-05).
Individuals who feel their access to community or work is limited may use the grievance process (IR-03) without retribution.

responsibilities.duty: Chooses activities, work, relationships and daily routines.
Gathers preferences, builds activity plans, arranges referrals and transportation, and reviews integration quarterly.
Support activities as chosen, document them, and report any barriers.
Writes integration and employment goals into the IHP and reviews them.
Resources community access and monitors outcomes.

documentation: Preferences and goals in the IHP
Employment referrals and contacts
Weekly activity plans and community activity log
Transportation records
Quarterly integration reviews
Any rights restriction documentation (IR-02)

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: All planned and unplanned transfers, discharges and terminations of services; Executive Director, Program Director, nurse, DSPs and planning team
policies.purpose: To make sure any move out of a [AGENCY NAME] home is planned with the individual, safe, respectful and documented, and that no person is evicted or discharged without due process, notice and help finding a new place to live.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will not discharge, transfer or terminate services of an individual except for a reason that is documented, discussed with the individual and guardian, and carried out under the requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A and DDD. Eviction is a defined term in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3 and is treated as a serious action: the Executive Director verifies the notice, transfer and appeal requirements in the current N.J.A.C. 10:44A text and DDD rules before any involuntary discharge, and documents that verification.

Transition is planned by the planning team (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3), including the individual, guardian and support coordinator, so that the individual has a safe, suitable place to go and continuing services. The dates of transfer or discharge are recorded in the individual's record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)).

The individual's funds and belongings are returned with a signed inventory (IR-05, IR-06). The individual keeps all rights during the process, and objecting or filing a grievance is never a cause for retribution (IR-03).

An emergency transfer (for example, hospitalization or imminent danger) is handled under HW-04 and BEH-04, and the agency continues planning with the team.

definitions.definition: End of residence or services at [AGENCY NAME], whether chosen by the individual or required by the agency.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: the involuntary removal of an individual from the residence by the licensee.
The written plan developed with the individual and the team for the move, covering supports, health, funds, belongings and follow-up.
The DDD-funded support coordinator who assists the individual to find a new provider or setting.

procedures: When an individual says they want to move, or the agency or team believes a move may be needed, the Program Director meets with the individual and guardian within [3] business days to listen, record the individual's wishes and discuss options. The support coordinator is notified the same day.
For a voluntary move, the Program Director convenes the planning team within [7] days, plans visits to the new setting, sets a target date and assigns tasks for each team member.

The agency never starts an involuntary discharge on its own initiative. If the agency considers that it can no longer meet a person's needs or ensure safety, the Program Director first documents what supports, changes, training, behavior support (BEH-01), nursing or staffing have been tried, and reports to the Executive Director.

The Executive Director reviews the record, consults the support coordinator and DDD, and verifies the current notice, transfer and appeal requirements in N.J.A.C. 10:44A and DDD requirements. The review is written and signed. Discharge is considered only after the team has explored all reasonable alternatives and only when it is documented as the last resort.

The Executive Director gives the individual and guardian written notice stating the reason, the proposed date (consistent with the notice requirements verified in step 4), the individual's right to object, the grievance process (IR-03) and the right to contact the support coordinator and DDD. The notice is explained in plain language and the individual's preferred communication method (IR-09).

The Program Director ensures the individual is never discharged to a place without a safe, planned alternative and is never left without supports. The agency continues to provide full services until the transfer occurs.

The Program Director holds a transition planning meeting with the individual, guardian, support coordinator and receiving provider. The plan covers the date, transport, staffing during the move, health and medication information, behavior support and communication information, preferences and routines, important people, and follow-up.

The nurse prepares a health summary, current medication list and orders, immunization and TB records as applicable, upcoming appointments and pending tests, and sends them to the receiving provider with the individual's or guardian's consent (IR-04). Medications are released with a signed count under HW-01.

The Program Director and DSPs help the individual pack and say goodbye in a way the individual chooses. Belongings are inventoried against the admission inventory and signed for by the individual or guardian (IR-06). Furniture and items the individual bought stay with the individual.

The Executive Director or designee reconciles the individual's personal funds, gives a final accounting and returns all funds and any account documents with a signed receipt, within [30] days or sooner as the agency's funds policy requires (IR-05). Any amounts owed are handled under IR-07 and are not held back from belongings.

On the day of transfer or discharge, the Program Director records the date, time, destination, who accompanied the person and what was sent, and enters the date in the individual's record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)). The critical information log and staff are updated (REC-03).

If the individual moves out due to hospitalization, death or emergency, the Program Director follows HW-04, HW-05 and BEH-04, notifies the guardian and support coordinator immediately and keeps the individual's belongings secure and inventoried.
Within [7] days after the move, the Program Director contacts the individual and new provider to check how the individual is doing and offers information as needed. A follow-up note is written.

The Program Director completes a discharge summary within [14] days, covering the reason, services provided, progress on goals, status at discharge and referrals. The record is closed and retained under REC-01.

The Executive Director reviews all discharges and voluntary moves quarterly (GOV-05) to find causes, including whether any involuntary discharge occurred and whether alternatives were explored, and reports patterns to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Take part in decisions, may object or grieve, and sign receipts for funds and belongings.
Approves any involuntary discharge after verifying current requirements, issues notices, and ensures funds and belongings are returned.
Leads transition planning, coordinates the receiving provider, documents the dates and completes the discharge summary.
Prepares health summary and medications for transfer.
Helps identify the new setting and coordinates services.
Support the person during the move and protect belongings.

documentation: Record of the individual's request or the team's reasons
Documentation of alternatives tried and the Executive Director's verification of current requirements
Written notice (if involuntary) and grievance records
Transition planning meeting notes
Health summary and medication release record
Signed belongings inventory and funds accounting/receipt
Dates of transfer or discharge in the individual's record
Discharge summary and follow-up note

policies.title: Medication Administration, Self-Medication and Staff Competency
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, supervisors, nurses and designees who assist with or supervise medication; all individuals served in community residences and supervised apartments
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual receives medication safely, as prescribed, and with the greatest independence the planning team supports. To make sure only staff who are trained and have shown competency assist with or supervise medication.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows written procedures for medication administration and self-medication. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)17 (Written procedures for medication administration, including procedures for self-medication). Individuals self-administer medication to the extent possible. The planning team determines the extent, and the decision is documented in the individual's record and carried out under this policy (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(a)). If an individual cannot self-administer, [AGENCY NAME] or its trained designee assists with and supervises administration exactly as prescribed (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(b)). No staff member gives or assists with any medication until the staff member has completed medication training and demonstrated competency. Competency is demonstrated again every year (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(b)). A record is kept of all medication administered, showing at least the individual's name, the date and the medication name (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(c)). Medication is given only on the order of an authorized prescriber, including an Advanced Practice Nurse where permitted by the 2023 amendment to the rule. The procedures in this policy are designed around normalization, least restriction and person-centered planning, and are reviewed at least annually (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(a)).

definitions.definition: The individual takes or applies their own medication, with only the level of prompting or oversight the planning team has documented.
Trained staff help the individual take medication as prescribed and observe and record that it was taken.
Medication given as needed, only under the conditions stated on the prescriber's order and pharmacy label.
Documented demonstration, observed by a qualified trainer, that a staff member can perform medication tasks correctly and safely.
The record of every medication given or taken, including the individual's name, the date and the medication name.
A staff member named by [AGENCY NAME] who has completed medication training and shown current competency.

procedures: 1. Before admission and at each annual planning meeting, the Nurse Consultant or Program Director gathers the individual's current medication list, prescriber orders, allergies and pharmacy information. These are placed in the individual's record.

2. The planning team decides how much the individual can self-administer, based on the individual's skills, preferences and risks. The decision is written in the record as 'independent,' 'prompts/supervision' or 'staff assists.' It is reviewed at least annually and whenever the individual's condition changes.

3. For individuals who self-administer, staff teach skills at the level the team set, respect the individual's choices, and document observations. They report any missed doses, confusion or unsafe practices to the Program Director and nurse the same day.

4. Medication is stored in a locked, clean location with temperature and access appropriate to the product. Individuals who self-administer have a secure place of their own that matches their plan. The House Manager checks storage weekly.

5. Before assisting with any medication, a staff member must complete medication training and pass a competency demonstration with a qualified trainer. The Training Coordinator records the date and the trainer's and trainee's signatures. The Program Director authorizes the staff member in writing as a medication designee.

6. Each year before the anniversary of the last competency date, the staff member repeats the competency demonstration. A staff member whose competency has lapsed is removed from medication duties until it is renewed. Another trained staff member covers that duty.

7. Staff accept only medications with a current prescriber order and a pharmacy label. Orders may be written by an authorized prescriber, including an Advanced Practice Nurse. Staff do not change, crush, split or stop medication unless the order or pharmacist says it is allowed.

8. At each dose, the trained staff member checks the individual's name, medication, dose, route, time and allergies against the label and MAR. They offer the dose, watch it being taken, and immediately record the individual's name, date, medication and staff initials on the MAR.

9. For PRN medication, staff confirm that the label and order show the individual's name, date, medication, dosage, interval, the maximum amount in 24 hours, a stop date where appropriate, and the conditions for giving it. If any element is missing, staff do not give the medication. They call the nurse or prescriber for a clarified order.

10. Before giving a PRN dose, staff document the reason, the time, the amount and the check against the 24-hour maximum. After giving it, staff document the effect. They notify the nurse or prescriber if the PRN is used more often than expected.
11. If an individual refuses a medication, staff do not force it. They document the refusal, notify the nurse or on-call supervisor the same day, and follow the prescriber's direction.

12. A medication error includes a wrong medication, dose, time, route or individual, and an omitted dose. When one occurs, the staff member immediately makes sure the individual is safe, calls the nurse or prescriber for direction, and calls 9-1-1 if there is a life-threatening reaction (HW-04). The staff member writes an incident report before the end of the shift and tells the Program Director. The Program Director decides whether the event is a reportable unusual incident (BEH-04).

13. Over-the-counter products, vitamins and herbal products are given only on a prescriber's or nurse's written order or approval. They are recorded on the MAR the same way as prescription medication.

14. At each shift change, staff count controlled medications with the outgoing staff member and sign the count record. Any discrepancy is reported to the Program Director immediately and handled as a possible incident under BEH-04.

15. Medications that are discontinued, expired or no longer needed are returned or disposed of as the pharmacist or nurse directs. Two staff members record the disposal, with date, medication, amount and signatures.

16. The Nurse Consultant or Program Director reviews MARs, PRN use, refusals and errors at least monthly and compares them with orders. Trends and corrective actions are reported to Quality Improvement (GOV-05).
17. When an individual moves, goes on leave or is discharged, the Program Director makes sure current medications, orders and a copy of the MAR are sent with the individual (PCS-05).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, authorizes designees, resolves compliance gaps, reviews errors and decides on incident reporting.
Reviews orders and MARs, answers medication questions, teaches the staff and supports the planning team's self-medication assessments.
Schedules medication training, arranges a qualified trainer for competency demonstrations and keeps certificates and signatures.
Give or supervise medication only when trained and competent; record each dose accurately; report refusals and errors immediately.
Decides the individual's level of self-administration and documents it in the record.
Take part in decisions about medication and tell staff about any concerns or side effects.

documentation: Planning team decision on self-administration in the individual's record
Current prescriber orders and medication list in the record
Medication Administration Record (name, date, medication, staff initials)
PRN documentation: reason, dose, time and effect
Medication training certificates and annual competency records with trainer and trainee signatures, kept in the administrative office
Controlled medication count sheets and disposal records
Medication error and incident reports
Monthly medication review notes

policies.title: Nursing Oversight and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: Program Director, nurse consultant, house managers, direct support professionals, and contracted health professionals
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's health care needs are identified, that nursing judgment is used where it is needed, and that appointments, follow-up and health records are coordinated with the individual's physicians.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes sure each individual receives general health care, and coordinates it with the individual's physicians and other health professionals. Tasks that need nursing judgment are done only by, or delegated through, a licensed nurse. Feeding-tube duties are delegated to nursing and are not performed by direct support professionals on their own (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a licensed nurse available as a consultant for staff and planning teams. Rule 10:44A is not understood to require a nurse for every residence, so this is a recommended practice that [AGENCY NAME] has adopted. The Program Director confirms current expectations with the NJ DHS Office of Licensing. [AGENCY NAME] verifies the professional credentials of any employed or contracted professional before that person provides services (STF-10). Medication is managed under HW-01 and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2.

definitions.definition: A New Jersey licensed nurse, employed or contracted by [AGENCY NAME], who advises on health care and oversees nursing tasks.
A licensed nurse's written assignment of a specific task to a trained staff member, with teaching, return demonstration and supervision.
Scheduling, preparing for and following up on medical, dental, vision and specialist care, and making sure information is shared with the people responsible for care.

procedures: 1. At admission, the Program Director collects the individual's health history, diagnoses, allergies, physician names, insurance cards and any health care directives. These are placed in the record (REC-01).

2. The Nurse Consultant reviews each new individual's health information within [NUMBER] days of admission. The review identifies health risks, needed monitoring, diets, equipment and any tasks that require nursing (HW-03, ENV-05).
3. The Program Director keeps the Nurse Consultant's current contact details and license number on file, and posts the contact number where staff can see it [PHONE].

4. The Program Director verifies the license and credentials of each nurse or other health professional before they begin work, and again at each renewal date. The verification date and the source used are recorded in the personnel or contract file.

5. Feeding-tube care and any other task that needs nursing judgment is performed only by the nurse or by staff to whom the nurse has delegated it in writing. The nurse documents the teaching, the staff member's return demonstration and the date of the next review. Staff who have not been delegated the task do not perform it.

6. The House Manager keeps a health calendar for each individual listing routine physicals, dental visits, vision and hearing checks, screenings, immunizations and specialist visits. The planning team and the individual set the schedule with the nurse.

7. Before each appointment, staff prepare a short written summary of current concerns, changes since the last visit and the current medication list. The staff member who goes with the individual brings it along.

8. After each appointment, the staff member records the findings, new or changed orders, and follow-up instructions on the appointment form, and gives it to the House Manager that day. The House Manager makes sure new orders reach the pharmacy, the MAR and the Nurse Consultant within 24 hours.
9. When the individual's condition changes, staff follow HW-04. The Nurse Consultant helps with follow-up and updates the care plan.

10. The Nurse Consultant reviews at least quarterly each individual's health records, MAR, health monitoring logs and appointments. Written findings go to the Program Director. Any needed corrections are assigned to a named person with a due date.

11. The Program Director makes sure health care information is shared with the guardian and involved family as the individual consents and the law allows (IR-04, IR-10). Information shared with outside providers is limited to what is needed.
12. The Nurse Consultant gives staff in-service training at least annually on topics identified through quality improvement or health trends. Attendance is recorded (STF-04).
13. The Program Director includes health-related findings, such as missed appointments, medication errors and hospitalizations, in the quality improvement review (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure nursing support is in place, verifies credentials and keeps the health coordination system working.
Assesses health needs, delegates and supervises nursing tasks, reviews records and trains staff.
Keeps health calendars, arranges appointments, makes sure orders are carried out and records are current.
Go with individuals to appointments as assigned, report health changes and carry out only the tasks they are trained and authorized to do.
Sets health goals and preferences with the individual.

documentation: Nurse Consultant agreement or job description, with license verification
Credential verification record for each health professional
Individual health history and annual health review
Written nursing delegation records for each delegated task, with teaching and return demonstration
Health care calendars and appointment summaries
Quarterly health record reviews
In-service attendance records

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, house managers, the nurse consultant and the Program Director
policies.purpose: To identify and monitor health risks, especially seizures and choking, so that staff respond quickly and consistently, and so that individuals have risk plans that fit their needs.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] monitors each individual's health and keeps a written risk plan in the record for every individual with a seizure disorder or a choking or swallowing risk. Each direct support professional completes specialized training within 90 days of employment in feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure and physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)). [AGENCY NAME] schedules staff so that at least one person on every shift has each specialized training that the individuals present on that shift require. Risk plans are written to be as least restrictive as safety allows and respect the individual's preferences. The Program Director verifies the current health care and over-the-counter medication requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A, subchapter 5, from the current rule text at each annual policy review.

definitions.definition: A written plan describing the individual's seizure types, triggers, warning signs, first aid steps, when to call 9-1-1, and what to record and report.
A written plan describing the individual's swallowing needs, food textures and liquid consistency, positioning, supervision level and emergency response.
Training in the topics required in the first 90 days of employment by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d).
Regular observation and recording of an individual's health, such as weight, vital signs, intake, bowel function, skin and seizure activity, as ordered or set by the nurse.

procedures: 1. At admission and at each annual review, the Nurse Consultant assesses each individual for seizure, choking and swallowing risk, falls, skin breakdown, dehydration and other medical needs. Physician records and the individual's own report are used.

2. For each individual with a seizure disorder or a choking risk, the Nurse Consultant writes a risk plan within [NUMBER] days of admission. The plan is reviewed with the individual, the guardian and the physician, and is filed in the record.

3. Each seizure risk plan includes seizure types, triggers, a step-by-step response, how long a seizure may last before 9-1-1 is called, what rescue medication is ordered and who may give it, and recovery care. It also includes how and when to notify the nurse and guardian.

4. Each choking risk plan includes the diet texture and liquid consistency ordered, how the person is positioned and paced during meals, the supervision level, the equipment, and the emergency response. It must be consistent with the diet order in ENV-05.

5. The Program Director gives each staff member the risk plans for the individuals they support before the staff member works alone with those individuals. The staff member signs that they read the plans and had a chance to ask questions.

6. Within 90 days of hire, the Training Coordinator makes sure each direct support professional completes the specialized training in feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure and physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans. Training certificates are filed (STF-04).

7. The shift scheduler checks each schedule before it is posted. Each shift must have at least one person with each specialized training that the individuals on that shift need. If the shift lacks one, the scheduler fixes it before the shift starts and informs the Program Director.

8. Staff record seizure activity on the seizure log. For each seizure they note the date, start time, duration, description, what happened before and after, interventions, and who was notified. The Nurse Consultant reviews the log at least monthly.

9. In a seizure emergency or choking emergency that meets the criteria in the risk plan, staff call 9-1-1 first and then follow HW-04. They start first aid steps for which they are trained while waiting.

10. Staff carry out health monitoring as ordered, such as weights, vital signs and intake. They record results in the same shift, and report out-of-range results to the nurse or on-call supervisor right away.

11. After any seizure that is new, unusually long or follows a change in pattern, and after any choking episode, the staff on duty notify the nurse and Program Director the same day. The Program Director decides if the event is a reportable incident (BEH-04). The nurse updates the risk plan if needed.
12. The Nurse Consultant updates the risk plans after any hospital stay, medication change or change in swallowing, and at least annually. The Program Director retrains staff on changes.
13. Each month the Program Director reviews seizure, choking and health-monitoring data for patterns and reports them to Quality Improvement (GOV-05).
