policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care (Danielle's Law)
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contracted workers who work in or with the residence
policies.purpose: To make sure a change in an individual's condition is noticed and acted on promptly, and that every life-threatening emergency gets an immediate 9-1-1 call.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)6 (A procedure for handling medical emergencies that includes the requirement to call 9-1-1 in the event of a life-threatening emergency, in accordance with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-5.1 et seq. (Danielle's Law), and N.J.A.C. 10:42A). Any staff member who believes an individual is experiencing a life-threatening emergency calls 9-1-1 immediately, before calling a supervisor, nurse or anyone else. Staff do not wait for permission. This policy also meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)7 (Training in life-threatening emergencies through a curriculum developed by the Division). Training in life-threatening emergencies is included in new employee orientation (STF-03) using the Division curriculum. Within 90 days of employment each direct support professional completes first aid and CPR from an ECC-compliant provider, and the certificate is kept on file (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a)). Each residence keeps a first aid kit that includes a CPR mask and protective gloves, as stated in the DHS 2023 webinar on N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.1(g). Staff who fail to follow Danielle's Law face disciplinary action by [AGENCY NAME] and may face penalties under the statute. Reportable incidents are reported to the state under BEH-04.

definitions.definition: A situation in which a reasonable person would believe the individual's life is in immediate danger, such as not breathing, no pulse, choking, severe bleeding, unresponsiveness, a prolonged seizure, or signs of stroke or heart attack.
Any noticeable change in an individual's physical, mental or behavioral state, such as new pain, fever, appetite change, confusion, fall, injury or loss of skills.
N.J.S.A. 30:6D-5.1 et seq., which requires staff of community residences to call 9-1-1 first for a life-threatening emergency.
First aid and CPR training that meets Emergency Cardiovascular Care guidelines.

procedures: 1. Staff who see signs of a life-threatening emergency call 9-1-1 right away. They give the address, the individual's condition and what has been done. They stay on the line until told to hang up.

2. While waiting for emergency responders, staff give the first aid and CPR for which they are trained, use the first aid kit and CPR mask, and keep the individual safe and comfortable. A second staff member, if available, unlocks the door and meets the ambulance.

3. Only after 9-1-1 is called, staff notify the on-call supervisor [PHONE], and then the nurse, guardian and family. They give the on-call supervisor the time of the call, the individual's condition and the hospital destination.

4. A staff member goes with the individual to the hospital, or follows as soon as another staff member can cover the residence (STF-09). Staff bring the face sheet, medication list, insurance cards, guardian contact details and the individual's communication information.

5. For a change in condition that is not life-threatening, staff record what they saw, take vital signs if trained and ordered, and call the nurse or on-call supervisor right away for direction. If staff are unsure, they call 9-1-1.
6. The nurse or on-call supervisor decides whether the individual needs the doctor, urgent care or emergency care and tells staff what to do. Staff document the instructions and follow them.
7. Staff add the change in condition to the communication log (REC-03). They tell the next shift in person at shift change.
8. The Program Director notifies the guardian of any hospital visit, injury or serious change in condition on the same day. The notice is recorded in the record.

9. Before the end of the shift, the staff member writes an incident report with the facts. The Program Director decides within the time set by DDD whether the event is a reportable unusual incident and reports it as required under BEH-04. If there is any question about whether it must be reported, the Program Director reports it.

10. The Training Coordinator makes sure the life-threatening emergency training from the Division curriculum is part of every new employee's orientation. Completion is recorded on the New Employee Orientation Checklist (STF-03).

11. The Training Coordinator tracks each direct support professional's first aid and CPR certification. Any staff member who has no valid certificate within 90 days of hire is not scheduled alone on a shift until certified. Certificates are filed in the administrative office.

12. The House Manager checks the first aid kit in each residence and vehicle monthly. Each kit must have a CPR mask and protective gloves, and used or expired items are replaced within 3 days. The checks are logged.
13. After each emergency, the Program Director leads a debrief within [NUMBER] days to review the response, the 9-1-1 call time and any gaps. Findings go to Quality Improvement (GOV-05).
14. All new staff sign that they have read this policy and understand that they must call 9-1-1 first in a life-threatening emergency. The signed form is kept in the personnel record.

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, the nurse consultant and the executive director
policies.purpose: To make sure that when an individual dies, the individual is treated with dignity, emergency care is provided as required, family and authorities are notified, belongings are protected, and the death is reviewed to improve care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats the death of an individual as a reportable unusual incident under BEH-04 and the unusual incident procedure required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b). The Program Director confirms the current DDD reporting timelines and reporting method at each annual policy review. Staff who find an individual without signs of life call 9-1-1 first, as required by Danielle's Law (HW-04), unless a valid physician-signed do-not-resuscitate order or other valid order applies and is on file. The guardian and family are told promptly and with compassion. The individual's belongings and funds are secured and accounted for. The death is reviewed internally and the findings are sent to Quality Improvement (GOV-05). Subchapter 5 (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.1 to 5.8) is checked for any additional health and safety requirements at each annual review.

definitions.definition: A structured internal review of the circumstances of a death, the care provided and any lessons that could improve safety.
A valid physician-signed order, kept in the record and followed according to New Jersey law, that says resuscitation is not to be attempted.
The person legally appointed to make decisions for the individual, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.

procedures: 1. A staff member who finds an individual who is unresponsive or not breathing calls 9-1-1 first, unless a valid DNR order applies. They follow HW-04, start CPR when trained and not prevented by a valid order, and stay with the individual.

2. If a valid DNR order applies, staff still call the on-call supervisor [PHONE] and the nurse immediately, who tell staff what to do. Staff do not move the individual unless emergency responders or the physician say so.
3. Staff cooperate with emergency responders, police and the medical examiner. They do not disturb the area, medications or records beyond what is needed for care, and they preserve evidence.

4. The on-call supervisor tells the Program Director and Executive Director immediately, and the Program Director notifies the guardian right away. The notification is made by phone or in person, not by text or email, and is recorded with the time and the person told.

5. The Program Director reports the death to DDD and the Office of Licensing and to any other required agency as an unusual incident under BEH-04, within the timelines in force. They confirm the timelines before reporting.

6. The Program Director arranges support for the housemates, who are told in an honest, age-appropriate and individualized way. The Program Director arranges counseling or chaplain support if they want it, and informs staff about grief support.

7. The Program Director secures the individual's room, belongings, valuables and funds. Two staff members make an inventory of belongings and sign it. The agency keeps personal funds and valuables until they are released to the legal representative (IR-05, IR-06).
8. The Program Director helps the guardian and family with funeral arrangements and respects the individual's known wishes, culture and faith.

9. Within [NUMBER] days of the death, the Program Director gathers the record, MAR, logs, incident reports, appointments and the medical examiner's or hospital's information. They then arrange a mortality review involving the Nurse Consultant and Executive Director.

10. The mortality review looks at the individual's health history, risks identified, care given, response to the emergency, timeliness of reporting, and any signs of abuse, neglect or other concern. If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected, the Program Director follows BEH-03 and BEH-05 at once.

11. The review team writes findings and recommended actions with a responsible person and due date. The report is given to Quality Improvement (GOV-05), and shared with DDD or the Office of Licensing as required.
12. The Program Director completes any billing and service closure steps (GOV-06, PCS-05). The agency keeps the individual's record for the required time (REC-01).
13. The Program Director offers staff debriefing and support, and follows up within [NUMBER] days to make sure recommended actions are done.

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, supervisors, clinicians, planning team members and the Program Director
policies.purpose: To support each individual with a positive, person-centered approach that prevents challenging behavior by meeting the person's needs, teaching skills, and using the least restrictive methods.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals using positive behavior support. This approach is based on normalization, age appropriateness, least restriction and person-centered planning (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(a)). A behavior support plan, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, is written only when the planning team finds it is needed, and is based on an understanding of why the behavior occurs. Plans emphasize prevention, skill building and the individual's preferences. They do not use punishment. Each direct support professional completes training in behavior support plans within 90 days of employment (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)). Any plan that limits an individual's rights must be reviewed by the Human Rights Committee and approved by the guardian where applicable (IR-02). It must also meet the HCBS settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c), including documented justification, informed consent and regular review. Restraint and seclusion are covered under BEH-02.

definitions.definition: As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, the written plan for an individual that describes strategies to teach skills and reduce challenging behavior.
A person-centered approach that changes the environment, teaches new skills and rewards desired behavior in place of punishment.
A review of what sets off, rewards and maintains a behavior, used to design the support plan.
The approach that places the fewest limits on a person's rights and freedom that can still keep the person and others safe.
The committee that reviews plans that restrict rights (IR-02).

procedures: 1. The planning team discusses the individual's communication, preferences, health, history and any behavior concerns at admission and at each annual plan review. They first look at whether health, pain, environment, routine or unmet needs are causing the behavior.

2. If the concern continues, the Program Director asks a qualified clinician [CLINICIAN / BEHAVIOR SPECIALIST] to complete a functional assessment. The assessment includes the individual's own view, where possible, and input from the guardian, family and staff.

3. The clinician writes a behavior support plan within [NUMBER] days. The plan includes target behaviors, likely causes, prevention strategies, skills to teach, how to respond, how progress will be measured and how the plan will be faded when possible.

4. The plan uses only positive and least restrictive methods. It does not allow physical punishment, humiliation, food or sleep deprivation, or the withholding of contact with family or personal items. If any strategy would limit a right, the Program Director follows IR-02 and BEH-02 before it is used.

5. The planning team, the guardian where applicable and the individual review the plan and give written consent. If the individual or guardian disagrees, the Program Director records the disagreement, tries to resolve it, and does not carry out the disputed part until it is resolved.
6. The Human Rights Committee reviews any plan that restricts rights before it is carried out, and at the interval it sets, as described in IR-02.

7. Within 90 days of hire, each direct support professional completes training on behavior support plans (HW-03, STF-04). Before working with an individual who has a plan, the staff member reads the plan, signs that they understand it, and receives hands-on coaching from the clinician or Program Director.
8. Staff collect data on the target behaviors, the antecedents, the response and the outcome as the plan says. They record data on each shift, and the House Manager checks completeness weekly.

9. The clinician reviews the data at least monthly, meets with the team, and changes the plan when it is not working or the behavior has decreased. The clinician writes the review and updates the plan or ends it when it is no longer needed.
10. The behavior support plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever the individual's needs change, as part of the plan meeting (PCS-02).
11. If an unplanned crisis occurs, staff use the crisis steps in the plan and follow BEH-02 for any restrictive measure. Staff report the incident under BEH-04 when it meets the criteria.
12. Staff give the individual feedback and support after a crisis, and the House Manager conducts a debrief with the staff that shift to learn what could help prevent a repeat.
13. The Program Director reports summary data on behavior incidents, plan use and restrictions to Quality Improvement every quarter (GOV-05).

Completes functional assessments, writes and reviews plans, trains and coaches staff.
Use positive strategies, follow plans exactly and collect accurate data.
Reviews the individual's needs, approves plans and monitors progress.
Reviews any plan that restricts rights.
Take part in developing the plan and give consent.

Human Rights Committee review record

Quarterly summary for Quality Improvement

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted staff, temporary agency staff and volunteers in every community residence, supervised apartment and supportive living setting operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect each individual's dignity, safety and rights by prohibiting seclusion and any punitive or convenience use of restraint or restriction, by limiting emergency physical intervention to a last resort, and by ensuring that every restrictive measure is reviewed by the Human Rights Committee and reported.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals through positive, person-centered approaches (see BEH-01). Services recognize that individuals have the same rights as other citizens, and exercising rights is never a cause for retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a)). Seclusion is prohibited. Restraint and restrictive interventions are never used as punishment, for staff convenience, as a substitute for adequate staffing or programming, or in place of a behavior support plan. A physical hold is permitted only as an emergency measure to prevent imminent serious harm to the individual or others, when less restrictive responses have failed or cannot work in time. It is used by trained staff, for the shortest time possible, and in a way that follows the current restraint and behavioral support provisions of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5 (Health and Safety, 10:44A-5.1 to 5.8) and current Division requirements. Mechanical restraint, chemical restraint (medication used to control behavior rather than treat a diagnosed condition), and any technique that restricts breathing, uses pain, or places a person face down are prohibited as agency policy. Any planned restriction of a right, such as locked access, restricted items or supervised-only access, is a rights modification. It must meet the supported-need conditions of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F) and be reviewed by the Human Rights Committee required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(e) and N.J.A.C. 10:41A. Every use of restraint is an unusual incident and is reported under BEH-04. Rights are not limited because an individual has a guardian or family (3.1(d)). House rules may not be used as a restraint or restriction (3.1(e)).

definitions.definition: Any manual, physical or mechanical method, or any medication used for behavior control, that restricts an individual's freedom of movement or normal access to their body.
A brief physical hold used only when an individual's behavior creates imminent risk of serious harm and less restrictive responses have failed or cannot work in time.
Involuntary confinement of an individual alone in a room or area from which the individual is physically prevented from leaving. Prohibited by this policy.
A planned limit on an individual's rights or freedoms (for example, locked access to food, money or exits) that must be supported by an assessed need and documented in the IHP.
A written plan, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, that describes positive strategies and responses to an individual's challenging behavior and is part of the service plan.
The committee used by the licensee under N.J.A.C. 10:41A to review restrictions and protect individual rights.

procedures: The Program Director reviews the current restraint and behavioral support provisions of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5, and any DDD or Office of Licensing guidance on restraint, at least annually and whenever the rules change. The Program Director records the review and updates this policy under GOV-04.

Staff first use the individual's behavior support plan and positive strategies (BEH-01): change the environment, offer choices, redirect, give space, and use calm communication. Staff document the strategies tried.

Seclusion is never used. Locking an individual in a room, or blocking a door so the individual cannot leave, is seclusion. Staff who see or hear of it must stop it immediately and report it under BEH-03.

An emergency physical intervention may begin only when staff reasonably believe serious harm to the individual or another person is imminent and less restrictive responses have failed or cannot work in time. Only staff with current training in [APPROVED CRISIS INTERVENTION CURRICULUM] and in the individual's behavior support plan (completed within 90 days of hire under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)) may apply a hold. Other staff stay with the remaining individuals and call for help.

Staff must never use a prone (face-down) hold, pressure on the neck, chest or back, restriction of breathing, pain compliance, mechanical devices, or medication to control behavior. If an individual's own prescribed protocol calls for a protective or medical device, it is handled through nursing orders and the IHP, not through this policy.

During any hold, one staff member continuously watches the individual's breathing, color, speech and signs of distress. If the individual shows any sign of medical distress, staff stop the hold and call 9-1-1 under HW-04.
Staff release the hold as soon as the imminent danger has passed. They never continue a hold to gain compliance, and they never use a hold to move a person who is not endangering anyone.

Staff call the on-call administrator ([PHONE]) during or immediately after any emergency physical intervention under STF-09. If the individual is injured or in distress, a registered nurse assesses the individual (HW-02) or the individual receives emergency care.

Before the end of the shift, the in-charge staff member completes the Restraint/Restrictive Intervention Report: individual, date and time, antecedents, strategies tried, technique, start and stop times, staff and witnesses, injuries, medical check, and who was notified.

The in-charge staff member completes the unusual incident report and notifies the guardian under BEH-04 within that policy's timelines. If there is any sign the hold was improper or injurious, or any allegation of abuse, staff also follow BEH-03 and BEH-05.

Within one business day, the Program Director reviews the report, speaks with the individual (offering a supportive debrief with a person the individual trusts) and debriefs the staff involved. The Program Director also decides whether retraining, plan changes or an investigation is needed.

After any restraint, the individual's planning team meets within [7] days to review the behavior support plan, look for triggers and unmet needs, and consider changes. Any change is recorded as an addendum to the IHP under PCS-02.

A planned restrictive measure is never started without the following in the IHP: the specific assessed need; positive interventions already tried; less intrusive methods tried and why they failed; a description of the condition proportionate to the need; data collection to show effectiveness; time limits with scheduled review dates; informed consent of the individual and guardian (IR-08); and an assurance the measure will cause no harm (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F)).

The Program Director submits each proposed rights modification and each restraint report to the Human Rights Committee under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(e) and N.J.A.C. 10:41A, following IR-02. The measure is not started until HRC review is complete, except for the emergency actions in steps 4 to 8, which the HRC reviews afterward.

The Program Director reports restraint data to the QI Committee at least quarterly (GOV-05): number of events by individual, staff, shift, location and duration, injuries, and trends. The data are used to reduce restraint use.

Training: all staff are trained on this policy during orientation (STF-03) and annually. Training includes alternatives to restraint, de-escalation, recognition of trauma, and the prohibition on seclusion. Training records are kept under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(e) and STF-04.

Staff who use restraint or seclusion outside this policy are removed from direct contact pending investigation and are subject to discipline up to termination. Staff who report such conduct in good faith are protected from retaliation (BEH-03).
The Program Director reviews each restrictive measure at least [quarterly]. Measures that are no longer needed are ended, and the end is documented.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt this policy, ensure resources for positive supports and training, and review restraint data at least annually.
Review rule changes annually, review every restraint report within one business day, convene planning team reviews, submit items to the HRC, and report data to QI.
Assess any individual after an emergency physical intervention and advise on medical risk.
Review proposed rights modifications and restraint events and make recommendations to the licensee.
Use positive strategies first, use holds only as in this policy, monitor the individual, document, and report before the end of the shift.
Review behavior support plans and restrictions after each event and on a set schedule.

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted staff, temporary agency staff, volunteers, governing body members and visitors at every [AGENCY NAME] residence
policies.purpose: To state in writing that abuse, neglect and exploitation are prohibited, to state the obligation to report every allegation, and to describe how [AGENCY NAME] prevents these harms and responds to them.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8.i, 2.2(b)8.ii and 2.6(a)2. (1) Prohibition (2.2(b)8.i): Abuse, neglect and exploitation of any individual served by [AGENCY NAME] are expressly prohibited. This includes physical, verbal, sexual, emotional or psychological abuse; neglect, including failure to provide needed supervision, care or medical attention; and exploitation, including misuse of an individual's money, property or labor. Falsification of records is also prohibited. These terms are used as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. Violation results in disciplinary action up to termination and referral to authorities. (2) Obligation to report each allegation (2.2(b)8.ii): Every employee, volunteer and contractor must report every allegation, suspicion or observation of abuse, neglect or exploitation, as required by N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10 and N.J.S.A. 52:27G-1 et seq. and Department policy. The rule text prints the first statute as '9:68.10'; [AGENCY NAME] applies it as N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10 and the Program Director verifies the citation against the current statute. No one may decide that an allegation is unfounded before reporting it, and no one may pressure another person not to report. (3) Prevention and orientation (2.6(a)2): The prevention of abuse, neglect and exploitation is covered in every new employee's orientation and in the Division basic training on preventing abuse and neglect that must be completed within 90 days of hire under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a). Exercising rights or making a report is never a cause for retaliation.

definitions.definition: As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: willful or harmful physical, verbal, sexual or emotional mistreatment of an individual, including any act that causes or is likely to cause physical or psychological harm.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, medical attention, food, shelter or protection an individual needs, whether by action or inaction.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: taking unfair advantage of an individual, including misuse of the individual's funds, property, benefits or labor for the benefit of another.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: knowingly making false entries in or altering records or documents.
The registry of persons found to have abused, neglected or exploited individuals with developmental disabilities, checked under STF-02.

Any report, observation, complaint or reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or exploitation, whether made by the individual, staff, family, a guardian or anyone else, and whether or not it can be confirmed.

procedures: The governing body adopts the written prohibition and reporting obligation above. The Program Director posts a one-page summary of both in each residence and in the administrative office, in plain language and in formats the individuals can understand (IR-09).

Before an employee has unsupervised contact with individuals, the employee completes the Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry checks and background checks (STF-02) and signs the Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Statement acknowledging the prohibition and the duty to report.

During orientation (STF-03), the trainer covers recognizing signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, the prohibition, the duty to report every allegation, and how to report. The trainee and trainer sign and date the orientation checklist (2.6(a)2).

Each direct support professional completes the Division basic training on preventing abuse and neglect within 90 days of employment, and a valid certificate is placed in the training file (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a), (e)). All staff review this policy annually.

Individuals are taught, in a way they understand, what abuse, neglect and exploitation are, that they will not be punished for telling, and whom to tell (IR-01). The individual's guardian and family receive the same information on admission (PCS-01).
If an individual is in immediate danger or needs emergency care, staff first call 9-1-1, protect the individual, and separate the individual from the alleged abuser (HW-04).

Any staff member who sees, hears or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation reports it immediately, by phone, to the Program Director or, if unavailable, the on-call administrator ([PHONE]) (STF-09). Staff do not wait until the end of a shift and do not investigate on their own.

Staff do not need the Program Director's permission to make an external report. Any person may report directly. The Program Director or designee makes the required external reports at the same time or immediately after the internal report. Reports go to the DHS/DDD abuse reporting line (DDD's published issues number is 800-832-9173; the Program Director confirms the current abuse reporting number with DHS at least annually and posts it) and, when the person involved is a child, to the NJ Department of Children and Families State Central Registry (1-877-NJ ABUSE). Law enforcement is called for suspected crimes. Reporting continues in line with BEH-04 and REC-02.
If the Program Director is the person accused, the report is made directly to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and to the external authorities.
The Program Director notifies the individual's guardian and family as permitted by the individual's rights and the investigating authority's instructions, and records the notice.

The Program Director starts the investigation process in BEH-05 and puts protective measures in place immediately. Accused staff or volunteers are removed from contact with the individual and others pending the outcome.
The individual receives medical care, a nursing assessment (HW-02), and offers of emotional support and counseling. The individual's right to make a report outside the agency is explained.
The report, the actions taken and the outcome are recorded on the unusual incident report (BEH-04) and in the critical information log (REC-03). Confidentiality is protected (IR-04).

No one is retaliated against for reporting. Retaliation, pressuring a person not to report, or falsification of a report is itself grounds for termination. Staff may also report concerns to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the governing body.
The QI Committee reviews allegations, substantiation rates, timeliness of reports and prevention actions at least quarterly (GOV-05).
The Program Director reviews this policy annually for any change in the statutes, the hotline numbers or Department policy and updates it under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt the written prohibition and reporting obligation, protect reporters from retaliation, and review allegation data.
Make or confirm required external reports, put protective measures in place, start investigations, post the current reporting number, and ensure training.
Never abuse, neglect or exploit; report every allegation immediately; cooperate with investigators.
Cover prevention in orientation and arrange the 90-day basic training with certificates on file.
Assess individuals after an allegation and document findings.

policies.title: Reportable Unusual Incidents
policies.applies_to: All staff at every [AGENCY NAME] residence; Program Director and administrators responsible for reviewing and reporting incidents
policies.purpose: To make sure every unusual incident is identified, responded to, reported to the right people on time, recorded, and reviewed so that individuals are protected and future incidents are prevented.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8 (a procedure for reporting all unusual incidents, including, but not limited to, abuse, neglect and exploitation) and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)3 (unusual incident reporting and investigating procedures covered in orientation). [AGENCY NAME] reports every unusual incident internally, immediately, and externally within the timeframes in the current DDD and Office of Licensing incident reporting requirements. Allegations of abuse, neglect and exploitation are always reportable and follow BEH-03. The Program Director keeps a quick-reference chart of the current DDD incident categories and reporting timelines in each residence and updates it whenever DDD issues revised requirements. Reporting is never delayed to gather more information. Incidents are recorded in the incident log and in the critical information log (REC-03) and are analyzed in the QI system (GOV-05).

definitions.definition: An event that affects or may affect the health, safety, rights or well-being of an individual, or the operation of the residence, and that is outside normal routine.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: information that staff on the next shift or on call need to know in order to keep individuals safe.
The employee designated on the staff schedule as responsible for the shift (STF-01).
The chronological record of all unusual incidents at a residence.

procedures: Staff are trained on this policy during orientation (2.6(a)3) and annually. They receive a copy of the incident category chart.
The in-charge employee first makes the individual and others safe, gets medical care if needed (calling 9-1-1 for life-threatening emergencies under HW-04), and stops any ongoing harm.

Incidents that are always reportable include: death (HW-05); allegations or suspicion of abuse, neglect or exploitation (BEH-03); missing person or elopement (BEH-06); any use of restraint or emergency physical intervention (BEH-02); injury needing treatment beyond first aid; emergency room visit, 9-1-1 call or hospital admission; serious medication error or refusal with risk (HW-01); suicide threat or attempt; police involvement or an individual's arrest; sexual incidents; theft or loss of an individual's funds or valuables (IR-05, IR-06); fire, evacuation or utility failure (ENV-02, ENV-03); vehicle accident (ENV-06); serious property damage; and other categories in the current DDD requirements.

The in-charge employee calls the Program Director immediately, and the on-call administrator ([PHONE]) after hours (STF-09). The employee does not wait until the end of the shift. If no one answers, the employee keeps calling the next person on the call list and records the attempts.

The Program Director or designee decides on external notifications. Verbal and written reports to DDD, the Office of Licensing, law enforcement or other authorities are made within the timelines in the current requirements, and the Program Director records the date, time, person contacted and any reference number.

The Program Director or designee notifies the individual's guardian and family as soon as possible, and no later than [the same day], unless the individual objects or an investigating authority advises otherwise. The notice is recorded.

Before the end of the shift, the employee who witnessed or discovered the incident completes the Unusual Incident Report with facts only: who, what, when, where, immediate actions, injuries, witnesses, notifications made, and the employee's signature and date. Opinions and blame are left out.
The in-charge employee records the incident in the incident log and adds an entry to the critical information log (REC-03) so the next shift is aware of any follow-up needed.

The Program Director reviews each report within one business day, confirms that notifications were made, assigns follow-up, and decides whether an investigation under BEH-05 is needed. Allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation always require an investigation.
The Program Director ensures follow-up care, such as a nurse assessment (HW-02), an appointment, a behavior support plan review (BEH-01) or a planning team meeting (PCS-02), and records completion.
If the Program Director is involved in the incident, the report goes to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
Incident reports are filed in a confidential incident file and a copy of the pertinent facts is placed in the individual's record (REC-01). Privacy is protected under IR-04.
Each month, the Program Director totals incidents by type, individual, location, time, shift and staff, and reports the totals to the QI Committee (GOV-05) at least quarterly.
The QI Committee reviews trends, identifies root causes, and approves corrective action. The Program Director verifies completion.
Incident records are available for inspection by the Office of Licensing (GOV-08). Required periodic reports to the State are prepared under REC-02.
The Program Director reviews the incident category chart at least annually and whenever DDD issues revised requirements and updates this policy under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Respond to and report every incident immediately and complete the report before the end of the shift.
Ensure safety, make immediate notifications, and update the incident log and critical information log.
Make or confirm external reports on time, review reports within one business day, assign follow-up, and report trends to QI.
Provide direction and make notifications after hours.

policies.title: Investigations
policies.applies_to: Program Director, investigators designated by [AGENCY NAME], and all staff who may be witnesses or subjects of an investigation
policies.purpose: To provide a fair, prompt and thorough procedure for investigating allegations of abuse, neglect and exploitation and other unusual incidents, protect the individual first, and ensure findings lead to corrective action.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)9 (a procedure for investigations). [AGENCY NAME] investigates every allegation of abuse, neglect or exploitation and every other unusual incident that raises a concern about the care, safety or rights of an individual. The individual's safety comes first: the individual is protected and the accused is separated from contact with the individual before the investigation begins. [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with the Department, DDD, law enforcement and the Department of Children and Families, and the agency's internal review does not replace or delay any external investigation. Investigators are impartial and have no conflict of interest. No one is retaliated against for reporting or participating in an investigation. Terms such as abuse, neglect, exploitation and falsification are used as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.

definitions.definition: A structured review that gathers facts through interviews, observation and record review to determine what happened and why.
Findings. Substantiated means the evidence shows the event occurred. Unsubstantiated means the evidence shows it did not. Inconclusive means the evidence is not sufficient to decide.
Actions taken at once to keep the individual safe, such as removal of the accused from contact, medical care and changes in supervision.
The person assigned by [AGENCY NAME] to conduct the internal investigation, who has been trained and has no conflict of interest.

procedures: The Program Director receives the unusual incident report (BEH-04) or allegation (BEH-03) and decides, within one business day or immediately for allegations, which incidents need an investigation. All allegations of abuse, neglect and exploitation are investigated.

The Program Director secures the individual's safety first: medical care, nurse assessment (HW-02), supervision changes, and removal of the accused staff member, volunteer or other person from contact with the individual and others pending the outcome. If a staff member is removed, this is neutral and not disciplinary until findings are made.

The Program Director or designee confirms that all required external reports were made (BEH-03, BEH-04) and asks the Department, DDD, law enforcement or DCF whether it will investigate and whether [AGENCY NAME] should hold its own interviews.

If an outside authority is investigating, [AGENCY NAME] does not interview witnesses or the accused in a way that interferes, unless the authority agrees. [AGENCY NAME] preserves evidence, provides records and staff schedules, and makes staff available.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] assigns a trained investigator who is not involved in the incident and does not supervise the accused. If the Program Director is involved, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or an outside investigator is assigned.

The investigator begins the investigation promptly, with a goal of starting within [24 hours] of the report and completing a written report within [10] business days, unless an external authority sets another timeline. Any extension is approved in writing by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] with the reason.
The investigator preserves evidence: incident reports, photographs, schedules, logs, medication records, video if any (IR-11), and personal items. The investigator keeps these in a secure file.

The investigator interviews the individual in a supportive manner and in the individual's communication mode, with a support person of the individual's choice if desired (IR-09). The investigator then interviews witnesses and the accused, takes notes, and does not promise confidentiality that cannot be kept.
The investigator reviews relevant records, including the individual's IHP, behavior support plan, incident history, training records and schedules, and the prior history of the accused.
The investigator writes a report with a summary of the allegation, steps taken, evidence reviewed, interview summaries, findings (substantiated, unsubstantiated or inconclusive), and recommendations.

The Program Director and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] review the report and decide on corrective action: discipline up to termination, retraining, supervision changes, plan changes, environmental changes, or referral to licensing boards or authorities. Substantiated findings against staff are reported to the Central Registry or other authority as required (STF-02, REC-02).
[AGENCY NAME] informs the individual and guardian of the outcome, to the extent permitted by law and the rights of others. The notification is documented.
The Program Director monitors the corrective action until complete and verifies the results. The individual is checked on regularly for [30] days after the investigation for new concerns.

Investigation files are kept confidential and separate from personnel and individual records, with a summary placed in the individual's record when appropriate (REC-01, IR-04). Records are retained as required in REC-01.
The QI Committee reviews investigation counts, timeliness, findings and corrective actions at least quarterly (GOV-05).
Investigation files are made available to the Office of Licensing during inspections (GOV-08).

responsibilities.duty: Assign investigators, approve extensions, review findings, and decide on serious corrective action.
Protect the individual, ensure external reports, support investigators, implement corrective action and notify guardians.
Be impartial, gather evidence, interview witnesses and write the report.
Cooperate fully, tell the truth, preserve evidence and keep information confidential.
Review investigation trends and the effectiveness of corrective actions.

Interview notes and witness statements
Evidence log and secured evidence
Protective measures record

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All staff at every [AGENCY NAME] residence, including temporary agency staff and the on-call administrator
policies.purpose: To protect individuals who leave a residence or supervised setting without staff knowledge or when it is unsafe, by planning for known risks, responding at once when someone is missing, and learning from each event.
policies.policy: A missing person is a serious emergency and an unusual incident reported under BEH-04. When an individual who needs supervision cannot be found, staff search the premises and immediately call 9-1-1 and notify the guardian. Elopement risk is assessed on admission and is addressed in each individual's IHP (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c)), which lists barriers and the supports, methods and responsible persons. The record contains a current photo and description of every individual. Individuals who are able to come and go independently under their IHP are not considered missing if they are within the limits, check-in plan and expected return time they and their team agreed to, because [AGENCY NAME] respects the right to freedom of movement (IR-01). Staff are on site whenever any individual is present, in line with supervision needs (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(d)), and an in-charge employee is designated for each shift (2.8(a)). That in-charge employee leads the response, and the remaining individuals are not left unsupervised. The procedure is part of the written procedure manual under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2.

definitions.definition: An individual who needs supervision or has a safety plan, and whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not where the IHP says he or she should be, or an individual who has not returned by the agreed time without explanation.
Leaving a residence, vehicle or program location without staff knowledge or permission, when the individual's plan requires supervision, and which may put the individual at risk.
A review of an individual's history, triggers, skills, medical and mobility needs, and community safety awareness, used to decide on supports.
A one-page form with a recent photo, physical description, medical needs, medications, communication method, likely locations, and contacts.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, the planning team completes an elopement risk assessment (PCS-01, PCS-02). The result, the supports needed, and the person responsible for each are written into the IHP.

The Program Director ensures every individual has a current Identification Sheet in the record and in a sealed, accessible place in the residence (updated at least [every six months] and after any change in appearance). The Sheet is shared with police when needed, with the individual's consent or as permitted by law (IR-04).

Supports for individuals at risk may include enhanced supervision, line-of-sight checks, door chimes, a check-in schedule, community safety training, and ID jewelry or a phone. Any restriction of freedom is approved as a rights modification under IR-02 and BEH-02. Locking an individual in a home is not allowed.
Staff review each individual's elopement plan and the Identification Sheet during orientation (STF-03) and whenever the plan changes. Staff on each shift know who is at risk (REC-03).

When an individual is not where expected, the staff member immediately tells the in-charge employee. The in-charge employee decides if the individual is missing: whether the person is outside the plan limits, overdue for the agreed return time, or at risk.

The in-charge employee organizes the response: one staff member checks the home, yard, vehicles and nearby areas immediately, while a second staff member prepares the Identification Sheet. Individuals remaining at the residence stay supervised at all times. If staffing is not enough to do both, the in-charge employee calls the on-call administrator ([PHONE]) (STF-09) for extra staff.

If the individual is not found right away, the in-charge employee calls 9-1-1 without delay, gives the description and last known location, and gives the Identification Sheet information. Staff do not wait for a set number of hours.
At the same time, a staff member calls the guardian and the Program Director or on-call administrator. If the guardian is not reachable, staff leave a message and keep trying and note each attempt.

Staff check likely locations from the IHP: work, day program, family, friends, favorite places and bus routes. Staff may drive a short search only if staffing allows, and do not leave other individuals alone.

Staff stay in contact with police and the on-call administrator until the person is found. They give police new information and keep a written timeline: last seen, time noticed, search actions, calls made, and results.

When the individual is found, the in-charge employee ensures safety, checks the individual for injuries, calls 9-1-1 for medical care if needed (HW-04), tells police and the guardian, and arranges for a nurse assessment (HW-02) within [24 hours]. The individual is treated respectfully and not punished.

The in-charge employee completes the Unusual Incident Report before the end of the shift and the Program Director makes external reports within required timeframes (BEH-04). The event is entered in the critical information log (REC-03).
If circumstances suggest neglect or abuse, such as inadequate supervision, the event is reported under BEH-03 and investigated under BEH-05.

Within [7] days, the planning team meets with the individual to talk about why the person left, any unmet needs or triggers, and what supports will help. The IHP and behavior support plan are updated with an addendum (PCS-02, BEH-01).
The Program Director reviews each missing person event, checks staffing and the staff schedule for the shift (2.8(a)), retrains staff if needed, and reports the event to the QI Committee (GOV-05).
The agency runs a missing person drill with staff at least [annually] at each residence and records results.

responsibilities.duty: Lead the search, call 9-1-1 and the guardian, keep other individuals supervised, and document the timeline.
Know each individual's risk and plan, report promptly, and follow the response steps.
Maintain Identification Sheets and risk assessments, make external reports, and review each event.
Provide extra staff and direction after hours (STF-09).
Assess risk, adjust the IHP and support the individual after any event.
Assess the individual after return.

Identification Sheet with photo
Missing person timeline
Unusual Incident Report and incident log entry
Critical information log entry
Guardian and police contact record
Post-event planning team notes and IHP addendum
Missing person drill records
Staff schedule showing in-charge employee for the shift

policies.title: Residential Environment, Siting and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] governing body, Program Director, maintenance staff and all staff at each community residence, supervised apartment and supportive living setting
policies.purpose: To make sure every residence is properly sited, lawfully approved, safe, accessible and homelike, and that required local and State approvals are obtained and kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates only in residences that meet the siting, size, safety and approval requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A. A community residence serves no more than 16 individuals, and a supervised apartment serves no more than 4 individuals per apartment (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3). A community residence is not located on the grounds of, or immediately adjacent to, a public institution serving a similar population (1.3). Before acquiring or leasing any housing, [AGENCY NAME] consults DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development, as the Office of Licensing requires. The agency keeps on file documentation of any required Fire Official inspection and registration with the Department of Community Affairs (DCA), and a certificate from the local enforcing authority or documentation that none is issued, as required in the Fire Safety and Physical Environment subchapter (10:44A-6.1 to 6.17). The Program Director confirms each requirement of that subchapter against the current text at least annually. Each residence is homelike, clean, in good repair, accessible to the individuals who live there under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the HCBS settings requirements (IR-01), and protects privacy and dignity.

definitions.definition: As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: a residence for up to 16 individuals with developmental disabilities, not on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution serving a similar population.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: an apartment serving up to 4 individuals, with staff support.
The municipal or county agency that issues the certificate of occupancy, certificate of continued occupancy or similar approval, or documents that none is issued.
Physical access and the ability of each individual to use the home safely, including adaptations such as ramps, grab bars, bathroom modifications and visual or auditory alerts.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3: permission to keep operating after a license expires when the inspection has been delayed.

procedures: Before looking at or committing to any property, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] contacts DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development, shares the proposed address, number of individuals and type of residence, and gets clearance as required. The contact is recorded.

The Program Director checks that the proposed site meets the siting and size requirements of 10:44A-1.3: maximum of 16 people per community residence, maximum of 4 per supervised apartment, and not on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution for people with similar needs. The result is written on the Site Review Form.

The Program Director checks zoning and obtains the local enforcing authority's certificate (certificate of occupancy or equivalent) or written documentation that none is issued. A copy is placed in the Residence File.

The Program Director obtains documentation of any required Fire Official inspection and registration with the Department of Community Affairs (DCA), and keeps copies in the Residence File and in the administrative office.

The Program Director reviews the Fire Safety and Physical Environment subchapter (10:44A-6.1 to 6.17) against the current text before opening a residence and annually, and records any items needing correction. Fire drill, evacuation, smoke detection and related requirements are carried out under ENV-02.

Before individuals move in, the Program Director completes an accessibility review with a nurse or therapist input as needed: entrances and exits, bedrooms and bathrooms, kitchen, common areas, and pathways. Needed modifications are listed with a completion date. The ADA and the access needs of the individuals living there guide decisions.

Individuals' bedrooms and living areas are set up to be homelike and to reflect their choices and belongings, with privacy protections and lockable doors where required by the HCBS settings rules, and visitors at times they choose, subject only to documented modifications approved under IR-02 (IR-01).

The Program Director or maintenance designee inspects every residence at least monthly (using the Environmental Checklist): cleanliness, repairs, safe floors and stairs, working lights, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, hot water temperature, locks, pest control, first aid kit (with CPR mask and protective gloves), and emergency numbers posted. Deficiencies are recorded with a date to fix them and a name responsible.

Urgent hazards are fixed or made safe immediately and the on-call administrator is called. If a hazard cannot be corrected promptly or the residence is not safe, staff follow ENV-02 or ENV-03 and the Program Director moves individuals to a safe place.

Repairs and requests from individuals about their home are recorded in a maintenance log. Individuals are asked at monthly house meetings if they have concerns or wishes about their living space, and results are documented.

For supervised apartment programs, the Program Director ensures the staff residence or office is located so staff can respond in a time that fits the supervision needs of the individuals (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(e)).

Insurance documents, local certificates, fire inspection and DCA registration documents, and the current license are kept current and readily available because the Office of Licensing reviews physical plant and insurance documents at annual and unannounced inspections (GOV-02, GOV-08).

Before any relocation, major renovation, change in number of individuals, or change in type of residence, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies the Office of Licensing and DDD, follows GOV-02, and obtains new approvals and clearances before the change.
The Program Director tracks expiration dates of certificates, registrations, inspections and the license on the Compliance Calendar and starts renewals at least [90] days before each date.
The Program Director reports environmental findings and completion of repairs to the QI Committee at least quarterly (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Approve sites, obtain DDD housing clearance, fund repairs and accessibility modifications, and maintain required approvals.
Check siting and approvals, complete monthly inspections, track certificates and renewals, and report to QI.
Complete repairs and routine maintenance and report hazards immediately.
Report hazards and repair needs, keep the home clean and safe, and respect individuals' space.
Are invited to choose how their rooms and common areas look and to raise concerns at house meetings.

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness, Evacuation Plan and Fire Drills
policies.applies_to: All community residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME], all direct support professionals and other employees, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect the lives and safety of individuals by ensuring each residence has a written, practiced plan for emergencies that require leaving the home, such as a fire or gas leak, and to ensure every employee knows how to carry it out.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written major emergency and evacuation plan for every residence and supervised apartment, and carries it out as written. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)5 (a procedure for implementing a plan to deal with major emergencies requiring evacuation from the residence, such as a fire or a gas leak). It also meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)4 (orientation on emergency procedures identified in the procedure manual: the emergency evacuation plan, emergency medical treatment, emergency coverage and on-call procedures, operation of the fire alarm system, and use of fire extinguishers). Each residence's plan is individualized to the building and to the mobility, sensory, communication and behavioral needs of the people living there. Fire safety and physical environment requirements in N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 6 (6.1 to 6.17) and the requirements of the local fire official and enforcing authority are followed. Evacuation drills are held at least monthly at each residence, and more often if subchapter 6 or the local fire official requires it. Drills are rotated across shifts and times of day, and the plan is reviewed after every drill and every real emergency. Emergencies that do not require evacuation, such as heat, cold or utility failure, are addressed in ENV-03. Life-threatening medical emergencies are addressed in HW-04.

definitions.definition: An event such as a fire, smoke, gas leak, carbon monoxide alarm, flood, structural damage or other hazard that makes it unsafe for individuals to remain in the residence.
A practice of the written evacuation plan in which all individuals and on-duty staff leave the residence to the designated assembly point, timed and recorded.
A safe, designated location outside the residence where everyone gathers and is counted after evacuation.
A pre-arranged safe place to take individuals if they cannot return to the residence after evacuation.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, an employee who provides direct support and supervision to individuals in the residence.

procedures: Before a residence opens, the Program Director writes a site-specific Emergency and Evacuation Plan. It includes a floor plan showing two exits from every sleeping area where the building allows, the evacuation routes, the assembly point, the location of fire alarm panels, extinguishers, the gas shut-off and the utility shut-offs, and the alternate shelter.

The Program Director obtains and files documentation of any required fire official inspection and registration, and the certificate from the local enforcing authority (or documentation that none is issued), as called for in N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 6.

The plan includes an individual evacuation profile for each person. It records mobility aids, need for physical assistance, sensory or communication needs, medications or equipment that must go with the person, and how to reduce distress. The profile is updated whenever the person's condition or Individual Habilitation Plan changes.

The plan names the staff role for each step: who calls 9-1-1, who assists which individual, who takes the individual profile sheets, medication list and emergency contact list, who takes the headcount, and who contacts the Administrator.

In an actual emergency, staff move everyone to safety first, call 9-1-1 from outside the building, take a headcount at the assembly point, and do not re-enter the building until the fire department or responding authority says it is safe.
In a gas leak or suspected carbon monoxide event, staff evacuate immediately, do not operate switches or phones inside, and call 9-1-1 and the gas utility from outside.

If individuals cannot return to the residence, the in-charge employee moves them to the alternate shelter. The in-charge employee also arranges for medications, adaptive equipment, food and staffing to go with them, and keeps continuous supervision.

The in-charge employee notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator notifies guardians and families, the DDD Community Services Office where required, and the Office of Licensing as required. The event is reported as a reportable unusual incident under BEH-04.

Smoke and fire alarm systems and fire extinguishers are tested and inspected on the schedule required by the fire official and N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 6. The Program Director keeps testing and inspection tags and records on file. Defects are corrected immediately, and staff are told whenever a system is out of service.

Evacuation drills are held at least monthly at each residence. They are rotated among shifts, including at least some overnight (sleeping-hours) drills, and across different exit routes. Individuals take part to the extent they are able, according to their evacuation profiles.

During each drill the in-charge employee records the date, time of day, shift, who took part, the time taken to evacuate, which exit was used and any problems. The record is signed and given to the Program Director within one business day.

The Program Director reviews each drill record within five business days. If the drill revealed a problem, the Program Director corrects it, for example by retraining staff, changing the route or revising an individual profile, and documents the correction.

New employees are trained on the evacuation plan, the operation of the fire alarm system, use of fire extinguishers, emergency medical treatment and emergency coverage and on-call procedures during orientation (STF-03), before working alone. This meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)4. Each new employee also takes part in a drill during the first month.
The evacuation plan is posted near the exits and in the staff area of each residence, in the format individuals can use, such as pictorial, large print or in another language.

The plan is reviewed at least annually as part of the annual procedure review (GOV-04). It is also reviewed after any real emergency, after any change to the building or its occupants, and when a fire official or surveyor makes a finding. The Compliance Officer checks the drill frequency and fire safety requirements against the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 6 at each annual review.
Drill results and emergency events are reported to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05) at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and ensures resources for alarm systems, extinguishers and inspections.
Writes and keeps current the site-specific plan; schedules and reviews drills; keeps inspection records; corrects deficiencies.
Directs evacuation, calls 9-1-1, takes the headcount, notifies the Administrator, and records drills.
Know and carry out the plan, assist individuals according to their profiles, and take part in drills.
Audits drill frequency and records; verifies the plan against current subchapter 6 requirements at each annual review.
Take part in drills to the extent of their ability and with the supports in their evacuation profiles.
