policies.title: Indoor Temperature and Utility Failure Emergencies (No-Evacuation)
policies.applies_to: All community residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME], all employees, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from harm when the home becomes too hot or too cold, or when heat, cooling, power, water or gas fails, in situations where an evacuation may not be required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] addresses emergencies where evacuation may not be required. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)5.i, which requires the major emergency procedure to cover situations such as an indoor air temperature below 68 degrees Fahrenheit or above 82 degrees Fahrenheit for four consecutive hours. Staff monitor and record indoor temperature during any heating, cooling or utility failure. Staff protect individuals using the alternate heating, cooling and relocation arrangements set out in this policy and in each residence's plan. Staff do not wait for four hours to act if any individual shows signs of heat or cold stress. An event that meets the criteria in BEH-04 is also recorded and reported as an unusual incident. If conditions become unsafe or a building hazard develops, ENV-02 applies and the residence is evacuated.

definitions.definition: Indoor air temperature below 68 degrees Fahrenheit or above 82 degrees Fahrenheit for four consecutive hours.
A loss of electric power, heat, cooling, water, gas or other essential service to the residence.
A written record of indoor air temperature readings with the date, time, location in the home, reader and actions taken.
A pre-arranged location, such as another [AGENCY NAME] residence, a family home, or a public shelter, where individuals can stay safely.

procedures: Each residence keeps working thermometers in the main living area and in sleeping areas. The Program Director checks that they work during the monthly home safety check.

A staff member who finds that heating or cooling has failed, or sees any thermometer reading below 68 or above 82 degrees Fahrenheit, tells the in-charge employee immediately and starts the temperature log.

The in-charge employee records the time of the first out-of-range reading. This starts the four-consecutive-hour measurement. The in-charge employee then takes readings at least every 30 minutes and logs each one.

The in-charge employee calls the Administrator or on-call administrator immediately (STF-09). The Administrator contacts the landlord, utility or service company and records the call and the estimated time of repair.

Staff protect individuals right away. In cold, they add blankets and layered clothing, close off unused rooms and use only approved safe heating equipment. In heat, they use fans, window air conditioners where available, cool drinks, light clothing and cooler areas of the home. Staff never use ovens, gas ranges, grills or unapproved heaters for heating.

Staff check each individual at least hourly for signs of heat or cold stress, such as confusion, flushed or pale skin, shivering, excessive sweating, lethargy, dehydration or changes in breathing. Staff pay extra attention to individuals with medical conditions, those who take medications that affect temperature regulation, and those who cannot say they are uncomfortable. Observations are recorded.
If any individual shows signs of distress, staff follow HW-04, call 9-1-1 for any life-threatening emergency, and notify the nurse.

If the temperature has not returned to the 68 to 82 degree range within two hours, or sooner if a person is at risk, the Administrator decides whether to move individuals to the alternate site. The Administrator starts the move at once if the home cannot be made safe, and in any case does not allow the four-hour mark to pass without a decision recorded in the log.

When relocating, staff take medications, medication administration records, adaptive and medical equipment, individual profiles, emergency contact lists and personal items. Staff keep continuous supervision, and the Administrator arranges adequate staffing at the alternate site.

For a power outage, staff use flashlights or battery lanterns, not candles. They protect any medical equipment, such as oxygen concentrators, suction machines and electric lifts, using backup batteries or oxygen cylinders. They keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed, and they discard food and refrigerated medications according to nurse and pharmacist direction and food safety rules (ENV-05).

For a water failure, staff provide bottled water for drinking, medication administration, hand hygiene and food preparation, and arrange alternate toilet and bathing arrangements. If safe water cannot be assured, the Administrator relocates individuals.
For a gas or carbon monoxide concern, staff follow the evacuation procedure in ENV-02 and do not treat it as a no-evacuation event.

The Administrator notifies guardians, families and the DDD Community Services Office as appropriate. The event is documented and, where it meets the definition of a reportable unusual incident, reported under BEH-04.

When conditions are restored, the in-charge employee records the time, completes the temperature log and confirms that individuals are well. The Administrator checks that equipment and food are safe before normal operations resume.

The Program Director reviews each event within five business days, documents lessons learned, and corrects any plan gaps such as a missing alternate site or equipment. Events are reported to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Contacts the repair source, decides on relocation, arranges the alternate site and staffing, and makes notifications.
Maintains thermometers, alternate site agreements and emergency supplies, and reviews every event.
Starts and keeps the temperature log, protects individuals, and calls the Administrator immediately.
Monitor individuals for heat or cold stress and carry out comfort and safety measures.
Advises on individuals at medical risk, medications and refrigerated supplies.

documentation: Temperature log with times, readings and actions
Individual health observation notes during the event
Record of calls to the landlord, utility or repair company
Alternate site relocation record, if used
Unusual incident report where applicable (BEH-04)
Post-event review and corrective action notes

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All community residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME], all employees, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among individuals and staff and to protect employees from exposure to bloodborne pathogens.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an infection prevention and control program in every residence. The program includes standard precautions, hand hygiene, cleaning and disinfection, a written Bloodborne Pathogen Exposure Control Plan meeting 29 CFR 1910.1030, first aid supplies, TB screening of employees, and prompt reporting and response to illness. Each first aid kit includes protective gloves and a CPR mask, consistent with the health and safety requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 (5.1 to 5.8). TB screening of employees is required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4 and is carried out under STF-05. The program protects individual dignity and privacy. Individuals who are ill are cared for in their own homes whenever it is safe to do so, and are not isolated in ways that violate their rights (IR-01, IR-02).

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all people at all times, including hand hygiene, gloves, and safe handling of blood, body fluids and sharps.
Disease-causing microorganisms in human blood or certain body fluids, including hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
A specific contact of eyes, mouth, mucous membrane or non-intact skin with blood or other potentially infectious material, or a needlestick or sharps injury.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 that identifies tasks with exposure risk and sets out protective measures, training, vaccination and follow-up.

procedures: The Administrator designates an Infection Control Coordinator, who is the nurse or [INFECTION CONTROL COORDINATOR NAME], to oversee this policy at all residences.
The Coordinator writes the Bloodborne Pathogen Exposure Control Plan, identifies job tasks with possible exposure, and reviews the plan at least annually and whenever tasks or procedures change.

Each residence stocks gloves, hand soap, alcohol-based hand sanitizer, disposable towels, face masks, disinfectant effective against bloodborne pathogens, biohazard bags and a sharps container where sharps are used. The Program Director checks stock at least monthly.

Each residence keeps a first aid kit in an accessible location. The kit contains protective gloves and a CPR mask in addition to other first aid supplies. The Program Director inspects each kit at least monthly and replaces used or expired items right away.

Staff wash hands with soap and water, or use hand sanitizer when hands are not visibly soiled, before and after assisting individuals, before preparing or serving food, before and after medication administration, after toileting or incontinence care, after removing gloves, and after contact with blood or body fluids.

Staff wear gloves when contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items is likely, and add gowns, masks or eye protection when splashing is possible. Staff discard gloves after each use and never reuse them.

Staff clean and disinfect bathrooms, kitchen surfaces and frequently touched surfaces on a daily schedule posted at each residence. They clean blood and body fluid spills promptly with disinfectant, using gloves.

Staff handle laundry that is soiled with body fluids with gloves, wash it separately in hot water and detergent, and do not shake it. Personal items such as razors, toothbrushes and nail clippers are never shared.
Staff place used sharps in a puncture-resistant container immediately and never recap needles. Containers are sealed when three-quarters full and disposed of through a licensed medical waste service.

[AGENCY NAME] offers the hepatitis B vaccine, at no cost to the employee, to every employee with reasonable expected exposure, within 10 working days of starting that work. An employee who declines signs a written declination and may change their mind later.

Employees receive bloodborne pathogen and infection control training during orientation (STF-03), before assisting with personal care, and then annually. Training covers the Exposure Control Plan, standard precautions, protective equipment, exposure response and the vaccine.

After an exposure incident, the employee washes the area right away, reports to the in-charge employee and the nurse immediately, and receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost, in line with 29 CFR 1910.1030. The Coordinator documents the incident.

Employees are screened for tuberculosis as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4. The results are filed in the personnel record under STF-05 and STF-06. Staff with symptoms of active TB are removed from direct contact until cleared by a health care provider.

Staff report any individual's symptoms of infection, such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, rash or skin infection, to the nurse and the in-charge employee on the same shift. The nurse directs care and contacts the health care provider (HW-02, HW-03).
Staff with symptoms of a contagious illness, such as vomiting, diarrhea, fever or a rash, do not work with individuals or prepare food until cleared under the Coordinator's return-to-work guidance.

When an individual has a contagious illness, staff support the individual in a way that protects others. This may include a separate bathroom if available, extra cleaning and masks. Any limits on the individual's movement are the least restrictive possible, are time-limited and are explained to the individual and guardian.

The Coordinator reports communicable disease and outbreaks to the local health department as required by New Jersey Department of Health requirements. The Administrator notifies guardians and, where criteria are met, files an unusual incident report under BEH-04.
Staff support individuals' immunizations, including influenza and other vaccines, according to individual choice and the health care provider's advice, and record them in the health record.
The Coordinator reviews infection data, exposure incidents and outbreaks quarterly and reports to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures resources and designates the Infection Control Coordinator; makes required notifications.
Maintains the Exposure Control Plan, trains staff, manages exposure follow-up and tracks infection data.
Ensures supplies, first aid kits and cleaning schedules are in place and followed in each residence.
Assesses ill individuals, advises on precautions and communicates with health care providers.
Follow standard precautions, report illness and exposure, and keep the home clean.

documentation: Bloodborne Pathogen Exposure Control Plan and annual review
Bloodborne pathogen and infection control training records
Hepatitis B vaccine offers, acceptances and declinations
Exposure incident reports and follow-up records
First aid kit and supply inspection logs
Cleaning schedules and sign-off logs
Employee TB screening results (see STF-05)
Outbreak and communicable disease reports

policies.title: Food, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All community residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME], all direct support professionals and the nurse, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To ensure individuals have safe, nutritious food that they choose, that meets their health needs, and that is prepared and served in ways that prevent choking, allergic reactions and foodborne illness.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual to choose what, when and with whom they eat, and prepares and stores food safely. The food and diet requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 (5.1 to 5.8) are followed. Modified diets, including texture-modified, thickened liquid, diabetic, allergy-related and tube feeding diets, are provided only under a written order from the individual's licensed health care provider or registered dietitian. Staff who assist with eating or feeding complete the feeding techniques training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d) within 90 days of employment, and feeding tube duties are delegated to nursing. Each individual with a choking risk has a written choking-risk plan (HW-03). Individual choice is not restricted except through the rights restriction process in IR-02.

definitions.definition: A diet changed in texture, consistency, content or amount by written order, for example pureed, mechanical soft, thickened liquids, low sodium, diabetic or allergen-free.
A written plan for an individual with swallowing or chewing difficulty that states food textures, positioning, supervision, pace of eating and emergency response.
Difficulty swallowing.
Nutrition and fluids delivered through a feeding tube, delegated to nursing.

procedures: At admission and at each annual Individual Habilitation Plan meeting (PCS-02), the nurse and planning team record each individual's food preferences, cultural or religious practices, allergies, dietary restrictions, and eating and swallowing needs.

Each individual chooses meals, snacks and mealtimes. Staff support individuals to plan menus, shop and cook as they are able and wish. Individuals have access to food at all times unless a rights restriction has been approved under IR-02.

The Program Director ensures that menus and available foods are nutritionally adequate and, when individuals have health conditions, consistent with their orders. Menus as served are kept for at least [MENU RETENTION PERIOD] and are available for review.

The nurse records every modified diet order in the individual's record with the ordering provider, the date, and the diet details. Orders are renewed or reviewed at least annually and whenever the individual's condition changes.

The modified diet is posted in a place that is accessible to staff but protects the individual's privacy, such as inside a cabinet door. A copy goes with the individual to outings, day programs and any hospital stay.

Staff prepare and serve modified diets exactly as ordered. A staff member who is unsure of the order checks with the nurse before serving. Staff do not substitute foods or textures without a new order.

Individuals with a choking risk have a choking-risk plan under HW-03. They are supervised at meals as the plan states, sit upright, eat at a safe pace, and receive foods in the ordered texture. Staff are trained in the Heimlich maneuver and CPR.

Staff are trained on food allergies, including recognizing and responding to an allergic reaction. An anaphylaxis response follows HW-04, including calling 9-1-1 and giving an ordered epinephrine auto-injector under HW-01.

Direct support professionals complete the feeding techniques training within 90 days of employment under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d), and the training is recorded under STF-04. Feeding by tube is carried out only by nursing or by staff delegated by the nurse under New Jersey nursing rules.
Staff wash hands before preparing or serving food (ENV-04). Staff with vomiting, diarrhea or open infected sores do not prepare food.

Staff store perishable food in a refrigerator kept at or below 41 degrees Fahrenheit and frozen food at 0 degrees Fahrenheit or below, check the temperature at least weekly, and keep cleaning products and medications apart from food.
Staff label and date leftovers, discard food that has passed its date or is spoiled, cook meat, poultry and eggs to safe internal temperatures, and clean food surfaces and utensils after each use.
Individuals who keep personal food in their rooms are supported to store it safely. Any limit on this is a rights restriction under IR-02.

Staff record significant changes in appetite, weight, chewing, swallowing, hydration or bowel habits, and report them to the nurse that shift. The nurse follows up with the health care provider (HW-02, HW-03).
For an emergency such as a power outage, the nurse and Program Director decide whether refrigerated food is safe to eat (ENV-03).

The Program Director inspects the kitchen, food storage and menu records at least monthly. The Compliance Officer reviews diet orders and choking-risk plans at least annually against the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 as part of the annual procedure review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Records diet orders, trains staff on modified diets and choking, delegates tube feeding tasks, and monitors nutrition and weight.
Ensures menus, food safety and storage routines, monthly kitchen inspections and training records.
Support food choices, follow diet orders and choking-risk plans, and report changes to the nurse.

responsibilities.role: Registered dietitian or health care provider
responsibilities.duty: Writes and reviews diet orders and nutritional recommendations.
Make choices about food, mealtimes and company, with support as needed.

documentation: Dietary needs and preferences in the individual's record
Written modified diet orders and renewals
Choking-risk plans (HW-03)
Menus as served
Refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Feeding techniques training records (STF-04)
Weight and nutrition monitoring notes
Monthly kitchen inspection checklists

policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All employees who drive or arrange transportation for individuals, all agency-owned, leased and approved personal vehicles used to transport individuals, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To ensure individuals are transported safely, with the supports they need, by qualified drivers in well-maintained, insured vehicles.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges transportation so individuals can take part in work, education, health care and community life of their choosing. Only employees who have a valid driver's license and an acceptable driving record may transport individuals. Every driver and escort is trained, within 90 days of employment as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d), in the use and transport of mobility devices and in the other specialized training that applies to the individuals served. Vehicles are insured, maintained and inspected. Emergency, medical, behavioral and incident procedures apply in vehicles in the same way as in the residence. Individuals are not denied transportation as a punishment or for convenience (IR-01, IR-02).

definitions.definition: The official driving record issued by the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, or the equivalent record from another state, showing license status, violations and suspensions.
A vehicle owned, leased or rented by [AGENCY NAME].
A wheelchair, scooter, walker, or similar device used by an individual for mobility.
Tie-downs, restraints and lap and shoulder belts designed to secure a wheelchair and its occupant in a vehicle.

procedures: Before an employee drives any individual, the Program Director obtains a copy of the employee's valid driver's license and a current driver abstract, and confirms the record is acceptable under the agency's driver standards ([DRIVER ELIGIBILITY STANDARDS]). The abstract is filed in the personnel record (STF-06).

The Program Director obtains a new driver abstract at least annually. An employee must tell the Program Director within one business day of any license suspension, revocation or new serious violation, and cannot drive individuals until reviewed.

Drivers and escorts complete the training in the use and transport of mobility devices and the other required specialized training under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d), within 90 days of employment. Staff do not transport an individual who uses a mobility device until they are trained and have been shown how to use the securement system. Records are kept under STF-04.
The Administrator maintains automobile liability insurance on all agency vehicles, with limits of at least [INSURANCE LIMITS], and keeps current proof of insurance and registration in each vehicle.

Staff may use a personal vehicle to transport individuals only with the Administrator's prior written approval, proof of the employee's insurance, and a satisfactory driver abstract. The employee is not allowed to ask individuals to pay for gas or mileage.

The Program Director schedules preventive maintenance for each agency vehicle according to the manufacturer's schedule. The Program Director also ensures every vehicle receives the State motor vehicle inspection when due and that records are kept.

Before each trip, the driver does a quick check of tires, lights, brakes, mirrors, fuel and that the wheelchair lift or ramp works, if there is one. The driver reports any defect to the Program Director and does not use an unsafe vehicle.

Each vehicle carries a first aid kit with gloves and a CPR mask, a fire extinguisher, emergency contact numbers, reflective triangles or flares, a flashlight, and, for individuals who need them, copies of emergency profiles listing medical conditions, allergies, medications and guardians.

Everyone in the vehicle wears a seat belt, as New Jersey law requires. Wheelchair users are secured in a four-point tie-down and a lap and shoulder belt, facing forward, and transferred to a vehicle seat when they can and wish to.

The driver does not use a hand-held phone, texting, or any distracting device while driving, and never drives while impaired by alcohol, drugs or medication. The driver is responsible for obeying all traffic laws.
The driver does not leave an individual alone in a vehicle unless the individual's plan allows it. In hot or cold weather, no individual is ever left in a parked vehicle.

The driver follows each individual's support and behavior plans while in the vehicle, such as seating, communication supports and planned calming strategies. If an individual's behavior becomes unsafe, the driver pulls over safely, applies the behavior support plan, and calls the on-call administrator (STF-09). Restraint is never used while the vehicle is moving (BEH-02).
For a medical emergency in a vehicle, the driver pulls over safely and follows HW-04, calling 9-1-1 for any life-threatening emergency, and then calls the Administrator.

After a crash, the driver calls 9-1-1 if anyone may be hurt, moves everyone to safety, gets medical care as needed and calls the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports the event as an unusual incident under BEH-04, informs the insurance carrier, and notifies guardians.
If a person goes missing during a trip, the driver follows BEH-06.
Medications that must be given during an outing travel in labeled containers with the staff who are trained to give them (HW-01).

The Program Director keeps the vehicle log, with trip purpose, driver, mileage, inspections, maintenance and incidents. The log is reviewed monthly. Crash and near-miss data go to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains insurance, approves personal vehicle use and receives crash and incident reports.
Checks driver abstracts and training, schedules maintenance and inspections, and reviews vehicle logs.
Drive safely, secure individuals, perform pre-trip checks and follow emergency and incident procedures.
Advises on medical needs during transport, including medication and positioning.
Use transportation to take part in their chosen activities and wear seat belts with the support they need.

documentation: Driver license copies and driver abstracts, annual updates
Mobility device and transport training records (STF-04)
Vehicle insurance, registration and inspection records
Maintenance and pre-trip check logs
Vehicle trip and mileage logs
Approval records for personal vehicle use
Crash and incident reports (BEH-04)

policies.title: Staffing, Supervision and In-Charge Designation
policies.applies_to: All residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME], all direct support professionals, supervisors, temporary agency staff and on-call staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each residence has enough trained staff on site, and a named person in charge on every shift, to meet the supervision and support needs of the individuals living there.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staffs each residence according to its approved program description and each individual's Individual Habilitation Plan (IHP). N.J.A.C. 10:44A sets no numeric staff-to-individual ratio and no awake-overnight requirement, so staffing levels are set by the program description and the individual supervision needs recorded in each IHP. A written staff schedule for at least two weeks is kept at each residence, showing the full names of staff, the on-site coverage required by the program description, and an in-charge employee for each shift (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(a)). In a group home or supervised apartment program, staff are on site whenever any individual is present, according to supervision needs (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(d)). Each specialized training required under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 is completed by at least one person on every shift (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(b)). Temporary agency staff are not designated in charge unless all N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 training is complete and this policy states that [AGENCY NAME] assumes responsibility and liability for them (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(a)). [AGENCY NAME] assumes that responsibility and liability, as stated in this policy.

definitions.definition: The employee designated in the written schedule as responsible for the residence and the individuals during a shift.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, an employee who provides direct support and supervision to individuals.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, an apartment in which up to four individuals live and receive supervision and support from agency staff.
Workers supplied by an outside staffing agency who are not employees of [AGENCY NAME].
The level and type of supervision each individual requires, as documented in the IHP and risk assessments.

procedures: For each residence, the Program Director writes the minimum on-site coverage by shift and day of the week, including overnight, into the program description. The coverage is based on the supervision needs recorded in each individual's IHP, health conditions, behavior supports, evacuation needs and the building layout.

The Program Director reviews coverage whenever an individual is admitted, discharged or has a change in condition or IHP, and at least annually. The Program Director adds staff when needs rise and records the reason.

The Program Director prepares a written schedule covering at least two weeks, with the full names of all staff, the hours of each shift, the on-site coverage required, and the in-charge employee for each shift. The schedule is posted or kept where staff and surveyors can see it at each residence.
Schedule changes are written on the schedule, with the date, the name of the staff member who changed, and the name of the staff member who replaced them. The schedule shows who actually worked.

In a group home or supervised apartment program, staff are on site at all times when any individual is present, according to the individual's supervision needs. A DSP does not leave the residence while individuals are present unless another qualified staff member has arrived.

When no individuals are present in the residence, staff need not be on site. In that case, the Program Director makes sure trained, paid agency staff who know the individuals are available for emergencies (STF-09).

For a supervised apartment program, the Administrator locates the staff residence or office so that staff can respond within the time that the individuals' supervision needs require. The response time is stated in the program description and tested by drill at least annually.

The Program Director names an in-charge employee for each shift, who is a DSP or supervisor who has completed orientation and the training required under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 (STF-03, STF-04). The in-charge employee knows how to reach the Administrator and on-call staff and has the emergency plan, critical information log and individual profiles at hand.

The in-charge employee is responsible during the shift for the supervision of individuals and staff, carrying out IHPs, giving or overseeing medication under HW-01, responding to emergencies, notifying the Administrator of incidents (BEH-04) and keeping the critical information log (REC-03).

The Program Director makes sure that each specialized training required under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d) (feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans) is held by at least one person on every shift, and checks this against training records (STF-04) when writing the schedule.
The Program Director does not schedule a new employee to work alone until orientation under STF-03 and the medication competency required by HW-01 are complete, if medication is part of the duties.

When temporary agency staff are used, the Program Director confirms before the shift that the agency staff member has passed background checks (STF-02), the required TB screening (STF-05), and the training for the individuals they will support. Agency staff are given orientation to the residence, the emergency plan and each individual's profile.

Temporary agency staff may be designated as in-charge only when they have completed all training required under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 and the certificates are on file. By this policy, [AGENCY NAME] assumes responsibility and liability for the acts of temporary agency staff in charge.

If a shift is left uncovered because of a call-out or emergency, the in-charge employee calls the Program Director or on-call administrator immediately (STF-09). The Program Director finds replacement staff from the on-call list, other residences, or approved agency staff. Staff do not leave their post until relieved, and mandatory overtime is limited so that staff are alert.

If coverage falls below the minimum in the program description and cannot be restored, the Administrator takes protective action, such as moving staff from another site, and documents the event. The Administrator reports it as an unusual incident under BEH-04 if an individual was put at risk.

The Program Director reviews schedules and actual hours worked against the program description at least monthly. Gaps, overtime, agency use and turnover are reported to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05), and the Administrator uses them to plan staffing.
Staffing and in-charge records are retained and available for inspection (GOV-08, STF-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the program description and ensures resources for staffing and for the agency's assumption of responsibility and liability for agency staff.
Ensures that staffing meets the program description, approves emergency staffing actions and reviews staffing reports.
Sets coverage levels, writes the two-week schedule, designates in-charge employees and checks training by shift.
Directs the shift, supervises individuals and staff, responds to emergencies and notifies the Administrator.
Remain on site and supervise individuals as scheduled, and report call-outs or inability to work promptly.
Audits schedules, in-charge designations and training by shift.

documentation: Program description with minimum on-site coverage
Written staff schedules of at least two weeks at each residence, with full names and in-charge designation
Records of actual hours worked and schedule changes
Training records showing specialized training by shift (STF-04)
Agency staff verification of screening and training
Records of coverage gaps and corrective actions
Monthly staffing review reports

policies.title: Background Checks, Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry
policies.applies_to: The licensee/owner, executive director (agency head), all employees, contracted and temporary-agency staff, interns and volunteers who may have contact with individuals receiving services, and the Human Resources designee and Program Director who administer screening.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from abuse, neglect and exploitation by making sure that no person with a disqualifying criminal history, a Central Registry listing or a Child Abuse Registry listing is paid, contracted or allowed contact with individuals served by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] screens every person who may have contact with individuals before that person is hired, contracted, assigned or allowed to work. No individual may have contact with individuals until every required clearance is on file and has been reviewed and signed by the Program Director. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)3 (a procedure for assuring compliance with the Central Registry) and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)20 (a procedure for assuring that no employee is included on the Department of Children and Families' Child Abuse Registry, as set forth at N.J.S.A. 30:6D-73 et seq. and 9:6-8.10f). Under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(b), the agency head is not paid or contracted until criminal history clearance is obtained under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69. The owner/licensee, if a different person, is also checked. Employee screening requirements apply to all employees who may contact individuals (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4). Contracted staff, temporary-agency staff, interns and volunteers who may contact individuals are screened to the same standard as employees. A person who is disqualified, or who is listed on either Registry, is not hired, or is removed from contact with individuals immediately if already working. Screening records are kept in the personnel file and are available to DHS inspectors at any time.

definitions.definition: The State Central Registry as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, which lists persons with substantiated findings of abuse, neglect or exploitation of individuals with developmental disabilities.
The registry maintained by the NJ Department of Children and Families (DCF) under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-73 et seq. and 9:6-8.10f.
A criminal history background check completed through the State-approved process under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69, with a result that does not disqualify the person.
The executive director or community agency head who manages the agency, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
Any employee, contractor, temporary-agency worker, intern or volunteer who may have contact with individuals receiving services.

procedures: Before any offer is made final, the Human Resources designee tells each candidate in writing that employment depends on clearance of the criminal history check, the Central Registry check and the Child Abuse Registry check.
The candidate signs a consent and disclosure form for the three checks. The Human Resources designee keeps the form in the personnel file.

The Human Resources designee starts the criminal history check through the State-approved process under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69 on the day consent is signed. The designee records the date submitted on the Screening Tracker.

On the same day, the Human Resources designee submits the Central Registry check using the process the Department prescribes. The designee also submits the Child Abuse Registry check through the DCF-approved process. Both submission dates are logged on the Screening Tracker.
The Program Director reviews each result when received. The Program Director signs and dates a Clearance Review Form that records the result of each check and whether the person may start.

No person with a pending check may start work, be placed on a schedule, orient in a residence with individuals present, or have any contact with individuals. Orientation that involves no contact with individuals may proceed in the administrative office only.

For the executive director/agency head: the Governing Authority confirms that criminal history clearance under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69 is on file before the person is paid or contracted, and the Governing Authority signs and dates the confirmation. The owner/licensee, if different from the agency head, is checked in the same way.

A result that is disqualifying under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69, or a listing on the Central Registry or the Child Abuse Registry, means the person is not hired, contracted or assigned. If the person is already working, the Program Director removes the person from all contact with individuals the same day.

The Program Director notifies the Executive Director the same day of any disqualifying or adverse result. The Executive Director decides what further action to take and documents it. If the result suggests a person already served may have been harmed, the Program Director follows BEH-03 and BEH-04.

Every employee must tell the Program Director within one business day if they are arrested, charged, or named in an abuse, neglect or exploitation investigation. The Program Director reviews the matter with the Executive Director and decides whether the person may continue to work with individuals.

The Human Resources designee re-checks the Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry for each employee at least annually, at the time of the performance evaluation, and records the date and result on the Screening Tracker.

Temporary-agency and contracted staff may not be placed until the staffing vendor provides written proof of all three clearances and the Program Director has reviewed it. The agency may instead run its own checks.

The Human Resources designee reviews the Screening Tracker monthly and reports any missing or overdue check to the Program Director. The Program Director corrects the problem within five business days.

Screening results are kept in a confidential section of the personnel file, in the administrative office, with the signed consent and the Clearance Review Form (see STF-06). Results are shared only with those who need them to make employment decisions and with DHS inspectors.

At each annual review of this policy (GOV-04), the Executive Director checks the procedure against the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4, 2.2(b) and 2.4 and any updated State screening instructions, and records the review date.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms clearance of the agency head and owner/licensee before any pay or contract; reviews screening compliance at least annually.
Makes final decisions on disqualifying or adverse results; ensures the agency complies with 10:44A-1.4(b) and 2.2(b)3 and 20.
Reviews every result, signs the Clearance Review Form, and removes disqualified persons from contact with individuals the same day.
Obtains consents, submits all three checks, maintains the Screening Tracker and files the results.
Cooperate with screening and report arrests, charges and investigations within one business day.

Criminal history clearance result for each person with contact, plus the agency head and owner/licensee
Central Registry result with date

Temporary-agency or contractor clearance proof
