policies.title: New Employee Orientation and Checklist
policies.applies_to: All new employees (including part-time, per diem and temporary-agency staff) who will work with individuals, the Program Director and the trainers who deliver orientation.
policies.purpose: To make sure every new employee understands the agency's philosophy, the rights and safety of the individuals served, and what to do in an emergency before working without supervision.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a documented orientation for every new employee before that employee works unsupervised with individuals. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)4, which requires a New Employee Orientation Checklist that includes at a minimum all of the requirements at N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)1 through 8. The agency's checklist contains the following items, each addressed in this policy: (1) 2.6(a)1: the organization's philosophy, goals, services and practices; (2) 2.6(a)2: the prevention of abuse, neglect and exploitation; (3) 2.6(a)3: unusual incident reporting and investigating procedures; (4) 2.6(a)4: emergency procedures identified in the procedure manual, including the emergency evacuation plan, emergency medical treatment, emergency coverage and on-call procedures, operation of the fire alarm system, and use of fire extinguishers; (5) 2.6(a)5: an overview of developmental disabilities and the special needs of the individuals served, such as medical or behavioral needs requiring tailored training; (6) 2.6(a)6: the employee's job description and the agency's personnel policies, including its drug testing policy; (7) 2.6(a)7: training in life-threatening emergencies through the curriculum developed by the Division; and (8) 2.6(a)8: training consistent with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6. The employee and the trainer each sign and date every item. Orientation is separate from the Division basic and specialized training that must be finished within 90 days of employment under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 (see STF-04). It also covers training in any relevant policies not otherwise covered (2.7(c)). Orientation is delivered by a qualified trainer (2.7(g)).

definitions.definition: The agency's signed record showing that each item at N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)1 through 8 was covered with the employee.
Work with individuals when no trained, oriented staff member is present to observe and direct the new employee.
A person with the knowledge, experience and, where required, credentials to teach the topic, designated in writing by the Program Director.
The employee who gives direct assistance and training to individuals, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.

procedures: The Human Resources designee confirms that all clearances required by STF-02 are on file before orientation begins at any residence where individuals are present.
The Program Director assigns a qualified trainer and a start date for each new employee and records them on the orientation schedule.
The trainer opens a New Employee Orientation Checklist for the employee on day one. The checklist lists items 2.6(a)1 through 2.6(a)8 and the 2.7(c) policy training.

Item 2.6(a)1: The trainer reviews the agency's philosophy, goals, services and practices, including person-centered planning, normalization, age-appropriateness and least restriction, and the Program Description (GOV-03).

Item 2.6(a)2: The trainer reviews the prohibition on abuse, neglect and exploitation, the signs of each, and the employee's duty to report every allegation (BEH-03). The employee signs the agency's statement of this prohibition.
Item 2.6(a)3: The trainer reviews unusual incident reporting and investigation procedures (BEH-04 and BEH-05). The employee practices completing an incident report form.

Item 2.6(a)4: The trainer reviews the emergency evacuation plan for each residence the employee will work in, emergency medical treatment (HW-04), emergency coverage and on-call procedures (STF-09), operation of the fire alarm system, and use of fire extinguishers. The employee demonstrates the evacuation route and extinguisher use.

Item 2.6(a)5: The trainer gives an overview of developmental disabilities and the individual-specific medical, behavioral, communication and support needs of the people the employee will serve, drawing on each person's current plan. The trainer notes any tailored training still needed.

Item 2.6(a)6: The employee receives the signed job description and the personnel policies, including the controlled dangerous substance testing policy (STF-08) and staff conduct (STF-07). The employee signs for each.

Item 2.6(a)7: The employee completes training in life-threatening emergencies through the curriculum developed by the Division. The trainer records the date and the provider of the training and files any certificate. The training includes calling 9-1-1 for life-threatening emergencies (HW-04).

Item 2.6(a)8: The employee receives training consistent with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6, including the exchange of contact information with involved family and guardians (IR-10) and drug testing of employees (STF-08).
The trainer reviews the other policies relevant to the employee's job that the checklist does not already cover (rights, confidentiality, medication and others) and records the date on the checklist.
The employee and the trainer each sign and date every checklist item as it is completed. An item is not signed until the employee can explain it or demonstrate it.
New employees work only alongside a trained, oriented staff member until the Program Director signs the completed checklist. The Program Director documents the date unsupervised work is allowed.
The Human Resources designee files the signed checklist in the personnel file and enters the 90-day training due date on the training tracker (STF-04).
At each annual review, the Program Director compares the checklist to the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a) and the content of orientation, and updates both.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns trainers, signs completed checklists, and authorizes unsupervised work.
Delivers each checklist item, checks understanding, and signs and dates each item.
Confirms clearances before orientation, files completed checklists, and sets the 90-day training due dates.
Completes every item, signs and dates each, and asks questions about anything not understood.

documentation: Completed New Employee Orientation Checklist signed and dated by employee and trainer for each item
Signed prohibition on abuse, neglect and exploitation statement
Signed job description and personnel policy acknowledgments
Life-threatening emergency training record or certificate
N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6 training record
Date the Program Director authorized unsupervised work
Orientation schedule and trainer designation

policies.title: Direct Support Professional Training
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals (DSPs), the in-charge staff on every shift, temporary-agency DSPs, the Program Director, and the qualified trainers.
policies.purpose: To make sure every DSP has the Division-required basic and specialized training and shows medication competency before giving care, and that the training is recorded in a form an inspector can review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides and documents all training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7. Within 90 days of employment, each DSP completes the Division basic training: DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid and CPR from an entity that complies with Emergency Cardiovascular Care (ECC) standards, with a valid certificate on file for each (2.7(a)). A DSP completes medication training and shows competency before administering any medication, and shows competency again every year (2.7(b)). Within 90 days of employment each DSP also completes specialized training in feeding techniques (feeding tube duties are delegated to nursing), mobility devices and transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans (2.7(d)). Training in relevant policies not covered in orientation is delivered by a qualified trainer (2.7(c), 2.7(g)). The agency may offer additional training without Division approval (2.7(f)). At least one person on every shift has completed each required specialized training (2.8(b)). A temporary-agency employee is not designated in-charge unless all 2.7 training is complete and the agency's written policy states that the licensee assumes responsibility and liability (2.8(a)). Training records are kept in the administrative office (2.7(e)).

definitions.definition: DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid and CPR, each with a valid certificate.
Training on feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizures and physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans, based on the needs of the individuals served.
A DSP's demonstrated ability to give medication safely, assessed and signed off before the first medication pass and every year after (see HW-01).
A log with each employee's hire date, 90-day deadline, completed courses, certificate expiration dates and annual competency dates.

procedures: On the hire date, the Human Resources designee enters the employee on the training tracker with the hire date and the date 90 days later.
The Program Director schedules Division basic training for each new DSP so that all of it, not just part, is finished by day 90. The target is day 60.
DDD Shifting Expectations: the DSP completes it and the trainer or Human Resources designee obtains and files the certificate.
Preventing abuse and neglect: the DSP completes it and the certificate is filed. It supports orientation item 2.6(a)2 (STF-03) and BEH-03.

First aid and CPR: the DSP completes a course from an ECC-compliant entity. The Human Resources designee files the valid certificate and records the expiration date on the tracker. A DSP renews it before it expires.

Medication: a DSP does not give any medication, in any residence, until medication training is complete and the delegating nurse or trainer has signed off competency (HW-01). The competency date is entered on the tracker.
The Program Director repeats the medication competency assessment every year. A DSP who does not show competency stops giving medication until retrained and re-assessed.

Specialized training: within 90 days of hire the Program Director completes the five specialized trainings listed in 2.7(d) for each DSP. Feeding techniques and feeding tube care are taught by nursing, and tube duties are delegated by nursing only (HW-02).

The Program Director reviews each individual's plan, so the DSP also gets person-specific training (for example the behavior support plan, seizure plan or diet) before working alone with that individual.
Policy training: the trainer delivers training in all relevant policies not covered in orientation, using a written curriculum or training plan.
Each training session is documented with the curriculum or training plan, the date, and the dated signatures of trainer and trainee. Any results the Division requires are filed with the record.

The Program Director checks the staff schedule (STF-01) each month, so at least one person on every shift has completed each required specialized training (2.8(b)). Gaps are filled by retraining or rescheduling.

Before the agency designates temporary-agency staff as in-charge, the Program Director confirms that all 2.7 training is complete. This designation is allowed only under the written policy in which the agency assumes responsibility and liability, and the signed policy is on file.

The Human Resources designee reviews the tracker every month and gives the Program Director a list of anyone with training due in the next 30 days. A DSP who has not met a 90-day requirement is not left in sole charge of individuals until the Program Director has reviewed the matter.
Additional trainings the agency chooses to offer are recorded in the same way. The Program Director may add to the plan when an individual's needs change.
Training records are kept in the administrative office, with copies of certificates in the personnel file (STF-06), and are available to inspectors.

responsibilities.duty: Schedules and verifies all training, signs off competency, confirms shift coverage of specialized training and designates in-charge staff.
Teaches feeding tube care and medication training and assesses medication competency (see HW-01 and HW-02).
Maintains the tracker, obtains certificates and reports upcoming and overdue training.
Delivers the curriculum and signs and dates each record.
Completes all training on time, renews certificates and shows competency.

documentation: Training tracker showing hire date, 90-day deadline and completion dates
Certificates for DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid/CPR
Medication training record and annual competency sign-offs
Specialized training records
Curriculum or training plan for each session
Dated trainer and trainee signatures
Any Division-required training results
Written policy and assumption of liability for temporary-agency in-charge staff

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted and temporary-agency staff, interns and volunteers who may have contact with individuals, and the Human Resources designee and Program Director.
policies.purpose: To keep individuals and staff safe from tuberculosis (TB) by screening every person with contact before they work and by tracking and following up on results.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires a TB screen for every employee who may contact individuals, as set out in the employee screening requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4. The screen is either a Mantoux tuberculin skin test (5 TU PPD) or an IGRA blood test. The test is completed within one year before the start of work or upon starting work, and the written result is given to the agency. No person has contact with individuals until the written result is on file. The agency also repeats the TB screen every year as its own standard. The Executive Director checks N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4 at each annual policy review, and any different interval required by the current rule applies. Results are kept in the personnel file (STF-06). Cost of the screening is paid by the agency as an employer expense, or by the employee's own arrangements where the employee prefers to use a personal provider.

definitions.definition: A tuberculin skin test using 5 tuberculin units, read by a licensed health care professional 48 to 72 hours after placement.
An interferon-gamma release assay, a TB blood test.
A document signed by a licensed health care provider that shows the type of test, the date and the result.
Any employee, contractor, temporary-agency worker, intern or volunteer who may have contact with individuals.

procedures: At the offer stage the Human Resources designee tells the candidate in writing that a TB screen is required, which tests are accepted, and the deadline.
The candidate provides a written result of a Mantoux 5 TU PPD or an IGRA test dated within one year before the start date, or is tested upon starting work.
The Human Resources designee checks that the result is in writing, names the test, shows the date and the result, and is signed by the health care provider.

A person whose written result is not yet on file may attend orientation in the administrative office only. The person may not have contact with individuals until the result is filed and the Program Director has reviewed it.
The Human Resources designee files the result in the confidential section of the personnel file, and enters the test date and the next due date on the Health Screening Tracker.
A negative result clears the person to work, once all other pre-work requirements are met (STF-02 and STF-03).

If a test is positive, the person is referred to a licensed health care provider or the local health department for evaluation. The person does not work with individuals until the evaluating provider gives the agency written clearance. The agency keeps that clearance in the personnel file.
For a person with a prior positive test, the provider's written evaluation and clearance, including any symptom review, is accepted in place of a repeat skin test.
The Human Resources designee reviews the tracker monthly and notifies each employee and the Program Director 45 days before the annual repeat screen is due.
An employee who does not complete the annual repeat by the due date is removed from contact with individuals until a written result is filed.

Any employee who has symptoms of TB, such as a cough lasting three weeks or more, fever, night sweats or unexplained weight loss, must tell the Program Director at once. The Program Director sends the employee for medical evaluation and keeps the employee away from individuals until cleared (see ENV-04).
Health information is kept confidential, is not placed in individual records, and is shared only as needed for exposure control or as the law requires (IR-04).

If an individual or employee is diagnosed with active TB, the Program Director notifies the local health department as directed, follows its instructions, and notifies the Executive Director the same day.
The Program Director checks that the screening records of all employees are complete as part of the quarterly personnel file audit (STF-06).

responsibilities.duty: Gives notice of the requirement, verifies and files results, maintains the tracker and sends reminders.
Reviews results, removes non-compliant staff from contact with individuals and arranges follow-up for positive results or symptoms.
Verifies the screening interval against the current rule at each annual review.
Obtains testing on time, provides written results and reports TB symptoms.

documentation: Written TB test result (Mantoux 5 TU PPD or IGRA) for each person with contact
Provider clearance for any positive test
Health Screening Tracker with test dates and next due dates
Notices of the requirement given to candidates
Records of removal from duty for overdue screening and the date of return
Annual policy review note confirming the current rule

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: The Executive Director, Program Director, Human Resources designee and all employees, contracted professionals and temporary-agency staff whose records the agency keeps.
policies.purpose: To keep complete, accurate and confidential personnel records that show each person is qualified, screened and trained, and that are ready for review by DHS inspectors at any time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for every employee, and for every contractor and temporary-agency worker who may contact individuals. The file holds the documents listed in this policy so that the agency can show compliance with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4 (employee screening), 2.5 (minimum staff qualifications, including verification of professional credentials under 2.5(f)) and 2.7 (staff training). Training records are kept in the administrative office with the curriculum or training plan and dated trainer and trainee signatures (2.7(e)). Inspectors review staff files, schedules, credentials, background checks and related documents during annual and unannounced inspections. The agency makes records available at once. Personnel files are confidential and are kept apart from individuals' records.

definitions.definition: The record for one employee, contractor or temporary-agency worker, kept in the administrative office.
Confirming with the issuing body that a license or certification required by law is valid, and recording the date and result.
A review of each file against the Personnel File Checklist.
Licenses or certificates required by law for employed or contracted professionals such as nurses.

procedures: The Human Resources designee opens a personnel file on the date of the conditional offer and keeps all files in locked storage in the administrative office, with electronic files protected by password and access limits.

Each file contains: the application and résumé; proof of identity; proof of age (18 or older for DSPs) and of high school diploma or equivalent or higher education as required by the position (2.5); and the signed job description.
The file contains the criminal history, Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry clearances, the signed consent and the Clearance Review Form (STF-02).
The file contains the written TB screening result and any provider clearance (STF-05), kept in the confidential health section of the file.

The file contains training records: certificates for DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid/CPR; medication training and annual competency sign-offs; and specialized training records (STF-04).

The file contains the signed New Employee Orientation Checklist (STF-03) and the signed personnel policy acknowledgments, including the drug testing policy and the prohibition on abuse, neglect and exploitation.

For any professional whose credentials are required by law, such as a nurse, the Human Resources designee verifies the license with the issuing body before the person starts and each time it is due for renewal, and files a dated printout or note under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5(f).

For the Executive Director, the file also shows the qualifications in 2.5(a): a bachelor's degree, five years of progressive developmental disability management experience, with at least two years at a supervisory or administrative level, and the CV. For a residence supervisor it shows a high school diploma or equivalent and one year of developmental disability experience (2.5(b)).
The file contains the employee's references, the results of drug testing required by STF-08, performance evaluations, corrective action records and any commendations.
The Human Resources designee uses the Personnel File Checklist to confirm that each file is complete before the employee's first unsupervised shift, and the Program Director signs the checklist.

The Program Director audits all files at least quarterly, and a sample of files monthly, using the checklist and the training and screening trackers. Missing items are corrected within 10 business days and the correction is documented.

Before each annual inspection and whenever DHS announces or arrives for an inspection, the Human Resources designee confirms that files, trackers and credentials are current and can be produced immediately (GOV-08).
Employees may review their own file on request, in the presence of the Human Resources designee. Others are given access only if they need it for their work or as the law or an inspection requires.
Entries are made only by authorized staff, dated and signed. No one backdates, alters or removes a record. Falsifying a record is a violation of STF-07.
Personnel records are kept for the period set in REC-01. Files of former employees are kept in locked storage, and are destroyed only according to REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Opens, maintains and secures files, verifies credentials and keeps the checklist and trackers current.
Signs file checklists, runs quarterly audits and corrects deficiencies.
Ensures records are complete and available for inspection, and ensures their own qualifications are documented.
Provide accurate documents, keep certifications current, and report changes.

documentation: Personnel File Checklist signed by Human Resources designee and Program Director
Application, identification, age and education proof
Signed job description
Background and registry clearances
TB screening result
Training and first aid/CPR certificates
Orientation checklist
Professional credential verification
Quarterly file audit reports and corrective actions

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted and temporary-agency staff, interns, volunteers, the Executive Director and members of the Governing Authority.
policies.purpose: To make clear the conduct expected of everyone who works with individuals, protect individuals from abuse, neglect, exploitation and loss of rights, and keep agency records honest.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] expects all staff to treat individuals with dignity and respect as adults with the same rights as other citizens, and to support their choices. This policy is designed on normalization, age appropriateness, least restriction and person-centered planning (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(a)). Abuse, neglect and exploitation of any individual are prohibited, and every allegation must be reported (see BEH-03, BEH-04 and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8). Staff may not retaliate against anyone for exercising a right, and no person may be penalized for exercising a right (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(a); see IR-01). Staff may not falsify any record. Falsification is a defined term in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, and for this policy it includes false or altered documentation of services, incident reports, medication records, EVV entries, time records, schedules, training records, drug test results, screening records and personal funds records. Staff may not have financial dealings with individuals or accept personal gain from them. Orientation covers these personnel policies (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)6; see STF-03). Violations lead to corrective action up to and including dismissal, and to reporting to outside authorities as required by law.

definitions.definition: Making, altering, omitting or destroying a record in order to deceive, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. It includes recording services that were not provided.
Using an individual, or an individual's money, property or labor, for the benefit of someone else, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
The limit between a staff member's role as a paid support and a personal, financial or romantic relationship.
Any punishment, threat or unfavorable treatment of a person because they exercised a right or reported a concern.

procedures: At hire, each employee receives this policy and the Staff Code of Conduct during orientation (STF-03, item 2.6(a)6). The employee signs that they have read it, understand it, and will follow it.
Staff treat each individual as an adult, address the individual by their preferred name, support their choices, respect privacy and speak and act respectfully at all times.

Staff do not abuse, neglect or exploit any individual. Any employee who sees, suspects or is told of abuse, neglect or exploitation follows BEH-03 and BEH-04 immediately, and reports every allegation.

Staff do not retaliate against, threaten or treat unfavorably any individual, family member, guardian or co-worker who exercises a right, files a grievance or makes a report. Retaliation is a separate violation.

Staff do not borrow from, lend to, sell to or buy from an individual. They do not accept gifts of more than nominal value, bequests or tips, and do not use an individual's money, card, property or vehicle for any purpose other than as set out in IR-05 and IR-06.

Staff do not hold themselves out as an individual's agent, guardian or representative, and do not serve as a witness or signer for an individual's financial or legal documents unless the Executive Director approves it in writing.
Staff do not enter into sexual, romantic or other personal relationships with individuals served. This applies regardless of whether the individual appears to agree.
Staff do not use an individual's photographs, name or information on social media or for any purpose other than the individual's services. Staff keep individuals' information confidential (IR-04).
Staff do not bring unapproved visitors to a residence, and do not take individuals on personal outings, or to their own home, without written approval of the Program Director.
Staff do not use alcohol, cannabis or any controlled dangerous substance while on duty, or report to work impaired. Staff follow the drug testing policy (STF-08).

Staff do not falsify any record. Staff document services at the time or right after they are provided, record only what they did or observed, and enter EVV and time records accurately. A correction is made by drawing one line through the error, adding the date and initials, and writing the correct entry. Records are never erased or overwritten.
An employee who is asked to alter a record, or who finds a falsified record, reports it to the Program Director at once, or to the Executive Director if the Program Director is involved.

Staff tell the Program Director within one business day of any arrest, criminal charge or substance-related charge, and of any investigation of abuse, neglect or exploitation in which they are named (STF-02).
Staff report any conflict of interest, such as a family relationship with an individual or a financial interest in a vendor, to the Executive Director for written review.

The Program Director investigates alleged violations promptly. Where abuse, neglect or exploitation is alleged, the matter is handled under BEH-05. The Program Director documents the finding and action taken, and removes staff from contact with individuals while an investigation is pending where needed for safety.

Corrective action may include coaching, written warning, retraining, suspension or dismissal, and is applied consistently. A record of the action is kept in the personnel file (STF-06). Where the law requires, the agency reports to DHS and other authorities (REC-02).
The Executive Director reviews this policy at least annually (GOV-04) and reviews conduct trends, including substantiated violations, in the quality improvement process (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, reviews conflicts of interest and decides corrective action on serious violations.
Reviews expectations with staff, supervises conduct, investigates reports and documents action.
Obtains signed acknowledgments and files corrective action records.
Follow this policy, protect individuals and their rights, keep records honest and report violations.

documentation: Signed Staff Code of Conduct acknowledgment
Orientation checklist entry for personnel policies
Record of arrest or charge reports and agency response
Conflict-of-interest reviews
Corrective action records in the personnel file
Investigation records (see BEH-05)
Record corrections showing date, initials and original entry

policies.title: Controlled Dangerous Substance Testing of Employees
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME] who work in or for a community residence (group home, supervised apartment or supportive living), including the Executive Director, residence supervisors, direct support professionals (DSPs) and any temporary agency staff placed with the agency. Also applies to the Administrator and Human Resources staff who run the program.
policies.purpose: To keep individuals safe by making sure no employee works while impaired by a controlled dangerous substance (CDS), and to set out how [AGENCY NAME] tests employees in line with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5. The policy also makes sure employees learn the drug testing policy at orientation.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)18 (written procedures for assuring compliance with the requirements for testing employees for controlled dangerous substances, in accordance with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5) and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)6 (the personnel policies of the organization, including its drug testing policies, are covered in new employee orientation). [AGENCY NAME] tests employees for controlled dangerous substances before employment and on a random basis during employment. Testing is done through a qualified laboratory and collection process. An employee with a confirmed positive result is removed from duty immediately and is not returned to work with individuals except as this policy allows. No employee may be alone with an individual or give supports once removed from duty. Test results are confidential personnel information and are never kept in an individual's record. The agency's testing practices follow the Medicaid/DDD provider requirements for pre-employment and random testing. The Administrator confirms the current statutory requirements with counsel at each annual policy review (see GOV-04).

definitions.definition: A drug or substance regulated as a controlled dangerous substance under New Jersey law, including illegally obtained drugs and prescription drugs used without a valid prescription or not as prescribed.
A CDS test given to a candidate after a conditional offer and before the person starts work or has unsupervised contact with individuals.
A CDS test given to an employee chosen by a neutral selection method, without advance notice and without regard to suspicion.
A licensed physician engaged by the testing vendor or the agency to review laboratory results and speak with the employee about legitimate medical explanations before a result is called positive.
Immediate removal of an employee from all work with individuals, including scheduled shifts, on-call duty and in-charge duty.

procedures: Policy owner: The Administrator is responsible for this policy. Human Resources carries out day-to-day testing tasks. The Administrator names a backup person for times when the Administrator is unavailable.

Vendor: Before opening, the Administrator contracts with [TESTING VENDOR/LABORATORY] for collection, laboratory analysis and MRO review. The contract is kept in the administrative file. The Administrator reviews it annually.
Pre-employment notice: Every job posting and offer letter states that employment depends on a negative CDS test and on the other pre-employment checks (see STF-02, STF-05, STF-10).

Pre-employment testing: After a conditional offer, Human Resources gives the candidate a written referral to the collection site. The test must be completed within [NUMBER] business days of the offer. A candidate may not start work or have contact with individuals until a negative result (or an MRO-cleared result) is on file.

Refusal or failure to appear: A candidate who refuses to test, tampers with a sample, or does not complete the test in the time allowed is not hired. An employee who does any of these things during employment is treated as having a positive result.

Random selection: At least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly], Human Resources, or the vendor if it provides this service, selects employees for random testing using a documented neutral method, such as a random-number generator or vendor pool. The method, date, pool size and names selected are recorded. Every employee has an equal chance of selection each time.

Random testing notice and timing: Selected employees are told on the day of testing and sent directly to the collection site. Employees on shift are accompanied or relieved so that supervision of individuals is not left uncovered. The supervisor arranges relief coverage under STF-09 if needed.

Prescribed medication: An employee who takes a prescribed medication that could affect a test result or the ability to work safely discloses this only to the MRO. If the MRO or the employee's prescriber advises that the medication limits safe work with individuals, the employee tells the Administrator about the work restriction only. The Administrator then decides on a temporary change of duties under the personnel policy.

Confirmed positive result: When the MRO reports a confirmed positive result, the Administrator is told the same day. The Administrator or a designee removes the employee from duty immediately and in writing, arranges safe transport home if impairment is suspected, and arranges replacement coverage so that required supervision continues.

Decision after removal: The Administrator decides whether the employee will be disciplined, terminated or offered a return-to-work process, according to the personnel policies and applicable law. Any employee returned to work is subject to follow-up testing as set out in the written decision. The Administrator consults counsel before any decision that could involve a reporting obligation to a professional licensing body or other authority.

Employees who are DSPs or in-charge staff: If a positive result affects a person assigned in-charge on a shift or on call, the supervisor names a replacement in-charge and updates the posted schedule and on-call roster (see STF-01 and STF-09).
Possible abuse or neglect: If a person suspected of CDS impairment may have harmed or neglected an individual, the supervisor follows BEH-03 and BEH-04 at once, in addition to this policy.

Orientation (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.6(a)6): During new employee orientation (STF-03), Human Resources gives each new employee the written drug testing policy, explains pre-employment and random testing, the consequences of a positive result or a refusal, and the confidentiality of results. The employee signs an acknowledgment, which goes on the New Employee Orientation Checklist and in the personnel file.

Confidentiality: Test results, MRO reports and related records are kept in a locked, confidential testing file in Human Resources, separate from the general personnel file and from every individual's record. Only the Administrator, Human Resources and counsel have access.

Temporary agency staff: Any contract with a staffing agency requires the agency to provide proof of equivalent pre-employment and random testing, and to remove staff who test positive. Temporary staff are not placed until the agency confirms a negative result in writing.

Annual review: Each year the Administrator reviews testing records, the random selection log and the vendor contract. The Administrator reports the number of tests, refusals and positive results (without names) to the Governing Body and to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the policy. Contracts with the vendor, takes reports of positive results, decides on removal and return, and reports test data (without names) to the Governing Body.
Issues test referrals, runs random selection, tracks completion, keeps confidential testing files and records the orientation acknowledgment.
Releases employees for random tests, removes any employee on shift from duty when directed, and arranges coverage so that individuals stay supervised.
Complete testing when selected, tell the MRO (not co-workers) about prescribed medication, and do not work while impaired.
Reviews the policy annually and aggregate testing results.

documentation: Signed orientation acknowledgment of the drug testing policy (New Employee Orientation Checklist)
Pre-employment test results and clearance date
Random selection log (method, date, names selected, test completion)
MRO reports and removal-from-duty notices (confidential testing file)
Vendor contract and annual review notes
Annual aggregate testing report to the Governing Body (no names)

policies.title: Emergency Coverage and On-Call Procedures
policies.applies_to: All residence supervisors, direct support professionals, in-charge employees, on-call supervisors and administrative staff of [AGENCY NAME], at every group home, supervised apartment and supportive living location.
policies.purpose: To make sure someone qualified and familiar with the individuals can always be reached and can respond in an emergency, including when staff are not on site, and to make sure shifts are covered when staff call out or must be removed from duty.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)7 (emergency coverage and on-call procedures). Staff are on site at a group home or supervised apartment whenever any individual is present, in line with each person's supervision needs (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(d)). When no individuals are present, staff need not be on site, but trained, paid agency staff who are familiar with the individuals are available for emergencies (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(c)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written on-call roster covering every hour, posts it with contact numbers at each residence, and makes sure an in-charge employee is named for every shift. The staff office or residence of a supervised apartment program is located so that response time meets the supervision needs of the individuals (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(e)). Emergency coverage does not replace 9-1-1: for life-threatening emergencies staff call 9-1-1 first (HW-04).

definitions.definition: A trained, paid agency employee, familiar with the individuals, who is assigned to be reachable by phone and able to respond when a residence needs emergency help or coverage.
The employee designated in writing for a shift who is responsible for the residence and the individuals on that shift (see STF-01).
Replacing or adding staff at a residence so that required supervision is maintained after a call-out, an emergency, a staff removal from duty or any event that leaves a shift short.
The time needed for on-call or supervisory staff to reach a residence or apartment from their location.

procedures: Roster: The Administrator, with the Residence Supervisors, prepares a written on-call roster at least two weeks ahead. It lists, for every day and hour, the on-call supervisor, a backup on-call person and an administrator contact, with full names and phone numbers. It is updated whenever a name or number changes.

Who may be on call: Only trained, paid agency employees who know the individuals and the residence's emergency plans may be on call. At least one person on the roster per shift has completed each required specialized training for the individuals served (see STF-04 and HW-01). Temporary agency staff are not placed on call unless STF-01 conditions are met.

Posting: Residence Supervisors post the current on-call roster and key numbers (on-call supervisor, backup, Administrator, 9-1-1 instructions, nurse (HW-02), poison control) in a staff-only location at each residence. Staff review them at each shift handoff.

Response expectation: The on-call person answers a call or text within [NUMBER] minutes and reaches the residence within [NUMBER] minutes when on-site help is needed. Both times are set to fit the individuals' supervision needs and the distance from the on-call person's location.
Life-threatening emergency: Staff on site call 9-1-1 first, as required by HW-04, and then call the on-call supervisor. Staff never wait for on-call approval before calling 9-1-1.

Other emergencies: For events that are not life-threatening (such as a staff injury, a vehicle problem, a utility outage, an environmental hazard or an individual's urgent need), the in-charge employee calls the on-call supervisor and follows ENV-02 or ENV-03 as applicable.

Staff call-outs: An employee who cannot work calls the Residence Supervisor or on-call supervisor at least [NUMBER] hours before the shift, or as soon as the employee knows. The supervisor records the call-out and begins the coverage process the same day.

Coverage order: To fill a short shift, the on-call supervisor first contacts [FIRST COVERAGE SOURCE, e.g., part-time or per-diem staff], then [SECOND SOURCE, e.g., staff from another residence], then agency-employed administrative staff who have completed all required training, and finally [APPROVED STAFFING AGENCY]. A residence is not left without required on-site staff when individuals are present.

Staff who leave: Staff do not leave the residence until relieved by the next scheduled person or by a replacement approved by the in-charge employee or on-call supervisor. Leaving an individual without required supervision is neglect and is handled under BEH-03.

In-charge designation: Whenever coverage changes, the supervisor updates the posted schedule and names the in-charge employee for the shift in writing. The in-charge employee reviews the Critical Information Log (REC-03) on arrival.

Individuals away from the residence: When no individuals are present (for example, all are at day programs or away), staff may be off site, but the on-call roster stays in effect and the on-call person is available to respond to emergencies as 2.8(c) requires. The supervisor records on the schedule that the residence is unoccupied.

Supervised apartments: The Administrator documents the location of the staff office or residence for each supervised apartment program, and the estimated response time from there. The Administrator reviews it when an individual's supervision needs change or when staffing locations change, and revises the arrangements if the response time no longer fits.

Emergency evacuation or relocation: If a residence must be evacuated or an individual cannot stay (ENV-02, ENV-03), the on-call supervisor sends additional staff so that every individual is accompanied during relocation and at the alternate site.

Communication after any activation: The on-call supervisor enters in the Critical Information Log (REC-03) a dated and signed record of the activation, the action taken, who responded and when. If the event is a reportable unusual incident, the supervisor follows BEH-04.

Testing the system: Once each quarter, the Administrator or a designee tests the on-call system by calling the on-call and backup numbers at an unannounced time and recording whether they answered and how fast they could have responded. Failures are corrected right away and reviewed through GOV-05.
Annual review: The Administrator reviews on-call experience, response times and coverage gaps each year, and updates this policy through GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures an adequate, trained on-call system, approves the roster, reviews quarterly tests and ensures budget and staff for emergency coverage.
Prepares and posts the two-week schedule and on-call roster, records call-outs, and arranges coverage.
Remains reachable, responds within the set times, arranges coverage and enters activations in the Critical Information Log.
Calls 9-1-1 for life-threatening emergencies, contacts the on-call supervisor for other emergencies, and keeps the residence supervised until relieved.
Know where the roster is posted, follow call-out and handoff rules, and do not leave their post unrelieved.

documentation: Two-week staff schedule and on-call roster (current copies posted at each residence; prior copies kept)
Call-out log and coverage record
Critical Information Log entries for emergency activations (REC-03)
Quarterly on-call test records
Supervised apartment staff office location and response-time documentation
Annual review notes

policies.title: Staff Qualifications, Hiring Standards and Credential Verification
policies.applies_to: The Governing Body, Administrator, Human Resources and every person who hires, supervises or contracts staff for [AGENCY NAME]; and every candidate, employee and contractor in the positions below.
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who works with individuals meets the minimum qualifications in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5, that required professional credentials are verified, and that each position on the table of organization has a job description submitted to DDD for review and approval.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(i)2: after the Office of Licensing approves the procedure manual, [AGENCY NAME] submits job descriptions to the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD), for each position on the table of organization, for review and approval. The agency hires only people who meet the following minimum qualifications (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5). The Executive Director (licensee) has a bachelor's degree, five years of progressive experience managing developmental disability services (at least two years supervisory at a senior or administrative level), and knowledge of program design, staff development and fiscal and qualitative standards. A Residence Supervisor has a high school diploma or equivalent and at least one year of experience in developmental disability services. A Direct Support Professional (DSP) is at least 18 years old, has a high school diploma or equivalent, can communicate with the individuals with whom they work, and can provide the direct assistance or training the individuals require. The agency verifies any professional credential required by law for employed or contracted professionals. Background clearance and screening requirements (STF-02, STF-05, STF-08) must also be satisfied before start dates.

definitions.definition: The chart of all agency positions and reporting lines included in the procedure manual (see GOV-03).
A written description of a position's duties, qualifications, reporting line and required training, submitted to DDD for approval for every position on the table of organization.
Developmental disability management experience with increasing responsibility, at least two years of which were supervisory at a senior or administrative level.
A license, certification or registration that the law requires for a given professional role (for example, nursing), which the agency must verify before the person works.
A person such as a nurse, clinician or consultant who provides services under a contract rather than as an employee.

procedures: Job descriptions: Before opening, the Administrator drafts a job description for each position on the table of organization (GOV-03), including Executive Director, Residence Supervisor and DSP, and any nurse, clinician or administrative positions the program uses. Each states minimum qualifications that are at least as strict as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5, reporting line, duties, required training and physical and communication requirements.

Submission to DDD: After the Office of Licensing approves the procedure manual, the Administrator submits the job descriptions for each position on the table of organization to DDD for review and approval, as 10:44A-1.4(i)2 requires. The date submitted, the DDD contact and the DDD response are recorded in the administrative file. The agency does not hire into a position before DDD approval of its job description unless DDD confirms in writing that it may.

Changes: When a position is added or a job description changes materially, the Administrator updates the table of organization, sends the new or revised job description to DDD for review, and updates the manual under GOV-04.

Posting and recruiting: Human Resources uses the DDD-approved job description for postings and states the minimum qualifications, the drug test and background clearance requirements, and any required communication skills (such as a language needed by an individual served).

Application review: Human Resources collects a signed application, resume or CV, three professional references for candidates in management positions, and proof of education (diploma, GED/equivalent or degree). Candidates who do not meet the minimum qualifications are not interviewed.

Age and education verification: For DSPs, Human Resources verifies age 18 or older with government-issued photo identification, and verifies a high school diploma or equivalent by copy of the diploma or transcript, or by a verification letter. A copy is kept in the personnel file.

Experience verification: For Residence Supervisors, Human Resources contacts prior employers to confirm at least one year of developmental disability experience. For the Executive Director, the Governing Body confirms the bachelor's degree, five years of progressive management experience and the two years of senior supervisory experience, using references and employer verification, and documents the finding.

Communication ability: The interviewer or Residence Supervisor confirms that the candidate can communicate with the individuals he or she will work with, using the individuals' communication needs identified in IR-09 and PCS-02 (for example, language or use of augmentative communication). The finding is recorded on the interview form.

Ability to provide direct assistance or training: The Residence Supervisor confirms during the interview and orientation (STF-03) that the candidate can perform the assistance or training the individuals need, including lifting, transfer, personal care and implementing plans. Reasonable accommodations are considered under applicable law. Required skill demonstrations are documented before independent work.

Professional credentials: Before any nurse, therapist, behavior specialist, dietitian or other professional starts work, whether employed or contracted, Human Resources verifies the license or certification directly with the issuing body, prints or saves the verification, and records the license number and expiration date.

Credential tracking: Human Resources keeps a credential tracking sheet and reviews it monthly. Anyone whose license lapses is removed from duties requiring that credential the day it lapses, until verified again.

Background and other clearances: No offer becomes final, and no employee has contact with an individual, until the criminal history, Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry checks (STF-02), health screening (STF-05) and drug test (STF-08) are completed and satisfactory. No agency head is paid or contracted before criminal history clearance under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69, and the owner or licensee is checked too if different from the agency head.
Contractors: Contracts with professionals require them to keep their credentials current, give the agency proof on request, and meet the clearance and screening requirements that apply.

Temporary agency staff: The agency contract requires the staffing agency to provide proof that each person placed meets these qualifications. Human Resources reviews that proof before the first shift. Temporary staff are not designated in-charge unless the conditions in STF-01 are met.
Record: Each personnel file includes the job description, signed acknowledgment, proof of qualifications, verification notes and credential copies (STF-06).

Annual check: The Administrator audits a sample of personnel files each year for qualification and credential evidence, and reports results to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05). The Governing Body checks the Administrator's qualifications at hire and at each annual review.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies the Executive Director's qualifications, approves the table of organization and job descriptions, and reviews hiring compliance annually.
Drafts job descriptions, submits them to DDD, makes final hiring decisions in line with this policy and ensures no unqualified person works with individuals.
Collects and verifies proof of qualifications, verifies credentials, and keeps the tracking sheet.
Confirms the candidate's communication ability and ability to provide assistance, and documents the finding.

documentation: Job descriptions for all positions on the table of organization, with DDD submission date and approval
Application, resume or CV, references and proof of education
Age and diploma verification
Experience verification notes
Interview form showing communication ability and ability to provide assistance or training
Professional credential verifications and tracking sheet
Contract provisions and credential proof for contractors and temporary staff
Annual personnel file audit results

policies.title: Individual Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All staff who create, use, store or release records of individuals receiving services at [AGENCY NAME] group homes, supervised apartments and supportive living locations, and the Administrator and Residence Supervisors responsible for them.
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate, protected and available record is kept for every individual, as New Jersey licensing rules require, and to set a clear plan for the retention period.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps an individual file for each individual receiving services (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(a)). The files of group home and supervised apartment residents are kept at the residence (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)). Each file contains at least the individual's full name, date of birth and sex; Social Security number and Medicaid and other insurance numbers; and the dates of admission, readmission, transfer or discharge. The Individual Habilitation Plan (IHP) and the monthly documentation of progress are kept in the record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(b)). Records are protected as protected health information under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Part 164) and under IR-04. The agency has not yet confirmed the length of time that records must be kept. Until the Administrator receives written confirmation from the Office of Licensing and the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD) of the required retention period, and has checked Medicaid record requirements, no individual record is destroyed. After confirmation, the longest applicable retention period applies.

definitions.definition: The paper or electronic file that holds the information required by licensing rules and agency policy for one individual receiving services.
Individually identifiable health information covered by HIPAA (45 CFR Part 164), including demographic, service and billing information.
The Individual Habilitation Plan developed under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3 and PCS-02.
The minimum length of time a record must be kept after discharge or last service before it may be destroyed.
A separate internal communication log kept apart from individuals' records (REC-03).

procedures: File creation: On the day of admission (PCS-01), the Residence Supervisor opens an individual file at the residence and records the individual's full name, date of birth, sex, Social Security number, Medicaid and insurance numbers, and date of admission. A second reviewer checks the entries within [NUMBER] business days.

Required contents: Each file also holds the IHP and monthly documentation of progress (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(b)), consents and releases (IR-08), health and medication records (HW-01, HW-02), guardianship papers and the other documents listed on the agency's record checklist [RECORD CONTENTS CHECKLIST]. The Administrator verifies the checklist against N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9 before opening and at each annual review.

Location and security: Group home and supervised apartment files are kept at the residence in a locked cabinet in a staff-only area. Electronic records require unique user logins and are backed up. Records are not left unattended in public areas or taken home.

Access: Only staff who need information to do their jobs, the individual, the guardian or authorized representative, and others permitted by law or by signed authorization may see a record (IR-04). The residence keeps an access and release log.

Who writes: Only trained staff make entries. Each entry is dated and signed (or electronically authenticated) with the full name and title of the writer. Entries are made at the time of the event or as soon as possible afterward.
Corrections: A staff person who makes an error draws a single line through it, writes the date and initials, and adds the correct information. Nothing is erased, covered or removed.

Monthly progress: The staff person responsible for each IHP objective writes a monthly progress summary. The Residence Supervisor reviews and signs it by the [DAY] of the following month, and files it in the record (PCS-02, PCS-03).
IHP filing: The current IHP, attendance sign-off and any addendum are filed within [NUMBER] days of the team meeting. Prior IHPs stay in the record.

Record review: The Residence Supervisor checks each record for completeness at least quarterly using the record checklist, and corrects missing items. The Nurse (HW-02) reviews the health portions. The Administrator reviews a sample of records each year for the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

Release and copies: Staff release records only under IR-04, with a signed authorization or other legal basis, and log what was released, to whom and when. Records are not sent by unsecured email or text.

Transfers and discharges: When an individual transfers or is discharged, the Residence Supervisor records the date, sends copies to the receiving provider only with authorization (PCS-05), and closes the record. The original record stays at the agency.

Retention (pending confirmation): Within 30 days of opening, the Administrator writes to the Office of Licensing and DDD to confirm the required retention period for individual records and checks Medicaid and HIPAA documentation requirements. The responses are kept in the administrative file. Until written confirmation is received, no individual record is destroyed.

Retention (after confirmation): Once the period is confirmed, the Administrator adopts the longest applicable period, enters it in this policy by revision through GOV-04, and records the earliest destruction date on each closed record.

Destruction: Closed records past the retention period are destroyed only with the Administrator's written approval, by shredding or secure electronic deletion. The agency keeps a destruction log with the individual's identifier, the date and the approver.

Billing and service documentation: Records supporting Medicaid claims, including service notes and EVV data, are retained and protected as GOV-06 requires. They are not destroyed until the Medicaid retention requirement has been confirmed.

Records during emergencies or relocation: The Residence Supervisor keeps an emergency copy of face sheets, medication lists and guardian contacts in the emergency go-bag (ENV-02), and protects it as PHI.
Breach response: Any lost, stolen or improperly disclosed record is reported to the Administrator the same day, and the Administrator follows IR-04.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures records meet licensing requirements, obtains written confirmation of the retention period, and approves destruction.
Opens and maintains the file at the residence, reviews monthly progress notes, performs quarterly record checks and controls access.
Reviews health and medication records for accuracy and completeness.
Make timely, dated and signed entries, correct errors properly and protect confidentiality.
Oversees HIPAA compliance, release logs and breach response.

documentation: Individual file for each person, kept at the residence
Record contents checklist and quarterly review results
Access and release log
Monthly progress documentation and current IHP
Written confirmation of retention period from the Office of Licensing and DDD
Record destruction log

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Governing Body, Administrator, Residence Supervisors, finance staff and any employee who prepares, signs or submits a report, application, response or notice to the NJ DHS Office of Licensing, the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD) or another State agency for [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To keep one calendar and one set of rules for what the agency must report or submit to the State, who is responsible, and how each submission is documented, so that no report is late, incomplete or inconsistent.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a State Reporting Calendar that lists every recurring and event-based report and submission to the Office of Licensing, DDD and other agencies. Unusual incidents are reported to DHS/DDD as BEH-04 sets out. The annual financial statement audit (required for agencies claiming $350,000 or more in combined Community Care Program and Supports Program reimbursement) and the Fiscal Sustainability Report (due 120 days after the end of the State fiscal year, about October 30) are handled under GOV-07 and GOV-06. Licensing application and license submissions are made to the Office of Licensing, and plans of correction for citations are submitted as GOV-08 sets out. The agency cooperates with annual and unannounced inspections by DHS, which may happen without limit or notice, and with the Office of Licensing's expanded enforcement posture, including provisional licenses and enforcement authority over developmental disability providers (P.L.2025, c.280). The agency has not confirmed every current reporting deadline. The Administrator therefore verifies each deadline against current DDD updates and the readopted N.J.A.C. 10:44A text each quarter and whenever DDD issues a notice, and the calendar is updated promptly.

definitions.definition: The agency's master list of required reports and submissions, with due dates, responsible person, source of the requirement, date last verified, and completion record.
An event that must be reported under BEH-04.
The annual report DDD requires from providers, due 120 days after the State fiscal year ends (about October 30).
The agency's written plan, submitted after a licensing inspection finds a violation, that explains how and when each violation will be corrected.
A license issued when an agency is only partly in compliance; two consecutive provisional licenses may result in non-renewal.

procedures: Calendar owner: The Administrator keeps the State Reporting Calendar and names a backup. The calendar lists each report, the authority, the due date or trigger, the preparer, the reviewer and the sign-off.

Core items on the calendar: (a) unusual incident reports to DHS/DDD (BEH-04); (b) annual audit and Fiscal Sustainability Report (GOV-07); (c) licensing application and license renewal submissions to the Office of Licensing; (d) plans of correction after inspections (GOV-08); (e) DDD provider approval, rate and billing submissions (GOV-06); (f) job descriptions to DDD (STF-10); (g) any notices DDD or the Office of Licensing adds.

Verification of deadlines: On the first business day of each quarter, and within five business days of any DDD update, Office of Licensing notice or announcement of the readopted N.J.A.C. 10:44A text, the Administrator reviews the calendar against the current text and updates it. The review date and source are recorded.

Unusual incidents: The in-charge employee notifies the supervisor and Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee submits the report to DHS/DDD within the time stated in BEH-04 and keeps a copy of the report and the submission confirmation. Follow-up and investigation reports (BEH-05) are submitted when required.

Annual audit: The finance lead determines each year whether the agency's combined CCP and Supports Program reimbursement reaches $350,000. If it does, the Administrator engages an independent auditor to perform an audit under generally accepted auditing standards, and the audit is submitted according to GOV-07.

Fiscal Sustainability Report: The finance lead begins the report at least 60 days before the due date, which is 120 days after the State fiscal year ends (about October 30). The Administrator and the Governing Body treasurer review it, and the Administrator signs it. The submission confirmation is filed.

Licensing applications and renewals: Application submissions follow N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4. Missing elements are supplied within 45 days of initial submission, because a late application may be denied and the applicant barred from reapplying for six months. The Administrator tracks the 60-calendar-day decision period and follows up if no written decision is received.

Application content: The Administrator keeps current copies of the items the Office of Licensing reviews, including table of organization, CVs, owner information, 24 months of service history with survey results and plans of correction, penalty and fine records, CPA examination of two fiscal years, and three professional references, so that updates can be submitted quickly.

Inspections: Annual and unannounced inspections are expected, and they increase beginning in 2026. The Residence Supervisor keeps staff files, schedules, credentials, background checks, physical plant documents and insurance documents ready at all times (GOV-08). Inspectors are admitted without delay, and the Administrator is told immediately.

Plans of correction: When an inspection finds a violation, the Administrator drafts a plan of correction within the time the Office of Licensing allows, assigns a person and a date for each correction, submits it, and tracks completion through GOV-08. Evidence of correction is kept.

Enforcement awareness: The Administrator tells the Governing Body of any provisional license, citation, penalty or enforcement notice within [NUMBER] business days. The Administrator also asks counsel to review the penalty provisions of P.L.2025, c.280, because the statute text has not been reviewed by the agency, and to advise on any changes to agency practice.
Housing: The Administrator clears any new housing location with DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development before acquisition, and records the clearance.

Review before sending: Every submission is checked by a second person for accuracy and consistency with agency records (for example, matching incident dates with the Critical Information Log in REC-03). A responsible officer signs.

Confirmation and filing: The preparer saves the confirmation, date sent, method and recipient. Copies of all State submissions are filed in the administrative file for the retention period the Administrator confirms under REC-01.

Missed or late reports: Any missed or late report is reported to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator contacts the State agency, submits the report as soon as possible, and reviews the cause through GOV-05.
Annual review: The Governing Body reviews the State Reporting Calendar, any late reports and inspection history each year, and updates this policy through GOV-04.

policies.title: Internal Communication and Critical Information Log
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME] who work in or oversee a community residence, including in-charge employees, direct support professionals, residence supervisors, nurses, on-call staff and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure critical information about individuals, the residence and staffing passes reliably between shifts and to management, and that action taken on it is documented, without placing it in any individual's record.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14 (a procedure, separate from individuals' records, for internal communication, to include the use of a separate log to document critical information and the action taken by the licensee to follow up) and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14.i (each log entry is dated and signed with the full name of the staff person making the entry). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a Critical Information Log at each residence. The log is separate from, and is never kept in, any individual's file (REC-01). Every entry is dated and signed with the full name of the staff member who makes it. Supervisors review the log each shift and document follow-up action. Staff keep entries factual and limit identifying details to what is needed to act on the information, and the log is protected as confidential under IR-04.

definitions.definition: Information that another staff member or manager must know to keep individuals safe or the residence running safely, such as a change in an individual's condition, a new risk or safety plan, an incident, an elopement concern, a medication change, a hazard, an environmental or equipment problem, a staffing gap or a directive from management.
A bound or secure electronic log, kept separately from individuals' records, in which critical information and the follow-up action taken are recorded.
What the agency did, and who did it and when, in response to a log entry.
The first and last name of the person making the entry, written out (not initials alone).

procedures: Log set-up: The Administrator provides each residence with a separate Critical Information Log, either a bound book with numbered pages or a secure electronic system with a locked, time-stamped audit trail. Columns or fields include date, time, entry, person making the entry (full signed name), follow-up action, person completing follow-up, date of follow-up and supervisor review signature.

Location: The log is kept in the staff-only area of the residence. It is never filed in an individual's record, and individual records do not contain copies of the log. If an entry must be shared with an individual's record (for example, a nurse assessment), a separate note is written in the record (REC-01).

What to enter: Staff enter critical information as soon as they learn of it, including changes in condition, incidents and near-misses, new or changed health or behavior supports, medication or diet changes, appointments or events that affect staffing, repairs or hazards, visitors with restrictions, communications from guardians, directives from the Administrator, nurse or supervisor, and any matter the in-charge employee decides another shift needs to know.
Emergencies first: In an emergency, staff first take action (call 9-1-1 under HW-04, protect individuals), notify the supervisor as BEH-04 requires, and enter the log after the individuals are safe.

How to write: Each entry is dated, timed and signed with the full name of the staff person making it (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14.i). Entries are factual, objective and brief. Staff use initials of individuals or an agreed identifier where possible, and avoid opinions and unnecessary medical or personal detail.

No altering: Entries are not erased, covered or removed. A staff person who makes an error draws one line through it, writes the date and signs. Late entries are marked as late and show both the date of the event and the date written.

Shift handoff: Before leaving, the outgoing in-charge employee tells the incoming in-charge employee all open items and entries from the shift. The incoming in-charge employee reads all entries since his or her last shift and signs or initials the log to show it was read.

Escalation: When an entry needs management action, the staff person notifies the Residence Supervisor, or the on-call supervisor outside business hours (STF-09), by phone right away and writes in the log who was notified and when.

Supervisor review: The Residence Supervisor, or the on-call supervisor on evenings and weekends, reviews all new entries at least once each shift or workday, signs the review column with a full name and date, and records follow-up action for each entry that requires it, or states that no action is needed.

Follow-up: For each entry that needs action, the supervisor assigns a person and a due date. The person who completes it writes the action taken, date and full name. Open items are carried forward until closed. The Residence Supervisor reports open items older than [NUMBER] days to the Administrator.

Administrator review: The Administrator reviews each residence's log at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly] to check for patterns, late follow-up or items that need agency-level action, and signs and dates the review. Patterns are given to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-05).

Incidents and reportable events: If an entry describes a reportable unusual incident, abuse, neglect, exploitation or a missing person, staff follow BEH-03, BEH-04 or BEH-06 immediately. The log entry does not replace incident reports, and incident reports are not replaced by the log.

Confidentiality: Staff do not share the log's contents with anyone outside the agency and do not photograph or copy it, except as the Administrator authorizes for an inspection or legal reason (IR-04, GOV-08). Electronic logs require individual logins and are backed up.

Training: New staff are trained on the log during orientation (STF-03) and are checked on a sample entry in their first week. The Residence Supervisor reviews entries for missing signatures or full names and coaches staff.

Retention and archiving: Full logs are kept for the retention period the Administrator confirms under REC-01. A closed bound log is labelled with its dates and stored securely at the agency. Closed logs are not destroyed before that period is confirmed.
Annual review: The Administrator audits a sample of entries each year for completeness, signature compliance and timely follow-up, and updates this procedure through GOV-04.
